1. Executive summary

The Budget comes amid global economic storms caused by the conflict in the Middle East and the illegal invasion of Ukraine, which have pushed up costs for families and businesses. In response, this Budget matches immediate action today with the big structural changes needed for the future.

The Budget meets the moment to steer Britain through this period of global pressures. It will provide breathing space for families and businesses, particularly with energy costs. At a time when households and businesses are under pressure, the Budget rejects broad-based tax rises, and is protecting most individuals and businesses from tax increases.

At the same time, this Budget commences the big changes needed to put the country on a better path. It will unlock good growth in every postcode by putting places in control of their economic future, and by backing a new wave of wealth creators. It will kickstart work on the big challenges facing the country to give people hope for the future, from bringing energy bills down for good, to building more social housing, to boosting the UK’s national security. This will build Britain’s resilience to make the country more secure and better off.

Fiscal discipline in this Budget will provide the bedrock for the economy to continue to grow and to deliver the vision that the Prime Minister and Chancellor will set out at the 10 Year Plan and the next spending review.

It is a Budget that will deliver breathing space today, and fresh hope for the future.

1.1 The economy and the public finances

Since the start of the conflict in the Middle East, all G7 countries have seen their borrowing costs rise to, or near to, highs not seen for decades. This means the UK is spending more on servicing its debt, with the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecasting the UK will pay an average of £14 billion per year in extra government debt interest compared to the Spring.

The UK economy is showing signs of resilience. Since the start of the Parliament, whole economy investment is up by 6.9%, business investment is up by 7.5%, and productivity growth exceeded 2% last year. The UK recorded the joint-fastest GDP growth in the G7 in the first half of this year, and the OBR has upgraded its growth forecast for 2026 to 1.2%. More recent GDP data has continued to exceed expectations, with growth of 0.7% in the three months to August alone.

1.2 Breathing space for Britain

Despite this resilience, the conflict in the Middle East has hit the UK’s growth outlook. Many families continue to feel their finances being squeezed. The cost of doing business – from energy bills to regulation to planning constraints – continues to weigh on investment and growth.

Fiscal discipline underwrites every promise this government makes. Reducing borrowing increases the UK’s ability to absorb global shocks, helps bear down on inflation, and creates breathing space for households and businesses. Fiscal discipline underpins economic stability, national security and sustainable growth. The government has therefore ensured that all policy at this Budget is fully funded over the forecast.

At a time when people, businesses, and the economy are under pressure and need breathing space, the Budget rejects broad-based tax rises. Instead, the government has chosen to use some of the headroom established last year to absorb the impact of higher debt-interest costs from the conflict in the Middle East.

The government continues to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer:

  • The stability rule is met by £15 billion in 2029-30, before rising to £22 billion in 2030‑31. Higher debt interest costs from the conflict more than account for the reduction of headroom in 2029-30 since Spring. This is what a buffer is for – to be used when needed before being rebuilt as soon as conditions allow.
  • The investment rule is met by £24 billion in 2029‑30, putting debt on a stable trajectory while continuing to deliver over £120 billion of additional investment this Parliament compared with the previous government’s plans.

The OBR’s forecast shows the government’s plans reduce borrowing over the forecast and put debt on a downward trajectory: borrowing falls to 1.8% of GDP by 2031‑32 and debt is lower at the end of the forecast (2031‑32) than it is now (2026‑27).

The IMF has forecast that the UK’s fiscal plans stand out from those of its peers. The UK has delivered the biggest reduction in borrowing in the G20 this year, and is on track to have the lowest level of borrowing in the G7 from 2029.

Energy bills

This Budget represents a shift in the government’s approach to energy. The conflict in the Middle East has put bills up for households and businesses. This Budget provides immediate relief, while offering longer-term reform to make sure the energy system works for households and businesses.

The government has made substantial progress on clean power. The focus now is to unleash cheap electricity, cutting bills to reindustrialise the country. The government must be disciplined in managing every aspect of energy costs, while building the assets needed to provide energy security to protect British businesses and households from volatile international gas prices, and to build the grid, which has not kept pace with demand. This Budget is the start of a new energy pathway on which the 10 Year Plan will build. This government will prioritise cheaper energy – to help British businesses to compete, and to provide breathing space for households. Cheaper electricity will boost electrification, increasing the UK’s energy security and helping to decarbonise the whole economy. This Budget will:

  • Support households with the cost of energy – extending the VAT cut to electricity to July 2027, which is expected to take around £50 off the annual Ofgem price cap in April 2027, and launching a £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment, which will provide a £100 payment directly into bank accounts from January 2027 for households in England in council tax bands A-D, supporting up to 20 million households. Devolved governments will receive their share of this funding via the Barnett formula. To help fund this, the government is temporarily increasing the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.
  • Extend the 5p fuel duty cut and freeze, while maintaining the Heavy Goods Vehicle (HGV) road tax holiday, to 1 July 2027 — keeping fuel duty as low as at any point in over 16 years and substantially lower in real terms, while the red diesel rate remains at its lowest level for over 20 years.

Alongside this immediate support, this Budget kickstarts the long-term action required to get energy costs down for good:

  • Controlling energy costs – no new policy costs will be put on bills until a comprehensive Cost Control Framework is in place at the spending review in 2027, which will set budgets for components of energy costs, including policy costs.
  • Prioritising a cheaper energy mix and procuring new generation only where it lowers bills, benefits the system, and can be accommodated by the grid.
  • Progressing next steps in breaking the grip of gas on bills with a consultation published alongside this Budget on wholesale Contracts for Difference, fixing the price paid to some renewable projects to protect British homes and businesses from volatile gas prices.

From 2027 onward, the government will:

  • Deliver the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, meaning 10,000 energy intensive manufacturing firms will get a 20-25% electricity discount, starting in April 2027, including a back payment for 2026-27.
  • Abolish gas standing charges, coupled with targeted mitigations to ensure this is delivered fairly.
  • Introduce a new Energy Debt Circuit Breaker to tackle energy debt, saving all billpayers around £30 by 2030.
  • Reform electricity standing charges – with further details to be announced next year.
  • Scrap the planned new tax on gas bills (the Gas Shipper Obligation), so that government rather than consumers fund the costs of hydrogen projects.

Targeted support for households

The Budget also gives households breathing space by:

  • Temporarily reducing tariffs on over 100 food and drink products.
  • Delivering the new Pension Tax Allowance – meeting the government’s commitment that pensioners with incomes at or under the value of the full new State Pension will not be brought into paying tax because of State Pension uprating in this Parliament.
  • Supporting working people by increasing the National Living Wage and the National Minimum Wage rates by 3.9%, expanding parental pay, (including to self-employed fathers and partners for the first time), and permanently increasing the tax-free mileage rates for those who rely on their own vehicle for work.

Targeted support for businesses

Small businesses create jobs and keep communities thriving. In addition to helping businesses with the cost of energy, the Budget will address wider costs on businesses by:

  • Delivering the government’s commitments on business rates by funding an extra 20% reduction for pubs, music venues and social clubs, and by increasing the Small Business Rate Relief threshold so that a further 70,000 retail, hospitality and leisure (RHL) businesses pay no business rates at all. The government is paying for this by ensuring businesses with significant sales online pay the VAT they owe, by requiring online marketplaces to collect it on their behalf.
  • For all other retail, hospitality, and leisure properties, rates will be frozen for two years so that no property in those sectors faces an above inflation increase. Taken together, the decisions in this Budget mean that, from April, RHL businesses in England will see their business rates either frozen in real-terms, reduced, or cut to zero.
  • Making Small Producer Relief in the Alcohol Duty system more generous by providing £10 million per year of support to over 2,000 small alcohol producers across the UK.

Public spending

The government has stabilised public services after years of underinvestment and is maintaining the highest sustained level of public spending in four decades. Departmental day-to-day spending will be £40 billion higher each year by 2028‑29 than under the previous government’s plans. Capital investment will be £120 billion more over the Parliament than under the previous government’s plans. This has enabled the government to invest in communities: building new social and affordable homes, improving infrastructure, lifting children out of poverty, strengthening the NHS, and in securing a stronger and more resilient UK through investment in defence.

The government is taking a fundamentally different approach to public services, in line with the ‘Rewiring the State’ Cabinet statement published in July. Reforms will improve outcomes and increase efficiency at every level of government by:

  • Devolving decision-making by transferring resources to local leaders across England, supporting an integrated approach that gives places more power to target spending towards the biggest issues in their communities, and which more coherently joins up services, improving outcomes and efficiency.
  • Streamlining central government, including through the transformation of the Civil Service which will deliver significant reductions in its size and cost.
  • Harnessing transformative technologies like AI, where the Chancellor and Health Secretary have commissioned an independent review into NHS productivity and the opportunities presented by AI and technology to transform services for patients, ahead of the next spending review.

These reforms will reshape not only how government operates, but how public services are designed and delivered, shifting towards a more devolved, preventative and productive state. The next spending review will introduce a new category of ringfenced spending, preventative DEL, to deliver the government’s long-term approach.

The Budget fully funds the Defence Investment Plan through proactive management of capital pressures and reprioritisation of capital budgets. The 10 Year Plan will set out the long-term vision and priorities for the country. As the government continues to target investment into the country’s top priorities, it is not necessarily the case that all departments will see real-terms increases at the next spending review; putting the right resources into priorities is what any responsible government does.

The work to set a long-term vision for the country by transforming the state, reprioritising spending, and reforming welfare has already begun, with further details to be set out in the 10 year plan. The next spending review will act as a further enabler of this radical change and will take place in 2027.

Revenue raising

At a time when households and businesses are under pressure and need breathing space, the Budget rejects broad-based tax rises. It achieves this while ensuring that all policy at the Budget is fully funded over the forecast and raises the revenue to fund commitments on breathing space and energy in a fair, targeted and proportionate way. In doing so, it has protected most individuals and businesses from tax increases, giving them further space to breathe. The government is keeping to its commitments on tax, with no increase to the headline rates of income tax, National Insurance contributions, or VAT. The government is also maintaining the commitments in the 2024 Corporate Tax Roadmap.

The government is modernising the tax system, closing loopholes and ensuring that people and businesses pay the tax they owe. That includes modernising the taxation of company distributions, while protecting genuine commercial transactions including family successions; acting against non-compliance by online sellers, with the revenue reinvested in the high street through business rates support; ending the inconsistency in taxation between larger minicab operators; and ensuring the tax system does not allow overseas businesses to undercut UK firms.

The Budget also makes a small number of targeted choices to raise revenue fairly and help fund support for households and businesses. Banks will make a temporary additional contribution to help fund immediate household support. The government will increase tax on income from property and savings in a fair and proportionate way, while supporting tax-free saving by reversing the planned cut to the cash Individual Savings Accounts (ISA) allowance. The rate of Machine Games Duty for higher risk machines will increase to help pay for the real-terms freeze in business rates for RHL properties. Reformed capital allowances will strengthen the upfront incentive to invest while also raising revenue.

Good growth in every postcode

The government will transform the economy to deliver good growth in every postcode. The government will deliver greater public control, deliver more devolution and local leadership, back British businesses and set out a balanced approach to AI, addressing risks and pursuing opportunities. In this Budget and beyond, the government will deliver more investment, drive more innovation and help to create more jobs across every region and nation, through the following big shifts:

  • Public control of the essentials – the state will provide greater strategic direction, certainty and accountability to secure the foundations for growth, including in energy, transport, water, and housing – creating the conditions for businesses to invest and grow. It will provide additional funding for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to crowd in investment. The government will cut business costs and support innovation, saving businesses almost £800 million per year through further cuts to the administrative burdens of regulation, extending suspensions on tariffs, and introducing new cross-economy powers so firms can safely test new technologies faster. The government is also establishing a Better Regulation Executive which will set the direction for and drive implementation of the government’s vision for a streamlined and proportionate regulatory system.
  • Growth in more places – this Budget sets out a roadmap to fiscal devolution, the biggest transfer of power and resources out of Whitehall in a generation, empowering local leaders to partner with businesses and universities to drive growth and reindustrialisation. The government will extend devolution across the country and give mayors, strategic authorities and local authorities greater powers. Mayors will receive a share of income tax and business rates, while local authorities will retain more of their business rates. Alongside these powers, the government will establish Good Growth Funds to support mayors and local leaders across England to ensure there is investment and good growth everywhere. Devolved governments will receive equivalent funding via the Barnett formula.
  • Backing British Business – this Budget will support the next wave of British start-ups and scale-ups, including through a world-leading tax offer for founders and their companies. The Budget will use strategic public procurement and promotion to back British firms and develop a skilled domestic workforce. The government will also ensure talent can move to where it is needed most to help businesses thrive and provide opportunity for people to pursue their careers.
  • Building the UK’s independent AI capability with British values – AI is the greatest innovation of our time, yet carries significant risks which the government must address. At this Budget, the government will strengthen AI security and resilience, including through an additional £120 million for the AI Security Institute, and £165 million for a new National AI Biosecurity Initiative. It will invest £154 million to strengthen cyber defences and £40 million to establish a National Agentic Security Unit to investigate and respond to rogue agentic incidents. It will invest an additional £140 million in the Sovereign AI Unit to back promising UK AI companies to scale and succeed here. It will also set out a new Data Centre Covenant, establishing the tests that strategic data centres are expected to meet, including the contribution they make to communities and the UK’s economic interests, matched by government action to support the capacity needed for technological sovereignty.

Fresh hope for the future

The Budget starts the big changes needed to put the country on a better path – from housing to national security – building Britain’s resilience to make the next generation better off.

Fresh hope on housing

Having a place to call home is foundational. It provides safety, stability and security. At this Budget, the government is prioritising housing investment in all its forms, supporting families across the country to thrive. The government will:

  • Build more social and affordable homes by providing an additional £1.5 billion to deliver around 10,000 homes in England. This funding will be prioritised for Social Rent, especially council homes, taking total investment in the Social and Affordable Homes Programme to more than £40 billion over 10 years.
  • Deliver the Prime Minister’s promise to end rough sleeping by providing further funding to ensure that people have a route off the streets, not just this year, but every year.
  • Help more people find and keep a home by helping 70,000 households to get onto the housing ladder, confirming £4.7 billion for the new Your First Home equity-loan scheme for first-time-buyers and setting out its final details.

Over the next 10 years, the government will start to deliver the largest council housebuilding programme since the post-war era, and continue to drive up private sector housebuilding, helping more people benefit from a safe and secure home. Next steps will be set out in the 10 Year Plan, which will detail reforms to ensure that councils have the capacity to start building at scale again, significantly reduce the complexity and cost of the development process, and release public land for affordable housing.

Fresh hope for every generation

The government is determined to deliver a system that invests in young people’s success, rather than paying for failure. And the government will ensure elderly people can get the care they need. The government will:

  • Support young people into work: The government refuses to write off the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training. This Budget strengthens pathways into work by delivering the Jobs Guarantee for eligible 18 to 24-year-olds on Universal Credit and investing £100 million in local apprenticeship services. Early next year, the government will publish a White Paper in response to the publication of Alan Milburn’s final report and the conclusion of the Timms Review.
  • Adjust the Triple Lock from the next Parliament to help fund a new settlement for older people: a state pension that rises every year, personal care free at the point of use and a high-quality National Care Service in England to give peace of mind in later life. The Prime Minister has agreed with Baroness Casey that her Independent Commission on Adult Social Care will now report in 2027.

A safer Britain

Safeguarding our national security is the first duty of any government. This government will meet this commitment to the people of Britain and its allies in the face of a new era of threat. The government’s fully funded Defence Investment Plan will deliver stronger front-line military capability, supporting jobs, businesses and economic growth across the UK.

At the spending review next year, the government will also set out the details of how it will meet its NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030. This is necessary for the security of the UK. It also presents an opportunity to do things differently, working more closely with the private sector to build defence industry capacity alongside delivering new and innovative defence capability. The Budget will launch a new Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce to maximise the contribution of private and international finance to UK defence, and confirms a new commitment for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use and other sectors that support our national security, sovereign capability and resilience.

The government is making available over £10 billion of additional financial support to Ukraine. This is alongside its enduring commitment to £3 billion a year in military support until 2030-31 or for as long as needed, recognising that Ukraine’s security is vital to global security.

Built on the rock of fiscal discipline, this Budget provides breathing space to families and businesses in the here and now, drives good growth in every postcode and offers fresh hope for the future.

2. Economic and fiscal outlook

The UK’s economy and public finances have proven resilient despite major external shocks, with the joint fastest growth in the G7 so far this year.[footnote 1] GDP per person, real household disposable income (RHDI) per person and business investment have all grown by more in the first two years of this Parliament than they did in the five years of the last one.[footnote 2] Government borrowing is falling, by more than £15 billion in 2025‑26 compared with the year before.[footnote 3]

The conflict in the Middle East is a significant shock, affecting all economies. Ending the conflict, fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz and repairing the damage to energy infrastructure is the single biggest priority to improve the global outlook, including for the UK. However, the path of the conflict – and the resulting economic and fiscal impacts – remains highly uncertain.

The UK’s workers and firms have been resilient this year, but the government will not be complacent given the headwinds from the conflict in the Middle East. At this Budget, the government is providing households and businesses with breathing space to help them manage higher energy and other commodity prices, while continuing to deliver on its commitment to fiscal discipline. The government is meeting the fiscal rules and bringing down borrowing across the forecast, helping to bear down on inflation, mortgage rates and the cost of business.

2.1 Economic and fiscal context

The UK had the joint-fastest growth in the G7 across the first half of 2026.[footnote 4] Real GDP grew by 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2, and cumulative growth across the first two quarters is 0.5 percentage points higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) expected in its March forecast.[footnote 5],[footnote 6] Stronger-than-expected outturns have led a range of forecasters, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), to upgrade expectations for 2026 compared with earlier this year.[footnote 7] In its October World Economic Outlook (WEO), the IMF forecast the UK to grow by 1.3% in 2026, 0.5 percentage points higher than its expectations in April 2026.[footnote 8] More recently, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) estimates that GDP in the three months to August 2026, which was released after the OBR closed the pre-measures forecast to new data, rose by 0.7%, continuing to exceed market expectations.[footnote 9],[footnote 10]

Source: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, HM Treasury calculations.

Living standards have grown since the start of this Parliament, with GDP per person growing by 2.0% and RHDI per person rising by 1.8%.[footnote 11] Household income has been supported by growth in real wages, which have now risen consistently for three years and grown more in the first two years of this Parliament than they did over the first decade of the previous government.[footnote 12]

GDP growth in 2026 has been broad-based across all sectors of the economy (production, construction and services).[footnote 13] Despite headwinds from the conflict in the Middle East, demand has remained robust, with household consumption rising by 1.0% in the first half of the year.[footnote 14] Retail sales have grown, rising by 0.7% in Q3 2026.[footnote 15] External demand has held up, supporting UK growth, as key trading partners have remained relatively resilient, with G7 economies (excluding the UK) growing by an average of 0.4% in Q2 2026.[footnote 16] This has helped support demand for UK exports, which were 4.2% higher in Q2 2026 than the same period last year.[footnote 17]

Whole economy investment has risen by 2.7% so far this year, supported by strong business investment, which grew by 4.8% in the first half of this year.[footnote 18] In this Parliament, whole economy and business investment have both already increased by more than they did over the entirety of the previous one, rising by 6.9% and 7.5% respectively, compared with 6.4% and 4.8% in the previous Parliament.[footnote 19] Recent strong growth has helped to push whole economy investment to its highest share of GDP since 1990 and business investment to its highest share in almost a decade.[footnote 20] Strong growth in whole economy investment reflects the government’s commitment to both protecting capital investment in infrastructure and public services, and providing the stability and certainty that allows firms to invest.

There is some evidence that AI-related investment is contributing to the strength in business investment and GDP growth. Over the first half of 2026, other buildings and structures, intellectual property products and information and communications technology (ICT) equipment and other machinery and equipment have contributed over three-quarters of the headline business investment growth of 4.8%.[footnote 21] These asset classes encompass many of the physical and intangible capital inputs needed to develop and deploy AI, including software, research and development and computing equipment. Investment activity has been particularly robust in sectors most closely associated with its adoption, for example information and communication, which has contributed over a fifth of UK GDP growth so far this year.[footnote 22]

Chart 1.2: Contributions to headline business investment growth (H1 2026)

Source: Office for National Statistics, HM Treasury calculations.

UK productivity growth strengthened over the past two years, rising for six consecutive quarters, the longest sustained run of quarterly growth in almost a decade. Over the past two years, productivity has grown at an annualised rate of 1.3%, compared with an average rate of 0.5% per year between 2015 and 2024.[footnote 23]

The labour market has remained subdued in 2026, with little change in headline indicators. Unemployment has fallen across the year to 4.7% while the number of employees has fallen slightly.[footnote 24],[footnote 25] Hiring is subdued, but employment remains close to record highs: there are only two peacetime years in the last 150 years when the employment rate was higher than it is today.[footnote 26],[footnote 27] At 75.3%, today’s employment rate is above the G7 average.[footnote 28],[footnote 29] The strength in employment masks persistent challenges for some groups, particularly young people, with almost one million young people not in employment, education or training, which rose by over 100,000 in the last five years of the previous government.[footnote 30]

Box 1.A: Measuring the UK’s productivity performance

Productivity growth (output per hour worked) is the long-run driver of economic growth, higher wages, and living standards. Headline measures of productivity growth are calculated as output divided by total hours worked. The source for hours worked in the economy is the Labour Force Survey (LFS). In recent years, falling response rates have significantly affected the quality of the LFS, making it more difficult to estimate reliably the number of workers and the hours they work. The LFS is also weighted to population projections, which could not anticipate recent changes to net migration levels.

In response to these challenges, researchers began to use alternative sources of employment information from surveys such as HM Revenue & Customs payrolled employees (known as RTI, real time information) and workforce jobs (WFJ). Since 2024, the ONS has published an alternative approach to productivity measurement using RTI data and this year recommended users focus on the RTI productivity measure.[footnote 31]

The RTI-based measure suggests that productivity growth was weak across 2022 and 2023, before rebounding strongly since late 2024.[footnote 32] RTI productivity has grown at an annualised rate of 1.3% since Q2 2024, and grew by 2.2% in 2025, compared with an average growth rate of 0.5% between 2015 and 2024.[footnote 33] These rates of productivity growth are above the OBR’s medium-term productivity forecast for annual trend productivity growth of 1.0%, which is based on the LFS measure.[footnote 34]

In September, the ONS published improved estimates of productivity growth from 1997 to 2024, updating the measurement of employment and average hours worked used in productivity calculations, bringing their methodology more closely in line with international best practice.[footnote 35] This new approach indicates that the long-run decline in average hours continued after 2010, rather than stabilising as indicated by existing LFS-based measures. The revised trajectory for average hours implies a stronger trajectory for productivity growth: average annual productivity growth between 2007 and 2024 is estimated to be 0.9%, revised up from 0.5%. The component approach suggests that productivity growth still slowed following the Global Financial Crisis, from 2.0% in 1997‑2007 to 0.9% in 2007‑2024, but this is less than previously thought and brings the UK more closely into line with international peers, although pre-existing productivity gaps remain. The new approach suggests a more positive long-run outlook for UK productivity growth.

Resilience

Decisions made since the start of this Parliament have increased the resilience of the UK economy. The government’s fiscal strategy is delivering lower borrowing and helps the Bank of England to maintain price stability, while supporting a step change in public investment of £120 billion this Parliament compared with previous plans. Last year, the government reduced the deficit to the lowest level for six years, to 4.4% of GDP. [footnote 36]

Energy prices increased sharply following the start of the conflict in the Middle East, pushing up inflation and weighing on the global economic outlook. Following the disruption to transits through the Strait of Hormuz in February, wholesale monthly average Brent crude oil prices rose by around 60% by October, while wholesale monthly average UK natural gas prices increased by nearly 200%.[footnote 37] The government wants to see an end to the conflict, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and restoration of the supply of energy. This would significantly improve the domestic and global outlook.

Before the onset of the conflict, inflation had been falling and was forecast to return to target this year. Inflation continued to fall until June, when it reached 2.6%, with households still protected by the Ofgem energy price cap, which was largely set before the outbreak of the conflict. Inflation has since risen to 3.5% in September, with the majority of the rise driven by motor fuel inflation caused by the conflict.[footnote 38] The OBR expects inflation to peak at 3.8% in Q1 next year, before falling again, with the outlook sensitive to wholesale oil and gas prices. The UK is not alone in seeing inflation rise as a result of these global shocks, with the IMF raising the inflation forecasts for 2026 on average across G7 countries by 0.8 percentage points in its October 2026 WEO compared with its October 2025 assessment.[footnote 39]

Although inflation is rising, the economic effect on the UK is expected to be less acute than in 2022. Growth in clean power and changes to the energy market have reduced the UK’s exposure to global energy market volatility and the international gas price, while different domestic economic conditions from 2022, underpinned by monetary and fiscal policy, mean the domestic inflationary risk of the external price shock is lower.

Box 1.B: Energy prices and inflation

Higher global energy prices are affecting countries around the world. Liquid and motor fuel prices rose quickly following the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Petrol and diesel prices have risen by similar amounts across Europe: petrol is up 19% in Germany and 30% in France between February and October 2026, compared with 33% in the UK; diesel has risen by 31% in Germany and 42% in France, compared with 41% in the UK over the same period.[footnote 40] How such rises affect headline inflation depends on the composition of the consumer price basket in each country. At 59 parts per thousand, energy has a smaller weight in the UK CPI basket compared with the euro area where it is around 91 parts per thousand. Therefore, a similar change in energy prices will have a smaller direct effect on headline inflation in the UK. The overall energy intensity of the UK economy has fallen from 70% in 2020 to 58% in 2025, reflecting improvements in energy efficiency and changes in the composition of economic activity.[footnote 41]

Changes in the energy market since 2022 have reduced and delayed the pass-through of global energy price shocks into UK inflation. Structural changes have weakened the link between gas and electricity prices, with gas setting the wholesale electricity price around 60% of the time in 2025, down from around 90% in the early 2020s.[footnote 42] These changes include the growth in renewable generation, including a higher share of the electricity market being covered by Contracts for Differences.[footnote 43] Reflecting this, the current shock has fed through relatively more to household gas prices, with Ofgem price cap unit rates rising 8.7% from July to this October, compared with 0.8% for electricity. Removing VAT from electricity bills contributed to the smaller rise in electricity prices.[footnote 44] Pass-through to customers has been delayed by greater fixing and hedging behaviour. For businesses, in March 2026, 42% had at least half of their electricity prices fixed or hedged, and 45% had at least half of their gas prices fixed or hedged.[footnote 45]

The risk of large second-round effects – with higher headline inflation feeding into higher wages – and indirect effects pushing up non-energy prices is lower than in 2022 due to current economic conditions. The 2022 shock coincided with the pandemic recovery and a period when inflation was already rising, compounding its effects. In contrast, there is currently greater spare capacity in the economy. At a comparable point seven months after the respective shocks, core inflation was 2.8% in September 2026, compared with 6.5% in September 2022.[footnote 46]

Higher inflation has led to higher interest rate expectations, with households, firms and governments facing tighter financial conditions. Since the start of the conflict in the Middle East, UK gilt yields have increased broadly in line with the G7 average; all G7 countries have seen their borrowing costs rise to, or near, highs not seen for decades.[footnote 47]

There continues to be significant uncertainty around the conflict in the Middle East and its effect on the economic and fiscal outlook. There have been periods of high volatility in wholesale energy markets since the start of the conflict. The OBR estimates that real GDP growth could be 0.5 percentage points higher in 2027 and borrowing could be £12 billion lower in 2027‑28 if energy prices follow a lower path than assumed in its central forecast.

2.2 Economic and fiscal strategy

Growth

The government’s economic objective is to deliver good growth and sustained improvements in living standards in every part of the UK. Greater investment, innovation and skills enable workers and businesses to become more productive, while higher employment allows more people to contribute to and benefit from growth. The government is therefore mobilising public, private and international investment, ensuring the essential infrastructure and services that underpin growth are affordable and reliable, devolving power to enable genuine local economic leadership, and backing businesses that want to grow. Together, these support rising wages, household incomes and profits while enabling high-quality public services. Good growth is growth that is resilient, broad-based and reflected in secure and productive work, affordable essentials, and greater opportunity across the country.

Stability

Growth in every postcode requires families and businesses to feel confident making long-term plans. For that, they need a stable economic environment: price stability, sustainable public finances, and strong economic and financial institutions reduce uncertainty and incentivise investment. Fiscal discipline and the stability it creates therefore provide the foundations for the investment needed to deliver good growth.

Fiscal rules

The recent rise in global borrowing costs reinforces the government’s strategy to reduce borrowing, which helps to bear down on inflation and give families more breathing space. The fiscal rules remain unchanged and mean the government will deliver this strategy while enabling the public investment needed to drive long‑term economic growth:

  • The stability rule means that the current budget must be in balance or in surplus by the third year of the forecast, meaning that day-to-day spending is met with revenues, so that the government only borrows to invest.
  • The investment rule is a target to ensure debt, defined as public sector net financial liabilities (PSNFL) or net financial debt, is falling as a share of the economy by the third year of the forecast.

The OBR has confirmed that the government is meeting the stability and investment rules. There is a buffer of £15 billion against the stability rule and £24 billion against the investment rule. Net financial debt stabilises from 2028‑29, and is lower at the end of the forecast (2031‑32) than at the start (2026‑27).

The conflict in the Middle East has pushed up borrowing relative to the OBR’s March forecast. The OBR forecasts an average of £14 billion per year in extra government debt interest, compared with the March forecast. Higher debt interest costs more than account for the change in borrowing and the reduction of headroom against the stability rule, in 2029‑30. The government has chosen to use some of the headroom to absorb the impact of the conflict in the Middle East while the outlook is uncertain. This approach is in line with the purpose of holding headroom, which is to give the government the flexibility to weather shocks, reducing the need to make immediate changes in tax and spending plans when there are changes in the global and UK economy.

Reducing borrowing

Last year (2025‑26), ONS data shows that borrowing fell by 0.7% of GDP to its lowest level in six years.[footnote 51] According to the IMF, the UK has the fastest fiscal consolidation in the G20 this year (2026).[footnote 52] The government is continuing to reduce borrowing including by ensuring that, overall, policies at this Budget do not add to borrowing over the forecast.

To enable this path of borrowing, the government has been responsible in its cost-of-living support for households and businesses, in response to pressures from the conflict in the Middle East. In line with IMF steers, the government has ensured that any intervention has been timely, targeted and temporary.

Lower borrowing helps the Bank of England to reduce inflation, reducing mortgage costs for households and borrowing costs for businesses. The independent Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Bank of England is responsible for bringing inflation to target, and the MPC has the government’s full support in returning inflation to target sustainably. The government has published the remit for the MPC alongside the Budget to reaffirm that the Bank of England’s price stability objective is defined as 2% CPI inflation, which applies at all times.

Box 1.C: Fiscal stance and consolidation

The government is consolidating the public finances. Public sector net borrowing (PSNB) fell by 0.7 percentage points last year to 4.4% of GDP and continues to fall over the forecast to 1.8% in 2031‑32.[footnote 53]

Two-thirds of the reduction in PSNB will be delivered between 2024‑25 and 2028‑29, underpinned by detailed tax and departmental spending plans.[footnote 54] This demonstrates the government’s commitment to get borrowing down. Reducing borrowing is the way to reduce debt interest costs which more than account for the increase in PSNB, on average, since the OBR’s March forecast.

The government has already made progress towards its fiscal mandate to balance the current budget (day-to-day spending balanced against revenues). Last year the current budget deficit fell by 1 percentage point from 2.5% to 1.5% of GDP, the lowest current budget deficit outturn in six years.[footnote 55] The current budget is forecast to continue to improve. By 2028‑29, the government will have done 90% of the work to balance the current budget, with concrete plans that are underpinned by set departmental budgets and taxes.[footnote 56]

The primary deficit measures how much the government is borrowing in a way that affects the economy, by focusing on what the government controls (taxation, day-to-day spending, and investment) and excluding debt interest. Last financial year (2025‑26), the primary deficit fell by 0.8% of GDP, and next year (2027‑28) it is forecast to fall to its lowest level in 25 years.[footnote 57] The primary balance moves into surplus by 2028‑29 – which would be the first primary surplus since 2001-02 – and by 2031‑32, the OBR forecasts a 1.7% of GDP primary surplus.[footnote 58]

The cyclically adjusted primary deficit (CAPD) – which strips out changes to tax and spending related to the economic cycle – is already close to being eliminated. The OBR forecasts a surplus next year, for the first time since 2001‑02.[footnote 59]

Long-term fiscal sustainability

The government is committed to public finances that are sustainable for the long term. Sustainable public finances support economic growth, provide space for the government to protect households and businesses from future shocks, support private investment, reduce pressure on borrowing costs, and prevent unduly burdening future generations with debt.

By announcing an adjusted Triple Lock, the government is acting now to put the State Pension on a sustainable footing, while delivering a new settlement for older people: one that ensures pensioners continue to see a meaningful rise in their state pension each and every year; while building a National Care Service which will provide older people in England with personal care, free at the point of use.

Adjusting the Triple Lock will generate significant savings and materially improve the certainty of the State Pension spending trajectory. It removes the ‘ratchet’ effect, whereby the State Pension rises ever higher relative to earnings. Following the introduction of the adjusted Triple Lock, the State Pension will track earnings over time. Adjusting the Triple Lock is estimated to reduce State Pension spending by £15 billion a year by the late 2030s, and by £50 billion a year by the late 2040s.[footnote 61]

The adjusted Triple Lock builds on previous decisions to secure fiscal sustainability for the UK. This includes strengthening the tax base by introducing Electric Vehicle Excise Duty (eVED) to respond to the long-term decline in fuel duty receipts and tackling fast-growing tax reliefs, including by capping the amount of pension contributions that can be salary sacrificed. The government has also introduced a series of major, innovative reforms to balance sheet management including the Balance Sheet Framework, enacted at this Budget through the Strategic Asset Review (Chapter 2), and the Guidance on Managing Government’s Implicit Liabilities, with a second round of funding allocated for projects which reduce long-term costs to government.

The government is taking a fundamentally different approach to public services, in line with the ‘Rewiring the State’ Cabinet Statement published in July. Reforms will improve outcomes and increase efficiency at every level of government by:

  • Devolving decision-making by transforming resources to local leaders across England, supporting an integrated, place-based approach that gives places more power to target spending towards the biggest issues in their communities, and which more coherently joins up services, improving outcomes and efficiency.
  • Streamlining central government, including through the transformation of the Civil Service which will deliver significant reductions in its size and cost.
  • Harnessing transformative technologies like AI, where the Chancellor and Health Secretary have commissioned an independent review into NHS productivity and the enormous opportunities presented by AI and technology to transform services for patients, ahead of the next spending review.

2.3 Economic and fiscal outlook

Economic outlook

The OBR has revised up its growth forecast to 1.2% in 2026, 0.1 percentage points higher than in the March forecast. The OBR forecasts growth to slow to 1.0% in 2027 as the impacts of higher energy prices feed through to consumers and businesses and higher interest rates weigh on the economy. Growth then accelerates to 1.6% in 2028, 1.8% in 2029 before moderating to 1.7% in 2030 and 1.6% in 2031. This means that despite the conflict, the level of GDP ends up broadly unchanged at the forecast horizon compared with the March forecast.

The OBR has revised up its forecast for potential output in 2026. Stronger-than-expected GDP growth and business investment in the first half of this year have raised potential output growth to 1.6%, 0.3 percentage points higher than the March forecast. Overall, the level of potential output at the forecast horizon remains broadly unchanged from the March forecast.

The OBR has not revised its assumption on underlying total factor productivity growth which reaches 0.8% in 2030. However, strong business investment – which follows a higher path across the forecast – affects trend labour productivity through greater capital deepening, leaving it 0.2% higher in 2030 than in the March forecast. The OBR has revised its forecast for real business investment and now expects it to be 0.5% above the level in its March forecast by 2030.

A higher starting level of potential output and higher growth in investment means the level of GDP per person is forecast to grow by 5.9% this Parliament and expected to be 0.7% higher at the end of the forecast compared with March.

Employment has been stronger than expected this year, with the OBR now forecasting an increase in employment of around 200,000 more than it did in the March forecast. However, labour demand is expected to remain subdued into 2027. The OBR expects unemployment to rise to 5.1% in Q2 2027 before falling to 4.1% by the end of the forecast period. The OBR expects total employment to increase from 34.4 million in 2026 to 35.4 million in 2031, rising in every year of the forecast. Nominal earnings growth is expected slow in the near term, but more gradually than in the March forecast.

The conflict in the Middle East has directly affected the inflation outlook through increased energy prices and indirectly through increased production and transportation costs. The OBR judges there to be only modest second-round effects. Inflation is forecast to peak at 3.8% in Q1 2027 before returning to the 2% target by Q3 2028.

The Budget provides breathing space for households as uncertainty and volatility from the global energy shock puts renewed pressure on living standards. RHDI per person is forecast to fall by 0.6% in 2026‑27 then average 0.6% annual growth over the rest of the forecast. Action to provide breathing space for households is expected to reduce inflation by 0.1 percentage points in 2027.
