Financing

The Debt Management Office (DMO) net financing requirement for 2026‑27 is forecast to be £258.6 billion, an increase of £7.4 billion from the previous remit. This will be financed through £250.6 billion of gilt sales (an increase of £4.4 billion), as well as £8 billion from the sale of Treasury bills used for debt management purposes (an increase of £3 billion). The government’s financing plans for 2026‑27 are summarised in Annex A.

The central government net cash requirement (CGNCR) is £144.1 billion in 2026‑27, £6.9 billion higher relative to the OBR’s March forecast. This is lower than the increase in PSNB in 2026‑27, reflecting inflation-driven increases in debt interest which affect PSNB when inflation occurs, but impact CGNCR over a longer time horizon.

The government is committed to maintaining as diversified an investor base as possible to enhance the resilience of the government’s financing programme. In keeping with this, the government published a consultation response in May on expanding and deepening the UK Treasury bill market. Today, the government is providing further detail around the implementation of the measures announced by it earlier in the year. These details can be found in Annex A.

HM Treasury, the Bank of England and the DMO have been developing a model whereby all Asset Purchase Facility (APF) active gilt sales are made to the government and not to the market. HM Treasury would instruct the DMO via the Debt Management Account to purchase the APF gilts that the Bank Executive is selling as part of its implementation of the MPC’s multi-year plan. HM Treasury would in due course instruct the DMO to issue a corresponding amount of debt to finance such APF purchases through the annual financing remit. As set out in the Chancellor’s letter to the Governor on 17 September 2026, this model remains under review, such that, subject to a final decision to proceed, implementation could begin in a way that allows this to be incorporated into the DMO’s 2027‑28 annual financing remit, as set by HM Treasury ministers.[footnote 62]

3. Fiscal responsibility and public spending

The actions this government is taking to reduce waste, increase efficiency, and live within our means will lower borrowing to bear down on inflation and increase the UK’s resilience in the face of shocks. All policy at this Budget is fully funded over the forecast.

3.1 Public spending

The government is maintaining public investment at the highest sustained level in four decades. Day-to-day departmental spending is due to be over £40 billion higher each year by 2028‑29, and the government is increasing capital investment by £120 billion over this Parliament, both compared with plans set out by the previous government in spring 2024.[footnote 63],[footnote 64] This has enabled the government to invest in communities: building new social and affordable homes, improving infrastructure, lifting children out of poverty, strengthening the NHS, and securing a stronger and more resilient United Kingdom through investment in defence.

The Budget confirms that day-to-day departmental spending will continue to grow overall in real terms over the forecast period, but it will be more gradual, controlled and targeted. The 10 Year Plan will set out the government’s long-term vision and priorities ahead of the next spending review. The next spending review will take place in 2027. As the government continues to target investment into the country’s top priorities, it is not necessarily the case that all departments will see real terms increases at the next spending review – putting the right resources into priorities is what any responsible government does.

The Budget also reaffirms the government’s commitment to reform through devolution, prevention and the transformational use of technology. This will improve outcomes and deliver efficiencies and savings. The choices the government is making on spending means this Budget can reject broad-based tax rises and protect most individuals and businesses from tax increases.

3.2 Spending discipline

In June, the government announced £15 billion between 2026‑27 and 2029‑30 for the Defence Investment Plan. It confirmed that £10.3 billion would be funded by reprioritising public spending without taking resources away from day-to-day spending on frontline services, and committed to confirming the full funding plan at Budget.

This Budget confirms that the residual £4.7 billion will be funded through reprioritisation of capital budgets. This will be achieved by further reducing departmental capital budgets by 1% from 2027‑28 to 2029‑30 to raise £3 billion. An additional £1.7 billion over the period will be funded from unallocated contingency in the Treasury’s capital Reserve. This is fair and balanced, made possible through proactive management of capital pressures and reprioritisation.

The government has concluded its Strategic Asset Review, which has identified surplus assets for disposal as part of the Defence Investment Plan funding package. The Budget sets revised departmental budgets, reflecting individual departmental disposal targets.

The government’s approach to spending discipline is reflected across reprioritisation decisions that it has taken throughout this administration, including: reprioritising within the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government’s budget to fund an offer of a route off the streets this year for rough sleepers; cancelling the Digital ID scheme; and funding the £2 bus fare cap that will be in place over 2027 from savings within the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero’s budget.

3.3 Reforming the state

The government is taking a fundamentally different approach to public services, in line with the ‘Rewiring the State’ Cabinet statement published in July and the fiscal devolution roadmap published alongside this Budget. These reforms will improve outcomes and increase efficiency at every level of government by devolving decision-making, streamlining central government, harnessing transformative technologies, and addressing the long-term drivers of spending. Rewiring the state will result in a shift towards a more devolved, preventative and productive state.

The government is taking steps at this Budget to radically shift where and how decisions are made by transferring resources to local leaders across England. This shift will enable a more integrated and place-based approach: one that gives places more power to target spending towards the biggest issues in their communities, that breaks down decision-making siloes, and that more coherently joins up services to improve outcomes and overall efficiency. As a step towards this, and alongside fiscal devolution, the government is publishing guidance on place-based business cases, a new approach to appraisal that puts local objectives at the heart of decision making. These place-based business cases can use economic potential analysis to identify the constraints holding a place back and assess what is needed to realise its potential.

The government is working with the devolved governments and local and regional stakeholders in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to explore how the benefits of regional empowerment can be spread to all parts of the UK.

The Cabinet Secretary is leading the transformation of the Civil Service so that it is recognised for excellence in delivery, innovation and improved productivity. This includes a process – supported by departmental Non-Executive Directors – to deliver significant reductions in the size and cost of the Civil Service, through maximising the opportunities presented by AI adoption and digital transformation.

The government will deliver devolution, not delegation. Where powers and functions are transferred, they will not be duplicated at the centre. Through devolution and increased adoption of AI and technology, the Civil Service will become smaller, more strategic, and focused on the issues that are best addressed at the national level.

At Spending Review 2025, the government committed to reducing departmental administration budgets by 16% in real terms by 2029‑30. As a result of its plans to rewire the state, the government is going further by reducing departmental administration budgets by 20% by 2029‑30. This will realise savings from 2027‑28 and will save an additional £595 million in 2029‑30 compared with previous plans.

This streamlining of the Civil Service will be supported by £35 million to set up GovAI to provide civil servants with access to the latest frontier AI tools and capabilities, freeing up their time to improve public services, and supporting departments to build in-house AI capabilities, procure external solutions, and partner with innovative startups. GovAI will also manage a new Civil Service AI transformation fund of £50 million across 2027‑28 and 2028‑29, funded through reinvesting some of the savings realised by reducing administration budgets. The fund will turbocharge technology and AI deployment across the Civil Service to reduce unnecessary administrative burdens and improve outcomes, including by automating processes and streamlining workflows to boost productivity.

The government is ensuring its investment into the NHS is spent wisely. In 2025‑26, the NHS delivered efficiencies and savings worth over £10 billion, equivalent to 5.2% of its RDEL budget. Considerable progress has been made already to drive NHS productivity, freeing up staff time and making improvements for patients, including through new technology such as the NHS App, which is helping more than 39 million users to navigate their healthcare options and access their health records.[footnote 65] The government’s AI-supported diagnostic tools have already helped over four million patients receive faster lung cancer diagnoses or results, with the AI Diagnostic Fund supporting technologies focused on high-demand services for lung cancer, such as chest X-ray and CT diagnostics.[footnote 66]

To build on this, the Chancellor and Health and Social Care Secretary have asked Mark Bailie to lead an independent review on NHS productivity and AI, which will inform the next spending review. Reporting in early 2027, this will focus on the practical opportunities presented by AI and technology to transform services for patients and boost NHS productivity.

The government is also launching an AI Challenge Prize to incentivise UK‑based innovators and businesses to develop AI solutions to major frontline public service challenges, supported by £15 million of funding and administered by DCMS. The first competition will focus on the NHS, with a top award of up to £2.5 million for the most promising solution to a priority healthcare challenge.

Across the rest of government, progress is also underway and is continuing to unlock innovation:

  • Rolling out Ask HMRC, the government’s AI tool to support customers to navigate the tax system – this handled a record 6.3 million customer interactions in 2025‑26, supporting the government’s ambition that nine in 10 customers use digital self-service.[footnote 67]
  • Expanding access to Justice Transcribe, the government’s AI-enabled probation tool, to all probation officers, building on around 267,000 hours already saved and freeing up officers to spend more time supporting rehabilitation and reducing reoffending.[footnote 68]
  • Making MHCLG’s PlanAssist frontier AI tool available to all councils in England by the end of 2027, subject to further testing, to halve routine planning decision times and build capacity in the planning system. The government will also mandate the digitisation and publication of key planning documents as open data by the end of 2027, removing barriers to wider AI adoption.

3.4 Prevention

The government recognises that placing greater emphasis on early intervention can yield benefits in the long term and help to address the drivers of poor outcomes and cost. The government is committed to acting to address problems before they escalate, improving people’s lives and delivering better long‑term value for taxpayers.

To support this approach, the government will introduce a new category of ringfenced spending at the spending review in 2027, preventative DEL (PDEL). PDEL will help facilitate shared resource and accountability across budget holders, and will help protect programmes that generate benefits over the longer term. This approach is demonstrated in the government’s plans to tackle rough sleeping, where the £432 million invested at this Budget will provide individual relief whilst also reducing the significant fiscal cost of each individual sleeping rough, estimated at around £14,000 per year.[footnote 69]

The government is continuing to reform the Green Book, its guidance on appraisal, including to place greater value on the long-term benefits of investment. As part of this, the government is publishing a revised Green Book, formalising the reduction in the discount rate from 3.5% to 3.0%. This will strengthen the case for transformational projects that drive growth, wherever they take place.

3.5 Continuous improvement in public spending

The government is committed to continuously improving the way it spends taxpayers’ money, delivering better outcomes and stronger public services with the same, or less, money. At Spending Review 2025, departments published Efficiency Delivery Plans with total annual efficiency gains of almost £14 billion by 2028‑29. In 2025‑26, every large department was required, for the first time, to report against the Government Efficiency Framework, which is a common reporting standard that shows efficiencies – delivering the same or more for less – as distinct from savings.

In 2025‑26, departments delivered 4.1% of efficiency and savings, equivalent to around £16 billion RDEL and exceeding their 2% target for that year.[footnote 70] Reports through the Framework show that gains are increasingly being driven by structural improvements to the way the government operates. This focus is already delivering results:

  • DfE’s AI lesson-planning tool is saving teachers an average of around three hours a week, reducing administrative burdens and freeing up more time for teaching and other school responsibilities.
  • The NHS has focused on reducing reliance on temporary staffing in order to reduce costs, with agency expenditure falling by £900 million (43%) in 2025‑26 compared with 2024‑25.

Spending Review 2025 set bespoke departmental efficiency targets and delivery plans targeting day-to-day spending. To ensure value across all departmental spending, the government will introduce a minimum expectation of technical efficiencies for capital budgets. This will be reported as part of the Government Efficiency Framework.

The government is tackling public sector fraud. In 2025‑26, the Public Sector Fraud Authority delivered £403.6 million in audited counter fraud benefits, achieving 119% of its target.[footnote 71] It continues to assess Initial Fraud Impact Assessments in business planning to embed fraud prevention in programme design.

As part of wider reforms to how the government plans, assesses and uses its assets across public services, departments will be required to develop long-term asset strategies to inform funding decisions at the spending review in 2027. Alongside the work of the Strategic Asset Review, a revised Strategic Asset Management Plan process will help create a more efficient and sustainable public estate, improving the condition of public assets over time by ensuring they are maintained, invested in and rationalised in a way that delivers value for taxpayers.

3.6 Keeping the government’s tax commitments

Fiscal discipline underwrites every promise this government makes. At a time when households and businesses are under pressure and need breathing space, the Budget rejects broad-based tax rises. It achieves this while ensuring that all policy at the Budget is fully funded over the forecast, and raises the revenue to fund commitments on breathing space and energy in a fair, targeted and proportionate way. In doing so, it has protected most individuals and businesses from tax increases, giving them further space to breathe.

The government is keeping to its commitments on tax, with no increase to the headline rates of income tax, National Insurance contributions or VAT. The government is further modernising the tax system, closing loopholes and ensuring that everyone pays the tax they owe.

The government recognises the importance of a stable and predictable tax system to give businesses the certainty and confidence to make long-term decisions and invest in the UK. The government is therefore maintaining the commitments in the 2024 Corporate Tax Roadmap, and is taking steps to progress the roadmap commitment to explore simplification and improve the administration of the tax system.

3.7 A modern and fair tax system

The government is committed to a modern and fair tax system that works better for individuals and businesses, including by closing the tax gap. This Budget builds on progress already made and introduces reforms that make it easier for individuals and businesses to navigate the tax system and pay the right amount of tax at the right time, reducing error and unnecessary burdens. This includes launching a targeted, evidence-led programme to simplify specific areas of Corporation Tax, working with businesses and tax experts to reduce avoidable complexity, improve certainty and make the UK a better place to invest and do business in.

This builds on HM Revenue and Customs’ (HMRC’s) Transformation Roadmap published in July 2025, which set out the government’s vision for a more modern and efficient tax administration system, including through the continued rollout of Making Tax Digital.[footnote 72]

The government will modernise the existing Payments on Account system for Income Tax Self Assessment (ITSA), following consultation with stakeholders and affected taxpayers. From April 2029, taxpayers who already make Payments on Account will make smaller, more regular contributions towards their tax bill throughout the year, bringing payment closer to when income is earned. This will help taxpayers budget and plan for their tax obligations, reducing the risk of large, unexpected tax bills and making it less likely that they fall behind on tax due and build up debt. The government will continue to work with stakeholders and affected taxpayers on implementing this change. Alongside these reforms, the government will make it easier for around 160,000 employees to claim tax relief on employment expenses by removing the need to use ITSA solely to make these claims.

This Budget supports businesses through the use of data and technology to develop a more modern and efficient tax system. The government is setting out an implementation roadmap for requiring VAT e-invoicing from April 2029, reducing administrative burdens and improving efficiency. Alongside this, a Call for Evidence on modernising Corporation Tax administration will explore how technology can simplify the system and reduce burdens on business.

Building on the increased benefits expected from existing third-party data reforms, the government will consult on expanding third-party reporting requirements for property income data, improving the information available across the tax system to support compliance while reducing unnecessary interventions and burdens for taxpayers who are meeting their obligations.

In addition to these measures, the government is modernising the rules that determine how distributions from companies to individual (non-corporate) shareholders are taxed, ensuring that similar transactions are taxed consistently through a clearer framework. This will reduce opportunities for well‑advised taxpayers to structure how profits are taken out to secure a more favourable tax treatment that is not available to other taxpayers.

The reforms are designed to protect capital treatment for genuine changes in ownership, including families passing down their business, and in some cases make the relief more generous for demergers. The government will continue to engage with stakeholders on the technical detail of the reforms and will consult on draft legislation ahead of implementation in April 2028.

As announced at Budget 2025, the government will introduce Electric Vehicle Excise Duty (eVED), a new mileage-based charge for electric and plug-in hybrid cars, from April 2028. The government has listened to feedback received through the eVED consultation and will:

  • Introduce a mileage estimation tool to support motorists that will be available at launch in April 2028. The government is undertaking proof of concept work to assess how features such as benchmarking could help motorists to estimate their mileage.
  • Develop an opt-in system to make use of vehicles’ in-built connectivity. ‘eVED Connect’ will allow motorists to use this connectivity so that they do not have to report their mileage manually. The technology could also support mileage estimation for the coming year.
  • Develop an automated refunds model by 2030, making refunds easier and available in more circumstances, such as when a motorist overestimates their mileage or sells their car.
  • Work closely with industry and motoring representative groups ahead of implementation, and make available further guidance for fleet operators later this year.

The private hire vehicle market has grown and changed rapidly in recent years, highlighting inconsistencies in tax treatment between larger operators. This Budget ends this inconsistency by making larger operators liable for VAT on their full fare, in line with other goods and services, while protecting smaller operators. The government will shortly publish a consultation on the level of annual fare turnover this measure will apply to, with £50 million as the lead option.

The government is modernising the taxation of foreign sovereign investment, putting it on a statutory footing for the first time and giving greater certainty to sovereign investors. The new regime will bring certain real estate income and gains into UK tax, while maintaining a globally competitive offer for foreign sovereign investment in the UK, including through bespoke rules to access Real Estate Investment Trusts for investments in UK real estate.

The government has published a new multi-year plan to modernise the approach to the compliance of wealthy taxpayers. The plan sets out how HMRC will make better use of data, technology and specialist expertise to improve its understanding of wealthy taxpayers, make it easier for them to get their tax right first time, and identify and address non-compliance earlier. This will enable HMRC to focus on the greatest risks.

3.8 Ensuring everyone pays what they owe

As well as making it easier for taxpayers to get their tax right first time, the government is taking targeted action to ensure everyone pays their fair share. This includes strengthening HMRC’s ability to tackle non-compliance and recover unpaid tax, with investment at this Budget in an additional 670 compliance officers, building on previous commitments to recruit 5,500 additional compliance officers, by 2029-30.

The government is also taking action to ensure foreign firms have to pay the same tax as UK businesses. The government is closing a loophole which currently allows overseas businesses to sell services to some UK businesses without accounting for UK VAT.

In 2021, reforms were introduced to ensure that overseas sellers on online marketplaces pay the tax they owe. This was a step towards protecting the high street from unfair competition from overseas businesses. The government is now going further to tackle the non-compliance by UK sellers trading on online marketplaces that undercuts businesses on the high street who pay the tax they owe. The government will do this by making the marketplaces responsible for collecting VAT on sales by UK businesses, where those businesses are making more than £90,000 of sales through the marketplace. This policy will be implemented from October 2027 and will not impact personal sales through marketplaces. The money raised from this policy will be reinvested into the high street through reductions to business rates.

This Budget also announces that, alongside existing tools used to recover high-value debt, the government will provide HMRC with a new power to enable the direct recovery of lower-value tax debts from those who can afford to pay but repeatedly fail to do so.

The government continues to take action to close the tax gap. The changes announced at this Budget to modernise the tax system and ensure everyone pays their fair share take the total due to be raised from measures to close the tax gap announced during this Parliament to over £12 billion in 2029-30.[footnote 73]

By reducing administrative burdens and improving certainty, the government is supporting investment, productivity and growth in every postcode in the UK. The government will continue to identify opportunities to simplify and modernise the tax and customs system and will make further changes including at a Tax Update in 2027.

3.9 Making fair choices on revenue raising

The government is giving families breathing space now, including by extending the cut to VAT on electricity until July 2027, and providing a further £2.6 billion of support through the Household Energy Payment, with up to 20 million households in England receiving a direct £100 payment from January 2027 delivered through the council tax system. To help fund this, the rate of the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge will temporarily increase from 3% to 6%, from 1 January 2027 until 31 March 2028. This time-limited period will be legislated for in Finance Bill 2026-27 and will not be extended.

The rate of Machine Games Duty will increase from 20% to 25% on machine games with stakes over £1 from April 2027. This will increase the rate on higher-risk machines, which are more associated with gambling harm and commonly found in venues such as adult gaming centres. The revenue raised from this measure will help to pay for the freeze in business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure properties, so that no property in those sectors faces a real-terms increase. In order to protect pubs and seaside arcades, the government is maintaining the existing rate for lower-stake machines.

The government is keeping the rates of tax paid on earnings unchanged, while seeking an additional contribution from those with taxable income from assets. Budget 2025 increased the rates of tax on savings and property income by two percentage points across all tax bands from April 2027. The government will increase these rates by a further two percentage points from that date. This is a fair and proportionate approach, and 84% of income tax payers will be unaffected by these changes. This also raises revenue in a progressive way, so that those who earn more contribute more. Around half of the revenue raised from this change is expected to come from the top 10% of households.[footnote 74]

The government continues to support individuals to save, including through Individual Savings Accounts (ISA), the Personal Savings Allowance (PSA) and the Starting Rate of Savings (SRS). This means that basic rate taxpayers would need over £25,000 in savings in addition to any ISA savings before paying tax and those also eligible for the SRS could have up to £150,000 in savings in addition to their ISAs without paying tax.[footnote 75]

To continue providing generous support for savers, the government has decided not to reduce the cash ISA limit, so that it remains at £20,000. The government recognises the importance of making investment more accessible to savers, supporting households to build their wealth. The government launched targeted support in April to help more people access support on investment decisions and welcomed the launch of the industry-led ‘Invest for the Future’ campaign to promote the benefits of investing to the public. The government will now go further, working with the investment industry to explore a new ISA incentive for people investing in a stocks and shares ISA for the first time. The detailed design will be developed with industry.

The government is reducing the lifetime limit for capital gains eligible for Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) from £1 million to £500,000 from April 2027. This will ensure that three-quarters of BADR claimants will still receive relief on their entire gain, while supporting focus within the tax system for the start-up and scale‑up phases of business, when most investment decisions are taken.

The government is maintaining stability for businesses and investment through its commitment to the Corporate Tax Roadmap, capping the headline rate at 25%, currently the lowest in the G7, and maintaining the UK’s world-leading full expensing regime. At this Budget, the government has decided to raise revenue by reducing the main rate of writing down allowances by two percentage points, taking the rate to 12% from April 2027. At the same time, the government is increasing incentives for new investment by raising the main rate First Year Allowance (FYA) from 40% to 50% and maintaining stability for businesses by prioritising sticking to the Corporate Tax Roadmap. This maintains the UK’s international competitiveness, with the UK continuing to have one of the most generous capital allowance regimes in the world.

4. Breathing space

Price stability and sustainable economic growth are essential to raising living standards in the long run. The government’s commitment to fiscal discipline supports breathing space: bringing down borrowing helps bear down on inflation, mortgage rates and the cost of business. At the same time, the government is helping households and businesses manage the immediate pressures from global volatility. This Budget delivers breathing space by launching a new Household Energy Payment, freezing or cutting taxes for retail, hospitality and leisure (RHL) businesses on the high street, and protecting most individuals and businesses from tax rises – while kicking off longer‑term changes to get costs down, starting with energy costs.

The government recognises that households and businesses are feeling the effect of the conflict in the Middle East. Global energy prices have increased sharply since the start of the conflict and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February. The global shock has pushed up the price of energy imports. Inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) expects it to peak at 3.8% in Q1 2027.[footnote 76] For a sustained period, cost of living pressures have been the most pronounced for household essentials. Overall, consumer prices today are around 33% higher than the 2020 average, while household energy has seen an increase of 73% (Charts 3.1 and 3.2). A household filling a typical 55-litre family car now spends around £24 more at the pump for petrol and £32 more for diesel than they did before the conflict started.[footnote 77] Government action at this Budget to provide breathing space for households is expected by the OBR to reduce inflation by 0.1 percentage points in 2027.

In that context, this is a Budget to steer Britain through a period of global pressures, to grow the economy and to provide breathing space for families and businesses.

  • First, this government is continuing to deliver on its commitment to fiscal discipline: the stability that fiscal discipline creates provides the foundations for the investment needed to deliver good growth, and lower borrowing supports the Bank of England to reduce inflation.   • Second, at a time when families and businesses are under pressure and need breathing space, this Budget rejects broad-based tax rises, protecting most individuals and businesses from tax increases. Instead, the government is choosing to use some of the headroom established last year to absorb the impact of higher debt-interest costs from the conflict in the Middle East.
  • Third, this Budget takes the pressure off families and businesses now. The government has already removed VAT from domestic electricity for this winter and will cap bus fares at £2 and reduce business rates on pubs in 2027. 4.3 Supporting households and businesses with energy bills

Households are understandably worried about energy costs, given the sharp increase in global prices this year. This Budget provides universal support with energy bills by extending the temporary 0% rate of VAT on qualifying domestic electricity supplies in Great Britain for another three months, until July 2027. This extension is expected to take around £50 off the annual Ofgem price cap in April 2027.[footnote 82] To support households in Northern Ireland, the government is providing funding for the Northern Ireland Executive to provide comparable support with household electricity bills. Extended VAT relief is expected to apply in Northern Ireland from April 2027.

In addition, the government is launching a £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment to help households with the rising cost of energy. This will be directly provided to up to 20 million households via the Council Tax system, through a £100 payment for households in bands A-D in England from January 2027.[footnote 83] The devolved governments will receive their share of funding through the Barnett formula, which will enable them to provide similar support. Taken together, these decisions mean that almost all households in the UK will benefit from the extended VAT cut to electricity, which is expected to take around £50 off the annual Ofgem price cap in April 2027, and around 80% of households in England will gain further from the £100 Household Energy Payment. To help fund this, the rate of the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge will temporarily increase from 3% to 6%, from 1 January 2027 until 31 March 2028. This time-limited period will be legislated for in the Finance Bill 2026‑27.

The government also recognises that lower-income households are the most likely to feel the squeeze when energy bills increase. In 2024‑25, households in the bottom 10% of the income distribution spent over six times more on energy than households in the top 10%, as a proportion of net income (see Chart 3.3). The government estimates the Household Energy Payment will reach 83% of fuel-stressed households in England, and 88% of households in the bottom three income deciles.[footnote 84], [footnote 85] In addition, this Budget provides £100 million additional funding for local authorities in England to provide further targeted support to households acutely impacted by rising energy bills, some of whom are in council tax bands above A-D.

This intervention builds on action taken at the last Budget, including taking £150 of costs off bills in April 2026 by scrapping the Energy Company Obligation levy and funding 75% of the Renewables Obligation from the Exchequer.[footnote 86] It also comes on top of the targeted financial support worth over £50 million for low-income households who heat their homes with oil, which the government announced in March.

The government is also offering longer-term reforms to make sure energy institutions and markets work for households and businesses. This Budget kickstarts the long-term action required to get energy costs down for good. Household energy debt has almost tripled to over £5 billion (Q2 2026) following Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.[footnote 87] The government is publishing a new debt strategy to address this and act as a circuit breaker on energy debt. The strategy is expected to save a typical household almost £30 by 2030, via reforms to prevent debt building up and a one-off targeted debt relief scheme for eligible households.[footnote 88]

Gas standing charges are currently £108 a year on average for the typical billpayer.[footnote 89] They are paid by households even if they use very little gas. To give consumers more control over their bills, the government has asked Ofgem to abolish gas standing charges on domestic energy bills, aiming for delivery by the end of 2027 or as soon as possible after then. Ofgem will ensure that energy suppliers recover these costs through gas unit rates instead and work with suppliers and consumer groups to maintain a stable, fair and competitive retail market. While a significant majority will benefit from better control of their energy bills, a number of households may be less able to make the most of the reform. This change will be implemented fairly, including through the government setting out targeted mitigation. As well as abolishing gas standing charges, the government is also committing to reform electricity standing charges and will set out details next year.

Chapter 4 sets out further detail on energy bill support for businesses. This includes funding being confirmed at Budget for the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS) to cut electricity bills by up to 25% for over 10,000 energy-intensive businesses from April 2027; the introduction of a Cost Control Framework at the spending review in 2027 to set budgets for components of energy costs, including policy costs; and reforms to the energy market which will bring down the cost of energy in the long term.[footnote 90]

The government will shortly bring forward the Energy Independence Bill to legislate for some of the measures in this Budget.

4.4 Support with fuel prices and other motoring costs

The government recognises that high fuel prices from the conflict in the Middle East are continuing to impact motorists. In 2022, Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine led to soaring fuel prices, and the previous government introduced a temporary 12-month 5p cut in the rate of fuel duty. This has since been extended five times, including in May of this year, when the government extended it until the end of 2026 to support motorists and other fuel users in response to elevated fuel prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East.

Fuel prices remain significantly elevated, with diesel exceeding £2 per litre in October 2026.[footnote 95] To provide temporary breathing space to the 35 million motorists and businesses across the UK, the government is cancelling plans to add 5p back onto fuel duty from January 2027 and is extending the cut by a further six months to 1 July 2027.[footnote 96] The government is also deferring the planned Retail Prices Index (RPI) increase to 1 July 2027. The government will continue to monitor fuel prices over the coming months. Fuel duty is as low now as it has been at any point for over 16 years.[footnote 97] Taken together, the government’s decisions on fuel duty across this Parliament are expected to have saved the average car driver £230, the average light goods driver £472 and the average heavy goods vehicle (HGV) driver nearly £4,000, compared with plans under the previous government.[footnote 98]

As announced on 27 October, the government is also supporting employees and self-employed people across the UK who use their own vehicles for work by increasing tax-free mileage rates. In May, the government announced a temporary 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles for cars and vans. At this Budget, the government is making this permanent. This will mean around 2 million employees and 1 million self-employed people, including care workers, social workers, electricians and plumbers, will see £120 a year in additional tax savings if they drive 6,000 business miles. The government is also increasing the mileage rate above 10,000 business miles from 25p to 35p, allowing someone driving 15,000 business miles a year to receive up to £300 in additional tax savings from both upratings.[footnote 99]

The rise in fuel prices is also disproportionately affecting users of red diesel. The government is extending the 3.7p cut to duty on red diesel for a further six months to 1 July 2027, keeping the rate at its lowest level for over 20 years.[footnote 100] This will continue to provide breathing space to agriculture, rail freight and other fuel-intensive red diesel users. Additionally, in July the government introduced a 12-month holiday from vehicle excise duty (VED) for most HGVs, running to 1 July 2027, and saving £600 for a typical HGV on top of savings from cancelling the planned fuel duty increases.[footnote 101]

In addition, the government welcomes the publication alongside the Budget of Philip New’s independent review of the cost of charging electric vehicles (EVs) on the public network. The government is taking immediate steps to establish a taskforce to explore allowing drivers to use their domestic electricity tariff at local, lower-powered public charge points. This is a complex proposal that will take time to consider, so the government is also announcing £100 million over the next two years to reduce costs for local, lower-powered public chargers. Coming into effect from Spring 2027, this is expected to save the average EV driver without home charging and who charges on-street around £150 per year.[footnote 102] The Department for Transport (DfT) will set out next steps in due course.

4.5 Additional support for households

One of the biggest expenditures for families is the weekly food shop. At this Budget, the government is suspending tariffs on all UK imports of over 100 food products – from plant-based drinks and baked beans to dried fruits and chocolate – expected to reduce consumer costs by £120-185 million per annum. Combined with the package of tariff suspensions on food in June, this is expected to reduce consumer costs by £245-595 million.[footnote 103] Separately, following the impact of the conflict in the Middle East, the government is also temporarily suspending tariffs on fertiliser and kerosene heating oil. This will lower production costs for the UK’s agricultural sector and support households that rely on heating oil to heat their homes, including many people in rural areas and Northern Ireland. Food and kerosene suspensions will be in place for two years until December 2028. Fertiliser tariffs will be suspended until December 2027.

To support low-paid workers across the UK, the government is raising the National Living Wage and National Minimum Wages, which is expected to benefit around 2.3 million workers.[footnote 104] On 1 April 2027, the National Living Wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 per hour, equivalent to an increase of £910 in the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker on the National Living Wage.[footnote 105] The National Minimum Wage for 18- to 20-year-olds will also increase by 3.9% to £11.27 per hour. By accepting the Low Pay Commission’s recommendations in full this year, the government is ensuring workers are rewarded fairly for their work, while protecting jobs, backing businesses, and strengthening the conditions for economic growth.

The government will also introduce the Pension Tax Allowance from April 2027, which reduces the disproportionate administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax for those whose incomes only just exceed the Personal Allowance. Pensioners with incomes at or under the value of the full new State Pension will not be brought into paying tax because of State Pension uprating in this Parliament.

Looking ahead, the government is making long-term changes to improve support for families. This includes:

  • Expanding parental pay to make the system fairer, including to self-employed fathers, partners and adopters: from April 2029, eligible self-employed fathers, partners and adopters in Great Britain, who are currently excluded from the system, will be able to access parental pay. This is set to benefit over 150,000 parents per year, providing breathing space to affected families who previously would be excluded from support.[footnote 106] This comes in advance of the ongoing Parental Leave and Pay Review, which will conclude in early 2027.
  • Supporting children’s development from birth to school: the government is committed to increasing children’s readiness for school, with an ambition that at least 75% of children will reach a ‘good level of development’ by 2028. The government will provide up to £5 million a year for three years from 2027‑28 for organisations like Dolly Parton Imagination Library and BookTrust, increasing access to books for young children and helping improve their readiness for school.
  • Giving carers in receipt of Carer’s Allowance greater flexibility to work without the fear of losing out financially: the government will reform the Weekly Earnings Limit so that carers no longer lose their entire benefit for exceeding the limit by a single penny. Instead, earnings above the limit will be subject to a taper that reduces the benefit payment as earnings increase. This measure is expected to benefit around 48,000 carers in England and Wales. The taper will be implemented during 2030‑31 following the development of a new IT system that will automatically adjust payments in line with the taper.
