4.6 Supporting high streets and small businesses

High streets are at the heart of local communities. They are where many people go to work and the places that keep communities connected. The government has already started to give breathing space to those businesses that bring people together. The government is providing an extra 20% relief for pubs, social clubs and all but the very largest live music venues in England from 1 April 2027. This is in addition to the support introduced earlier this year, bringing the total relief to 35%. Taken together, this relief is a tax cut worth an average of over £3,000 per pub next year.[footnote 107]

At this Budget, the government is going further to support high streets, backing RHL businesses of all sizes, many of which had been facing significant business rates bill increases. The decisions in this Budget mean that from April 2027, RHL businesses in England will see their business rates either frozen in real terms, reduced, or cut to zero. The government will deliver this by:

  • Taking around 70,000 more high street businesses out of business rates through an increase of the Small Business Rates Relief (SBRR) thresholds to £18,000 for 100% relief (from £12,000) and £21,000 for tapered relief (from £15,000) for qualifying RHL properties in England from April 2027. From next year, an additional 3,500 pubs, 3,900 restaurants, 2,200 cafés and 1,700 hairdressers and beauty salons will pay no business rates.
  • Delivering a real-terms freeze of business rates bills for qualifying RHL properties in England in 2027‑28 and 2028‑29, so all RHL businesses have greater confidence to plan, invest and protect jobs. On average, over 14,000 restaurants will avoid an extra £7,500 paid over the two years and 120,000 shops will avoid an extra £3,250 paid over the two years.
  • Extending transitional support by extending the 2026 Supporting Small Business (SSB) scheme in England to those who were in receipt of 2023 SSB for a further year, so that around 37,000 small and independent ratepayers will continue to receive protection next year worth an average of £3,000.

As a result of this package, half of all RHL properties in England will not pay business rates at all and around 110,000 RHL properties will see their bills falling next year.

These measures will be funded in part by increasing the rate of Machine Games Duty from 20% to 25% only for higher-stakes machine games, protecting pubs and seaside arcades. They will also be partly funded by tackling non- compliance on online marketplaces through extending the online marketplace liability rules to UK businesses. Further detail is set out in Chapter 2. To go further, the government will continue to explore how the business rates system could better target online retailers in ways that minimise any indirect impacts for wider retail businesses, to fund support for the high street. The government will extend the existing Transitional Relief Supplement in England for a further two years. This 1p supplement only affects properties that have seen smaller increases or reductions in their business rates bills and will help fund the two-year real-terms freeze for qualifying RHL properties.

This fiscal support sits at the heart of a wider package to make high streets safer and easier places in which to do business. The Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) will launch its High Streets Strategy today, including committing to creating a ‘High Streets First’ principle for relevant public estates, Business Improvement Distinct reform, and work to clean up England’s high streets. It builds on commitments from MHCLG, with a £210 million package to revitalise derelict high street buildings, and work from the Home Office to crack down on organised crime operated through businesses on the high street. To support this, the government will also:

  • Take action against business rates avoidance in England: empowering local authorities to better take on avoidance by expanding the funding provided for challenging avoidance in court; and introducing a General Anti-Avoidance Rule, giving local authorities the powers they need to take on non-compliance.
  • Remove business rates reliefs for vape shops and Adult Gaming Centres, so that these reliefs are better targeted at businesses that support thriving high streets: from April 2027, vape shops and Adult Gaming Centres in England will no longer be eligible for the RHL multipliers, and vape shops will also lose eligibility for SBRR.
  • Engage with businesses and local government, following the mixed responses in the ‘Business Rates and Investment: Call for Evidence’, to understand how the system can better incentivise the reoccupation of empty properties.

The government is committed to a business rates system that supports growth in every postcode, strengthens local economies and gives businesses and local government greater stability. As next steps, the government will prioritise measures that support high streets, and that improve stability and predictability within the system. As set out in the fiscal devolution roadmap, the government intends to increase the share of business rates retained locally with the intention for 100% of business rates to be retained locally. The government will also explore how greater control of business rates policy could better support fiscal devolution and good growth, while protecting business certainty and fairness between places.

Support for the RHL sector announced at this Budget sits alongside wider measures to support small businesses across the UK. Small businesses are the backbone of the British economy, supporting around 13 million jobs. Earlier this month, the government accepted recommendations from the Small Business Regulatory Taskforce, which has seen government work in partnership with business leaders to identify and reduce the bureaucracy holding firms back. For small businesses, the government will make it simpler to bid for contracts, streamline ONS business surveys to reduce the number of data requests businesses have to fill out, and implement the government’s ‘Tell us Once’ ambition. To unlock the opportunities of AI, this Budget also confirms funding to pilot local partnerships to develop locally-led approaches to AI adoption, including working across local councils to help small businesses grow. Further detail is set out in Chapter 4. The government is also committed to tackling late payments to support small business cashflow. Together, these changes represent the future partnership between government and small business.

4.7 Further support for businesses

To maintain reduced import costs for businesses across the UK, the government is extending Business Suspensions applying to 269 goods which are otherwise due to expire at the end of 2026. Tariffs will remain suspended on products such as grape juice (20% tariff), tomato paste (14%) and bicycle tyres (4%) – benefitting businesses across the food and drinks, chemicals, plastics, hydrogen and automotive sectors. The government will also open a new window for businesses to request the suspension of tariffs on further products, giving firms an opportunity to identify where removing tariffs could reduce input costs and support competitiveness. This window will be open from 11 November 2026 to 3 February 2027.

Small alcohol producers make an important contribution to the economy and local communities. To provide further help, the government will make Small Producer Relief in the Alcohol Duty system more generous, providing £10 million per year of support to over 2,000 small alcohol producers across the UK, based on the government’s Alcohol Duty Evaluation report published alongside the Budget. The government will implement a more generous discount taper for products below 3.5% ABV – strengthening incentives to produce lower-strength products – and uprate the marginal discount for products between 3.5%-8.4% ABV by RPI+10% from 1 February 2027. To further support brewers, the government intends to introduce a ‘Guest Beer’ provision in the Pubs Code, covering England and Wales. This will support brewers to continue to gain access to the market, whilst giving consumers a greater choice of beers available at the pub.

More detail on measures to cut the cost of administrative burdens on businesses, including through more proportionate regulation, is covered in Chapter 4.

This Budget is reducing pressures on households and lowering costs for businesses in a fair, responsible way: providing breathing space now, and bringing hope for the future.

5. Good growth in every postcode

Good growth is how we build a stronger, fairer country, where people can enjoy rising living standards, find good work and rely on the public services and essential infrastructure that support everyday life. Its benefits should be felt in every part of the UK.

Productivity growth has slowed since the mid-2000s, weighing on living standards. Since 2010, real household disposable income per person has grown by around 0.8 per cent a year, compared with a long-run pre-financial crisis average of around 2.5 per cent.[footnote 108]

The UK also has persistent gaps in regional productivity.[footnote 109] Economic growth and jobs have been concentrated in London and the South East.[footnote 110] Regional disparities are a symptom of the national growth challenge but also hold growth back by leaving people and productive capacity underused.

The UK’s economy has proven resilient in the face of external shocks. Real GDP grew by 1.2% in the first half of the year, the joint-fastest growth in the G7.[footnote 111] There are signs productivity growth has picked up (see Box 1.A in Chapter 1).

However, further action is needed to sustain this momentum. In recent decades the UK has not done enough to strengthen the foundations of growth: investment, innovation, and good jobs and skills.

5.1 Investment

UK investment was the lowest in the G7 in 22 of the last 30 years, leaving workers and businesses with less of the capital they need to become more productive.[footnote 112]

Public investment has averaged 2.5% of GDP over the last 30 years, compared with 3.5% across the rest of the G7, leaving the UK with the G7’s joint-lowest public capital stock.[footnote 113],[footnote 114] The government is addressing this issue by increasing capital investment by £120 billion over this Parliament, compared with plans set out in Spring 2024.[footnote 115]

Private investment, which is three times larger than government investment, is an even bigger challenge. Business investment has grown by 7.5% since the start of the Parliament.[footnote 116] However, planning constraints and inadequate infrastructure reduce the returns to investing, while high input costs make some investments uneconomic. Risk aversion and limited access to scale-up finance can slow decision making, and policy uncertainty can increase costs and risk.

Places have often lacked the powers, long-term funding and flexibility to invest in their own economic opportunities. Regional government in the UK currently receives the smallest share of its funding from taxes and is most reliant on grants from central government of any country in the G7.[footnote 117]

5.2 Innovation

UK research is globally strong, with the highest measured impact per publication in the G7.[footnote 118] But these strengths are not translating consistently through the wider economy. The Global Innovation Index ranks the UK sixth overall but 15th for knowledge diffusion.[footnote 119] There is a particular challenge with scaling companies.

A dynamic economy in which successful firms can grow and capital and workers can move towards more productive uses supports the commercialisation and diffusion of new ideas. But declining job reallocation and a shrinking share of young firms suggest this dynamism has weakened in the UK,[footnote 120] and competition, backed by a strong independent regulator, plays a key role in supporting a more dynamic economy.

The possibilities of AI show what is at stake, with the OECD estimating it could add 0.4–1.3 percentage points to annual productivity growth over the next decade,[footnote 121] depending on the rate of diffusion and adoption that occurs.

5.3 Jobs and skills

The UK labour market remains strong by historical and international standards, with the employment rate at 75.3%.[footnote 122] However, there are now almost one million young people not in education, employment or training, while around 2.7 million people are out of work because of long-term sickness.[footnote 123],[footnote 124] Growth depends on connecting people with the jobs in which they can be most productive. The UK has one of the highest rates of tertiary education attainment in the G7, but this overall strength masks weaknesses in technical and vocational skills, which can leave businesses without the capabilities they need.[footnote 125]

This Budget takes actions to address these issues by strengthening public control, driving growth in more places, backing British businesses, and seizing the opportunities of AI while managing its risks. HM Treasury and No10 North will work together to drive good growth across the country.

5.4 Public control

Public control means government stepping in to ensure that life’s essentials are run for the public good: taking an active role in delivering essential services and infrastructure on which people, businesses and places depend, by increasing investment, affordability and accountability. This may include direct provision or ownership, but also a strategic state providing leadership through setting direction, coordinating investment, reducing the cost of business, and shaping markets for public benefit.

Affordable and reliable energy, water, transport and housing are the foundations of a productive economy. On 29 September, the Prime Minister announced commitments to reform the UK energy market, a strengthened Water Bill to repeal the statutory ban on public ownership and to give Mayors stronger oversight powers over the sector, and the largest council housebuilding programme since the post-war era.

At this Budget, the government is taking steps to:

  • Bring down energy costs for business and support electrification.
  • Deliver infrastructure and housing faster and at lower cost.
  • Provide strategic public investment, including to help mobilise private finance.
  • Reduce business costs through more proportionate regulation and faster, more predictable decision making.

This Chapter also sets out the government’s approach to AI.

The government will set out further reforms to exercise greater public control as part of the 10 Year Plan.

Bringing down energy costs for business

The cost of energy is one of the biggest barriers to growth in the UK. In the second half of 2025, household electricity prices in the UK were higher than in all but three EU states.[footnote 126] Industrial energy prices for all UK business types are consistently amongst the highest in the EU.[footnote 127] The UK is exposed to volatile international fuel markets. High electricity costs also make decarbonising the whole economy more difficult.

The government will introduce a new comprehensive Cost Control Framework (CCF) at the spending review in 2027 that will set budgets for components of energy costs, including policy costs, to ensure government action drives bills down over the next 10 years. Until that CCF is in place, no further policy costs will be placed on bills unless they bring bills down or are essential for security of supply.

The Gas Shipper Obligation tax on gas bills will not be introduced as planned, providing savings for businesses and households across the country. Instead, the government will publicly fund Hydrogen Allocation Round 1 contracts and any future hydrogen contracts – for example, Hydrogen Production Plant 1 – if the government commits to them, subject to value for money.

Cheap, clean power benefits billpayers, energy security and decarbonisation. To ensure that the government’s continued commitment to clean power always means cheaper power, the government will ensure that it only procures clean power when it lowers bills overall and can connect to the grid. Allocation Round 8 will lower bills, as well as deliver a good outcome for energy security and climate.

To tackle high energy costs for businesses, the government is delivering one of the most significant interventions in business energy costs in a generation. From April 2027, the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme will support over 10,000 eligible manufacturers in Great Britain, cutting their electricity bills by up to 25% and bringing electricity costs closer to other economies in Europe.

In addition, the main rate of the Climate Change Levy on electricity will be frozen from 1 April 2028. This will help to reduce electricity costs in real terms for businesses. This comes on top of the removal of Carbon Price Support from April 2028, as announced earlier this year. This will simplify the carbon pricing landscape and remove £18/tCO2e on fossil-fuel powered electricity generation, helping to reduce energy bills. This is worth £235 million over the next five years.

To drive down costs, the system must also deliver infrastructure cheaper and faster. As announced by the Prime Minister, Great British Grid will work alongside existing network operators to increase competition and support delivery of grid upgrades and reforms. Competition in offshore electricity networks has delivered hundreds of millions of pounds of bill savings, and building on this success, competition will shortly be introduced into onshore electricity transmission networks.[footnote 128]

The government is publishing a consultation response on strategic demand connections which will confirm the use of powers in the Planning and Infrastructure Act to prioritise grid connections for strategically important projects.

The government is delivering a golden age of nuclear power in the UK. This includes giving the green light to Sizewell C, delivering the UK’s first Small Modular Reactor programme, and a significant investment in our world-leading nuclear fusion programme. Significant progress has been made, with the Technology Partner Contract for the Gwyndod project signed with Rolls-Royce SMR in April 2026. Gwyndod represents the most significant industrial investment in North Wales for a generation: Great British Energy – Nuclear has awarded almost £900 million in supply chain contracts to date, hitting their targets for more than 70% of these going to UK registered companies.

The government has committed to deliver fully the findings of the Fingleton Nuclear Regulatory Review, the most significant reset of the UK’s nuclear regulatory system in over 20 years. This will make both deploying new civil nuclear and renewing the deterrent quicker and cheaper to build, while ensuring robust safety and environmental standards. A significant number of the recommendations have been fully implemented already or will be completed through the introduction of the Nuclear Regulation Bill early next year. All reforms should be delivered by the end of 2027.

The government will set out further detail on reforming and improving the efficiency of the electricity market in the 10 Year Plan. This will include how siting and investment decisions are made by generators, constraint management, system pricing, and balancing and settlement arrangements, building on the reformed national pricing programme set out earlier this year. These reforms will reduce system costs, make markets work better for consumers, and encourage electrification.

The government will review accountability across the energy system – setting clearer expectations for the roles, responsibilities, priorities and outcomes of the National Energy System Operator (NESO), Ofgem and the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ).

The consultation on wholesale Contracts for Difference has been published today to progress the government’s plans to delink electricity from volatile international gas prices. The government intends to consult on Market Arrangements for Gas, with further details to be announced in due course. Further reforms to the Contracts for Difference scheme will be delivered before the opening of Allocation Round 9.

As the UK transitions to clean power, net zero and to support the country’s energy security, the government is clear that oil and gas will remain a part of our energy mix for decades to come. Therefore, the government is continuing to take a pragmatic approach to the North Sea – providing stability, supporting jobs and ensuring the sector continues to make a significant contribution to the UK economy.

Established within the National Wealth Fund (NWF), the Energy Wealth Fund (EWF) will invest in renewable and low-carbon energy infrastructure across the UK, helping to unlock growth and supporting the low-carbon economy. To support this, £2 billion for the EWF will be provided to the NWF. The EWF will be linked to the government’s future revenues from the North Sea, ensuring investment in the energy transition.

The government is legislating for the Oil and Gas Revenue Levy in Finance Bill 2026‑27 to ensure it is ready to take effect immediately after the Energy Profits Levy ends, which will be 1 April 2030 or earlier if the price floor is triggered. This legislation will provide the oil and gas sector with the certainty and predictability it needs to keep investing in the North Sea, while ensuring it pays its fair share of tax on excess revenues in times of unusually high oil and gas prices in future.

DESNZ is reprioritising its budget to contribute towards the Defence Investment Plan. The government is prioritising delivery of mature carbon capture, usage and storage (CCUS) and hydrogen projects at the Teesside, Merseyside and North Wales clusters, maintaining grant funding for the Viking Cluster while exploring progressing projects in development through private investment and government loan or equity investments, subject to approval. This will save £200 million capital grant from CCUS and £500 million from hydrogen. The government will also save £1 billion capital grant from the Warm Homes Plan (WHP). The government remains committed to heat pump deployment and will maintain the Boiler Upgrade Scheme at current funding levels of £400 million in 2027‑28 and rising broadly in line with inflation thereafter. The government has also launched the Warm Homes Loan Scheme to support heat pump and clean technology uptake. The majority of WHP funding for low-income households and social housing, delivered by mayors and councils, is protected. After a £200‑million saving, Great British Energy (GBE) and GBE-N retain £8.3 billion across the spending review period.

The government is actively looking at how loan or equity investments can support the continued development of future CCUS and hydrogen projects this Parliament, including for the Acorn Cluster, while ensuring a return on any investment for taxpayers. Subject to value for money and affordability, up to £300 million may be available for strategically important hydrogen projects. Projects in the Second Hydrogen Allocation Round will also shortly be progressed to the Invite to Offer stage, with funding to be considered as part of the next spending review.

Delivering infrastructure faster and driving down costs

The Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 included reforms to reduce the delay and cost associated with judicial reviews. The changes are beginning to show results, with the judicial review concerning Stonestreet Green Solar concluding in six months, compared with a previous average of 1.4 years.[footnote 129]

The government has made 60% more decisions on major infrastructure projects compared with the same time in the previous Parliament.[footnote 130] In September, the Chancellor set out a wider agenda to reduce administrative friction and get decisions made more quickly. This Budget takes that agenda forward:

  • The government intends to extend the Fingleton Review’s ethos and findings more widely across other infrastructure sectors. As a first step, Rachel Skinner CBE will chair a review of rail infrastructure costs, reporting in six months’ time. Separately, building on the Review’s recommendation to indemnify nuclear developers, the government is exploring offering indemnities to developers of other critical projects.
  • The government will bring forward legislation at the earliest opportunity to reduce the risk that legal challenges leave essential projects in limbo. This will let Parliament designate and authorise the country’s most critical infrastructure projects and will help ensure legal challenges are raised and resolved earlier.
  • The government will seek to repeal unnecessary duties to consult, moving away from habitual, box-ticking consultation towards more participatory policymaking.

The government will publish an updated Infrastructure Pipeline before the end of the year, giving investors, industry and the supply chain greater certainty on the UK’s infrastructure programmes, projects, and funds. It will set out over £750 billion of planned investment over 10 years and an expected workforce requirement of over 650,000 people, helping industry plan.[footnote 131]

Within the business rates system, exceptional increases in rateable values can create particular challenges for strategically important infrastructure investment with long-term horizons. The government will legislate to provide further support for those most acutely affected, such as airports, once the current transitional relief package expires.

Box 4.A: Building more homes

The UK has around 4.3 million fewer homes than it would have if its housing stock per person matched its European comparators.[footnote 132] Despite significant progress on planning, the cost of building a home is at a record high, both due to underlying inflation of materials and labour costs, and increased burdens due to regulation and policy costs.

The government has already taken bold steps to boost housebuilding, including substantial pro-growth reform of the planning system, improving the performance of the Building Safety Regulator, and speeding up planning decision making. To provide further certainty for house builders, the government will not make major changes to building regulations for the remainder of this Parliament – except to continue improving building safety, including implementing the recommendations from the Grenfell Inquiry. In addition, the government will continue to consider how amendments to regulations could support development by being more proportionate. This will give industry and councils greater confidence to invest, build, and deliver homes.

The government will also introduce an exemption from Biodiversity Net Gain requirements for residential brownfield developments on sites up to 1.5 hectares, supporting its ambitions for brownfield land to be the first port of call for development. This will make it cheaper and simpler to build both council and private houses.

As set out in Chapter 5 – the government is also announcing new steps on council housebuilding and home ownership which will drive additional supply.

Mobilising private finance through strategic public investment

Over this Parliament, the government has already increased the firepower of our Public Financial Institutions (PuFIns) from £106.8 billion to £208.9 billion. The National Wealth Fund (NWF) has committed £10.9 billion to date, mobilising £21 billion of private finance and creating or supporting 83,000 jobs.[footnote 133] From inception through to the end of 2025‑26, the British Business Bank (BBB) has deployed £9 billion of public funding, mobilising an additional £23 billion of private sector capital and guaranteeing £16 billion of lending. More than 260,000 businesses have benefitted from this finance.

Building on the PuFIns’ success in delivering investment across the UK, the government is going further by recapitalising the NWF and BBB with an additional £20.4 billion – taking the overall capitalisation of our PuFIns to £229.3 billion.

The NWF will be provided with an additional £15.4 billion of capital to support growth across the UK, including £2 billion for the Energy Wealth Fund. This will take NWF’s overall capitalisation from £27.8 billion to £43.2 billion. The additional capital is expected to create or support 100,000 jobs.[footnote 134] This will enable the NWF to commit to an extra £15.4 billion of investment and lending over the scorecard period, with businesses and projects drawing down this funding over a longer timeframe.

The NWF will work with the Office for Investment (OfI) to jointly deliver the Strategic Sites Accelerator (SSA), deploying a new concessional finance offer where needed. The SSA will mobilise around £700 million between the NWF and OfI to support reindustrialisation through the development of strategic investment sites.

The BBB will be provided with an additional £5 billion of capacity, taking its total financial capacity to £30.6 billion. This will enable it to deliver the £6.5 billion expansion of the Growth Guarantee Scheme and deliver £1.4 billion in new investment commitments in commercial equity, £165 million in funding for community lenders across the UK, and £450 million to launch a new venture debt product. Together, these three measures are expected to create or support more than 40,000 jobs over their lifetime.[footnote 135]

A new UK Export Finance (UKEF) guarantee jointly delivered with the BBB will widen access to finance for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) that export or intend to export when launched in 2027. UKEF will also make changes to the General Export Facility – a working capital guarantee – widening eligibility to include new exporters and making it quicker for lenders to access guarantees of up to £15 million.

UKEF’s new Flexible Finance pilot will provide up to £5 billion of guarantees, covering up to 80% of eligible commercial loans to selected overseas buyers and giving them greater flexibility to procure from UK suppliers.

PuFIn Financial Transactions are governed by the Treasury’s Financial Transaction Control Framework (FTCF). It ensures the use of Financial Transactions (FTs) is fiscally sustainable and that debt, defined as Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities or net financial debt, does not rise over time. PuFIns also have investment principles to ensure their investments deliver strong value for money.

Under the FTCF, the Treasury expects PuFIns to deliver a return above gilts over time, or to be transparently subsidised through government grant funding where they target a return below gilts.

Lowering the cost of business through more proportionate regulation

The government is committed to cutting the administrative burden of regulation for business by 25% by the end of the Parliament. Achieving the target will save £5.6 billion per annum in administrative costs, freeing up 280 million working hours to spend on growth, innovation and job creation.[footnote 136] The government is on track to deliver the target, with over £2 billion of net progress secured.[footnote 137]

At this Budget, the government has identified up to an estimated £640 million per annum of new gross administrative savings for business, including:[footnote 138]

  • Up to £290 million per annum from ongoing reforms to create a more proportionate company reporting framework.
  • An estimated £116 million per annum through delivering the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government’s (MHCLG) Home Buying and Selling Roadmap.
  • An estimated £105 million per annum from the Financial Conduct Authority’s work to develop a single flexible reporting framework for UK fund managers.

The government is establishing a new Better Regulation Executive (BRE), which will set the direction and drive implementation of the government’s vision for a streamlined and proportionate regulatory system that better enables growth, investment and innovation, and frees up public sector workers to focus on the front line.

The BRE will be a joint unit between HM Treasury and the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, will be overseen by a Ministerial Oversight Group including the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the First Secretary of State, and the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. A Chair will be appointed shortly. The BRE will work in close partnership with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade.

Box 4.B: Regulatory innovation

To enable growth and investment, while at the same time protecting consumers, the regulatory system needs to keep pace with innovation. The Regulation for Growth Bill will establish new cross-economy powers so businesses can safely test, refine, and scale innovative products and approaches faster.

The new powers will allow existing rules to be temporarily adapted, under strict controls and safeguards, to test new technologies and approaches. If a trial proves safe and effective, the powers will allow a route to permanence for the regulatory changes. Regional leaders will have an influential role in shaping and directing those trials and ensuring they reflect local growth priorities. The Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade will set out further details shortly.

The government is developing a pipeline of potential use cases, ready to deploy once the new powers are in place. In addition to those outlined in July, further potential use cases include:[footnote 139]

  • Enabling innovative defence capabilities – creating simpler ways to ensure autonomous systems can be developed in the UK, working through a newly-established, Ministry of Defence-led drone regulation unit.
  • Supporting high streets to thrive – ensuring the licensing system can operate more proportionately and consistently, for example by allowing councils to test making it easier for pubs, bars and restaurants to make better use of outdoor space.
  • Optimising environmental regulation – exploring testing more efficient approaches to the delivery of environmental regulation and the management of rural land and natural resources to reduce administrative burdens while maintaining environmental protections and standards.

5.5 Growth in more places

In recent decades, the UK has become one of the most regionally unequal advanced economies.[footnote 140] Concentration of economic activity in London and the South East has pushed up housing costs, acting as a drag on living standards, and seen other regions underperform their potential. This has gone hand-in-hand with the centralisation of government decision making.

In most major economies, power and resources are much less centralised, with strong local institutions invested in their place and empowered to get on and deliver.[footnote 141] This Budget takes decisive steps to change this current concentration of economic activity and to back growth in every postcode.

The government will:

  • Empower local leaders who are best placed to drive better decisions in their area.
  • Back national and local sectoral strengths to drive reindustrialisation across the UK.
  • Unlock the productivity potential of major city regions and growth corridors.

Empowering places

This Budget takes significant steps on English devolution. The Rewiring the State Delivery Plan will be published before the end of the year and will set out further details.

Local leaders need genuine control over resources, the certainty to plan beyond annual funding cycles, and the flexibility to be able to invest in their economies.

The Fiscal Devolution Roadmap outlines a new funding model for regional and local government. This includes income tax assignment for all Mayors beginning in 2028; increased business rates retention, with Mayors retaining a 20% share of locally retained business rates from next year, and with local and regional government retaining 100% of business rates income by the end of the decade; and plans to legislate for all Strategic Authorities to have the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. Fiscal devolution baselines will be set at the spending review in 2027.

The government is setting out its intention to take forward the first wave of new Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) Business Rates Retention Zones in Greater Manchester, East Midlands, Hull and East Yorkshire, Liverpool City Region, Tees Valley, West of England, North East, and York and North Yorkshire Strategic Authorities and the Greater London Authority, subject to Full Business Case approval and legislation. This will unlock commercial development, support the delivery of Mayors’ Local Growth Plans and projects in areas such as Stratford, Derby and Selby, and enable more tax to be spent where it is raised.

The government will continue to work with Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority to agree a zone to support the Biomedical campus and development in Cambridgeshire from 2028. The government remains open to receiving proposals from Mayoral Strategic Authorities who did not put one forward as part of this wave.

The government intends to provide an opportunity to put forward Business Rate Retention Zone proposals to areas with Foundation Strategic Authorities and local authority areas that come forward for devolution as they work through the process of establishing Strategic Authorities. This will be subject to proposals demonstrating exceptional economic additionality. The government will set out details shortly on how this offer can be taken up.

The government will support the rollout of Good Growth Funds across England. Alongside fiscal devolution, this will enable local leaders to bring together different funding tools into a single local investment approach and align Public Financial Institutions, pension funds and private capital behind local growth priorities to invest in catalytic regeneration and development. The government is determined to help local leaders deliver good growth immediately, and today the government is confirming £285 million in 2027-28, comprising £165 million to support places with a mayor in place in 2027 to establish Good Growth Funds and £120 million of incubator capital funding for areas transitioning towards a devolution deal or strategic authority status – extending funding to areas that did not receive the City Densification Fund announced earlier in the year. Funding for MSAs will be incorporated into fiscal devolution baselines, which will be set at the next spending review alongside the transfer of responsibilities from departments, so MSAs can have certainty that the funding provided in 2027-28 will continue into future years.

To support Good Growth Funds, the government is also confirming a bespoke borrowing facility of £1.5 billion for MSAs. This facility will be operational by April 2028, allowing MSAs to build up the capability necessary to operate devolved loan funding. The government will work in partnership with MSAs to develop this borrowing facility, and this will include mechanisms to enable concessional lending to support a broad range of locally determined projects. The devolved governments will receive additional funding through the Barnett formula. Principles of the borrowing facility are set out in the devolved chapter of the FT Control Framework. To enable those MSAs with City Densification Funds to keep delivering on local growth priorities quickly, the government is working with them to finalise the funding terms for the City Investment Funds.

The true benefits of devolution cannot be felt without building strong local institutions. The government has committed to delivering a plan to support the sustainability of strategic and local authorities, recognising they are the foundation of the public services that neighbourhoods and communities rely on, and are essential to its wider ambition to rewire the state. The Budget supports these ambitions by:

  • Delivering a growth package for English Local Authorities and Foundation Strategic Authorities that provides councils with greater financial flexibility and stability, increased local discretion and targeted support for investment and development. The government intends for local and regional government to retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade in place of grants from central government, with the share retained by local authorities increasing to at least 70%. This process will begin with MSAs receiving a 20% share of business rates from April 2027. The government will seek views from the sector on how best to achieve 100% business rates retention. These measures will strengthen local growth incentives and support councils to play a more active role in driving economic growth.
  • Supporting these efforts through the High Streets Strategy. Through the new £125 million Derelict Buildings Fund, the government will support English local authorities to transform buildings into what their communities need, from health centres to civic spaces. An additional £65 million will be invested in helping communities across England rescue and revamp beloved buildings and businesses at risk of closure, like pubs and sports clubs.
  • Providing an uplift to capacity and capability funding directly to Strategic Authorities, worth £150 million in 2027-28. This will support local leaders to continue building the resource and expertise required to manage greater powers, fiscal devolution and Good Growth Funds. Capacity and capability funding for Strategic Authorities will be incorporated into fiscal devolution baselines, which will be set at the spending review in 2027 alongside the transfer of responsibilities from departments so Strategic Authorities can have certainty that the funding provided in 2027-28 will continue in future years. The government will undertake a fuller assessment of Strategic Authority capacity and capability to inform funding baselines at the spending review in 2027. It has also published today an overview of how Public Financial Institutions and other investment bodies can support local places with investment capacity and capability, with a view of consolidating and simplifying this support over time.

This new model of government will be structurally embedded for the long term, and local people will be given the power to hold local leaders to account. The government is now in the final stages of agreeing 10 new devolution agreements:

  • Mayoral Strategic Authorities for Devon, Plymouth and Torbay; Hertfordshire; Lancashire; Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland; Stoke and Staffordshire; Surrey; Thames Valley (Oxfordshire, Berkshire and Swindon); and Wessex.
  • A Strategic Authority for Kent and Medway which will be Mayoral if the area’s Local Government Reorganisation outcome is compatible with this and Foundation if not.
  • A single Foundation Strategic Authority for Cornwall.

This will mean that over 90% of England’s population will have a devolution agreement in place. These areas will join Cheshire & Warrington, Cumbria, Sussex & Brighton, Hampshire & the Solent, Greater Essex, and Norfolk & Suffolk at the forefront of the government’s ambitious programme to expand devolution, and we will now work with the relevant councils to launch local consultations with key stakeholders, as the key next step in establishing new Strategic Authorities. We will continue working with all remaining areas – including places like Bedford, Central Bedfordshire, Luton, and Milton Keynes, where there is broad agreement but not yet local consensus – to agree a Strategic Authority as soon as possible, with the aim of achieving full devolution coverage by the end of 2028.

Through its Priority Projects Programme, No10 North will help places unlock their potential by joining up plans and agencies across government, business and academia. By partnering with local leaders, the programme puts local priorities at the heart of the government’s efforts to overcome barriers to growth. Many of the areas above are already developing strategies for growth and investment. The government will extend the Priority Projects Programme to these areas and those electing mayors for the first time in 2027 and 2028, helping them identify the projects that matter most to their economies and coordinate government support to drive delivery, including through the Prime Minister’s Situation Room. This will include support to develop strong business cases where required.

No10 North, alongside MHCLG, will also work with local leaders in places that are yet to come forward for a Strategic Authority, with a particular emphasis on supporting these places to find local consensus so that they can benefit from devolution as quickly as possible. No10 North will also help these places to develop shared growth priorities, identify joint projects, and strengthen the foundations for future devolution. Across every area, the government will encourage projects linked to local Industrial Strategy sectoral strengths and combine them with wider action on infrastructure, skills and investment needed to strengthen clusters across the UK.

The Budget will also accelerate delivery of priority projects in West Yorkshire Combined Authority, West of England Combined Authority, South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority (SYMCA), subject to business cases, by funding £28 million to expand the Leeds College of Building to accommodate over 2,000 new learners; crowd in significant private investment to Bristol Temple Quarter; and match fund specialist innovation space for early stage companies in the Don Valley corridor.

The government welcomes SYMCA’s agreement with Doncaster Sheffield Airport’s leadership to bring the airport into public ownership, and stands ready to work with SYMCA as they progress plans to restart flights from the airport.

The government reiterates its support for new mass transit systems as the Mass Transit Taskforce concludes its consultation phase. Taking into account the Taskforce’s conclusions, the government will explore ways to unlock these schemes, including new powers to help mayors.

The government will continue to support local projects across the UK through a new £80‑million Local Renewal Fund to support job creation, invest in local economic regeneration, maintain heritage assets and back local initiatives that boost economic growth.

Backing local strengths to reindustrialise the UK

Box 4.C: Reindustrialisation

Reindustrialisation is central to the government’s plan to build a stronger, fairer, and more resilient economy. With the Modern Industrial Strategy at its heart, reindustrialisation will support good growth in every postcode. It will ensure the UK is the best place for workers to build a career in thriving, globally competitive industries and for businesses, including the next generation of large, innovative British firms, to invest and grow.

Reindustrialisation means more good jobs around the country. It means more towns and cities making and innovating and having a stronger role in the national economy. It means more British-owned businesses exporting goods and services. The government will co-develop our approach with local leaders, business and investors, academia and trade unions over the months and years ahead.

The UK must look forward and champion our growth-driving sectors and the places that host them, from advanced manufacturing, defence, digital and technology, and clean energy to life sciences, creative industries and financial and professional business services, and the critical foundational industries that underpin our economic resilience.

Delivering reindustrialisation will not happen overnight. This government is taking decisive steps to boost competitiveness now and for the long term:

  • Devolution and a place-led approach to growth: the government will build new partnerships with local leaders, business and universities in which they are empowered to set their own priorities and identify opportunities. The government will work with them to align Local Growth Plans with our national growth strategy to prioritise where government involvement can have the greatest impact and maximise the agglomeration benefits of clusters. The government’s goal is a globally significant cluster in every nation and region.
  • Prioritising lower energy costs: businesses are held back by slow grid connections and energy costs. This Budget puts the UK on a different path, enabling more businesses in more places to grow.

  • Backing British business with the power of the state by:

  • Being bolder on public procurement across critical sectors, from start‑ups to steel. The government will use public procurement to build resilience and address supply chain vulnerabilities, as already shown with the decision to build three new floating docks for the Royal Navy’s submarine service in British shipyards, directing £6 billion into local economies.
  • Ensuring the UK’s world-class research base can support the development of the companies of the future with £1 billion of UK Research & Innovation (UKRI) investment in innovation clusters across the UK.
  • Confirming the NWF and BBB will deploy an additional £20.4 billion of capital to back UK strategic industries and places.
  • Using the Regulating for Growth Bill to ensure regulation keeps pace with innovation – from new defence capabilities, to innovative medicines and medical devices – and enabling firms to test, refine and scale new technologies faster.
  • Introducing reforms to make the UK’s migration system the most pro‑business in Europe for high-skilled workers.
  • Protecting key supply chains like steel, via trade defence measures, and chemicals through the £350 million Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund.

The government is working with local leaders to support investment in Industrial Strategy sectors. For example, the government is already supporting Team Plymouth and Team Barrow to make the most of generational defence investments that are creating thousands of new jobs. The Plymouth place‑based business case has identified an opportunity to maximise the benefits of defence‑led growth. Team Plymouth will receive £3 million to help those not in education, employment or training (NEETS) get into the growing local defence industry while addressing skilled labour shortages faced by business.

The No10 North Priority Projects Programme will build on this, joining up agencies across government, business and academia and aligning plans with wider action on the infrastructure, skills, and investment needed to strengthen sectoral clusters across the UK.

UKRI is promoting innovation across the UK by focusing £1 billion of investment over the next four years into priority innovation clusters aligned with existing Industrial Strategy clusters, and by devolving Local Innovation Partnerships Fund settlements to Established Mayoral Authorities from 2028. UKRI is supporting university partnerships and promoting research commercialisation through its £19.75 million Collaboration for a Sustainable Future Programme and through £16 million of proof-of-concept funding. To drive regional growth, UKRI will work with organisations in regions across the UK to identify additional Research & Development- (R&D‑) intensive businesses in Industrial Strategy sectors which could act as host organisations on the endorsed funder pathway of the Global Talent visa route by spring 2027.

UKRI is investing in world-leading science and innovation clusters across the UK, including:

  • £424 million to transform the John Innes Centre and the Sainsbury Laboratory at Norwich Research Park into a world-leading national hub for plant and microbial science. This will deliver 4,000 square metres of cutting-edge research and innovation infrastructure.
  • Over £85 million to transform the Offshore Renewable Energy Catapult’s facilities in Blyth into a world-leading hub for testing the next generation of wind turbines, cementing the North East’s position at the vanguard of clean energy innovation.
  • Over £75 million into the CoSTAR network of state-of-the-art labs anchored in Yorkshire, Dundee, Belfast, Buckinghamshire and Surrey – providing both a powerful national infrastructure for the UK Creative Industries while giving local clusters access to the world-class R&D capabilities they need to compete globally.

The government is also announcing three new public-private investments in life sciences, totalling over £1 billion and backed by almost £70 million in grant funding, delivering on the Modern Industrial Strategy and reinforcing the UK’s position as a global leader in life sciences. Convatec will invest over £500 million over the next decade in a new global R&D hub in Manchester, accelerating product evaluation and strengthening its end-to-end UK research and manufacturing capability.[footnote 142] Vertex Pharmaceuticals will invest over £300 million in a new facility in Oxford, accelerating research into creating transformative medicines for people with serious diseases. Kindeva will invest £200 million in Loughborough, strengthening manufacturing of respiratory medicines, including next‑generation low‑emission inhalers.

Aerospace is one of the UK’s greatest manufacturing success stories, with a competitive advantage across prime manufacturers and supply chains. The government is announcing a plan for a multi-decade cooperation agreement with Rolls-Royce starting with co-investment in a joint, 10-year, £2.5‑billion programme for next-generation gas turbine technologies for civil and defence aerospace. The programme will support 3,300 jobs in Rolls-Royce and its partners by the end of 2029, strengthening engineering skills and vital development and testing capabilities in the UK, including in Derby, the Midlands and Bristol.

The programme will unlock further investment from Rolls-Royce over time to advance the development of more efficient and lower-emission propulsion technologies with potential applications across a range of future aircraft. This includes the next generation of narrowbody aircraft and other defence applications, with the potential to create tens of thousands of additional jobs and billions of pounds of further investment across the UK supply chain over subsequent decades.

This is backing British technology, skills and manufacturing capability to underpin the UK’s security and long-term prosperity, and is proof of reindustrialisation in action, driving forward the industrial base that underpins the UK’s success.

The cooperation agreement provides the framework under which any future support will be provided. This has not been contracted and funding is subject to award, negotiations and relevant legal processes.

Giving firms the confidence and security to invest and grow in Britain is a priority for the government. The UK and devolved governments’ consultation on the operation of the Vehicle Emissions Trading Schemes (VETS) Order, known as the Zero Emission Vehicle Mandate, closed on 23 October. The government aims to publish a shared response to the consultation by the end of 2026, with a view to any changes taking effect from the 2027 compliance year.

The government is also supporting UK foundational sectors. The Budget confirms funding for the £350 million Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund announced in May 2026, designed to support strategically important chemicals producers and sites, strengthen critical supply chains and help support thousands of skilled jobs. The fund will be launched by the end of this year.

The government intends to expand the scope of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) to include refined products, subject to consultation on the feasibility and impacts. This could help address carbon-leakage risks for refineries in Pembrokeshire, Cheshire, Hampshire and the Humber, giving British businesses confidence to decarbonise while retaining and renewing high‑value industrial capability.

Unlocking the potential of city regions

The government aims to realise the potential of the UK’s city regions, grow urban agglomerations, better connect surrounding areas into that growth, and build deeper connections into the rest of the country.

This is essential because in most major economies, cities and their surrounding regions are engines of growth. The UK is one of the most urbanised countries in the world – with 60% of the working age population in England living in the 20 largest functional urban areas – but our core cities have trailed the national economy and underperformed by international standards.[footnote 143]

London – The capital remains the driving force of the UK economy and one of the world’s most important cities. 5.6 Backing British business

The UK’s 5.7 million businesses are the drivers of wealth creation in the economy.[footnote 148] Delivering the government’s growth ambitions will require business, academia, local leaders and the public sector to work in lockstep, combining high ambition with close partnership to unlock investment, innovation and growth across the country.

Alongside other steps taken in this Budget, the government is backing British businesses by:

  • Supporting entrepreneurs to start, scale and stay.
  • Improving access to talent.
  • Using public procurement to drive growth and innovation.
  • Promoting international investment and trade.

Supporting entrepreneurs to start, scale and stay

As laid out in the ‘Entrepreneurship in the UK prospectus’, published alongside the Budget, the government’s ambition is to make the UK the best place in the world to start a business, scale it, and stay for the long term.

That is why the government is strengthening the tax environment for founders at every stage of the growth of their businesses, making it one of the most competitive in the world. The government will introduce a new Capital Gains Tax Founders’ Relief from 6 April 2027, offering a reduced 10% Capital Gains Tax rate on up to £10 million of lifetime gains, supporting the talented individuals who take risks to build and scale high-growth, innovative companies in the UK. This will further support those with a track record of creativity and resilience in building successful businesses to deliver even more UK jobs, growth and wider economic benefits in future.

The government’s plan to strengthen the tax environment also includes making R&D tax reliefs easier to access by simplifying administration and improving our venture capital schemes so that founders can raise capital with greater certainty.

The government will enhance our world-leading employee share ownership schemes by launching an expanded EMI2 (formerly CSOP). EMI2 will double the value of tax-advantaged options employees can hold from £60,000 to £120,000 from 6 April 2027, giving scaling businesses a more generous and flexible way to attract and retain talented employees as well as enabling those employees to share in the value they help their companies create.

To support entrepreneurs to take the first steps in starting a small business, the government is also tripling the generosity of the Trading Allowance from £1,000 to £3,000 from 6 April 2027.

The Budget is increasing access to finance for innovative start-ups and scale‑ups through a £5 billion uplift to the British Business Bank’s financial capacity, including £1.4 billion to invest in equity funds backing high-growth businesses and £450 million for a new venture debt product providing non-dilutive finance to innovative firms.

The Mansion House Accord should unlock around £25 billion of additional investment into UK private markets.[footnote 149] The government will work with pension providers, asset managers and the wider industry to build on existing commitments, accelerate the deployment of capital into innovative, scaling businesses, and support the UK’s scale-up ecosystem.

At Budget 2025, the government announced UK Listings Relief to incentivise firms to stay and list in the UK, and confirmed it would continue to evaluate the wider impacts of Stamp Taxes on Shares (STS). The government has heard industry feedback that cutting STS could boost UK capital market competitiveness. The government recognises the potential economic benefits of such a change and will keep this under review as part of the government’s wider focus on supporting UK capital markets, having appropriate regard to the fiscal implications of any changes.

Box 4.E: Partnering with the financial services sector to drive growth

A competitive financial services sector enables growth across the UK, financing firms to start, scale, invest and create jobs. The government is delivering an ambitious 10-year Financial Services Growth and Competitiveness Strategy as part of our Modern Industrial Strategy.

The Chancellor today set out his priorities for the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee in his annual remit letter. The Chancellor welcomed the Committee’s conclusions from its review of bank capital requirements to date, including proposed reforms to the leverage ratio and releasability of capital buffers, and asked for these changes to be delivered quickly. The Chancellor also set out his expectation that the next stage of the review should deliver further proposals to ensure the UK’s bank capital framework is internationally competitive, promotes competition, and supports investment in the economy.

The government is also:

  • Modernising how the sector is regulated through the Financial Services and Markets Bill, including reducing the overall burden of the Senior Managers and Certification Regime by 50%.
  • Working with industry and regulators to make the UK the global destination of choice for next-generation financial markets by 2030. The government will also explore the use of HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data in Open Finance, working with regulators and industry partners to test feasibility, while safeguarding the integrity of the tax administration system.
  • Building the talent base that will underpin the UK’s future success. The government will shortly commission Progress Together to examine how career progression, socio-economic background and regional factors affect retention, to report by the Chancellor’s Mansion House speech in 2027.

Too often, a major barrier to new entrants is a lack of support with personal finances, with young entrepreneurs not always being those with the best ideas, but those with access to family support. The government will shortly pilot a Young Entrepreneurs Allowance, providing successful applicants with support towards their living costs during the first year of their business.

The government is bringing its support for high-growth, innovative businesses together through Scale UK, providing a clearer ‘no wrong door’ route to access existing programmes. This will include a new regional pilot, Scale UK – Connect, providing tailored support to 200 high-growth firms across the UK, with expert advice, investor connections and international opportunities.

Women make up just 21% of the digital workforce.[footnote 150] Led by the Women in Tech Taskforce, new voluntary Tech Forward and Inclusive Investment Standards will help to tackle the barriers women face raising capital and working in the technology sector. The government will also launch its scale-up women’s programme to support women founders across the UK. This builds on the Investing in Women Code and Invest in Women Taskforce initiatives.

The BBB has developed a pipeline of commitments to women-led funds of over £100 million, including first-time fund managers identified through Investor Pathways Capital, which tackles the barriers faced in accessing finance and investor networks.

Access to talent

Non-compete clauses in employment contracts affect millions of people, from tech employees to care workers. Workers trapped by these clauses are often held back and unpaid, missing out on opportunities and forced to spend time out of their chosen field, sometimes threatening their financial security. That also stunts innovation and inhibits the energy and dynamism our economy needs.

This Budget confirms that the government will legislate to make sure that non-compete clauses will no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising startups and scaling firms, and ensure that workers in the everyday economy are not prevented from moving jobs. These reforms will apply across the whole of the economy.

The government will also consult shortly to understand the wider use of restrictive practices. The government is keen to work with industry to ensure the action it takes is proportionate, evidence-based, and supports both the dynamism of the UK economy and protection of intellectual property.

The government will then set out a detailed position on all these issues in early 2027 in advance of legislating.

To ensure the immigration system supports a dynamic labour market and innovative firms, the government will deliver the most pro-business migration system in Europe for high-skill workers. The government has tightened the immigration system for low and medium-skill individuals while improving the offer to international talent. Since Budget 2025, the Global Talent visa-endorsed funder pathway has been expanded, giving more than 100 R&D-intensive businesses the ability to support the world’s best scientists and engineers to come to work in UK industry. To go further in attracting the world’s best graduates, the government will expand the High Potential Individual visa to support applicants with eligible qualifications from the top 150 of the world’s best institutions, with a proportional increase to the cap under the scheme. The government will also increase the duration of the Graduate visa to two years for graduates from high compliance universities where there are strong labour market outcomes.

The government is making the visa system work for all regions of the UK. By implementing changes to minimum salary requirements, the government will ensure that visa criteria better reflect labour market conditions across the UK, supporting employers across the entire country. The government will also work towards allowing the highest skilled workers to access a visa curtailment period of up to six months, allowing these highly skilled sponsored workers longer to find a new job. This will enable employers to locate and bring on board high-skill employees before they have to leave the country.

The government is committed to the UK being a leading destination for global talent and responding where issues emerge, which is why it has worked with the Global Talent Taskforce to identify and resolve barriers for those looking to move here. The government is taking action in this Budget to address the unavailability of double tax relief for some UK residents investing through US limited liability companies and make it easier for people with existing trusts to move to the UK. In line with that, and supported by emerging evidence next year, the government will continue to assess whether the residence-based regime is striking the right balance between international competitiveness, fairness and support for the public finances – and has shown its willingness to take action to ensure that balance is best achieved.

Using public procurement to back British businesses

The government is using public procurement to back UK industry and support local communities. A new National Procurement Policy Statement to be laid in Parliament in March 2027 will prioritise delivery of high-quality jobs, fair pay and skills opportunities, including pathways for young people.

The government will publish a new definition for a ‘UK supplier’ in public procurement by January 2027, taking action to better understand and track UK suppliers and subcontractors across public supply chains. For too long, broad definitions have allowed companies with little more than a UK post box to be classed as a UK firm. This will help ensure economic resilience in key supply chains, safeguarding UK sovereign capabilities. By maximising the UK’s domestic capabilities, alongside contracting with suppliers from our international allies, the government will ensure that procurement supports communities and that UK public services receive the best solutions on the market.

The government has published new guidance on applying social value in central government procurement. Businesses bidding for major government contracts will be judged on their commitment to creating high-quality jobs, tackling local skills shortages, and supporting young people into work.

The government will make sure that jobs and skills in local communities are at the heart of our procurement model, with a target of at least 3% for apprenticeships on large government infrastructure and construction projects.

The government is using procurement to bolster British industry by proactively shaping strategic markets, including the steel, shipbuilding, AI, and energy infrastructure sectors. For example, to improve pipeline visibility, the National Shipbuilding Office will have oversight of all future civil ship procurement. The Shipbuilding and Maritime Technology Action Plan will set out clear plans for this measure to support the UK shipbuilding industry.

Government procurement will also be used to support innovative and scaling companies. To help this, we intend to appoint an external Chair for the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST)’s Commercial Innovation Hub (CIH). They will use their experience to strengthen the role of the CIH in supporting departments to procure innovative solutions along with departmental Procurement Innovation Champions.

An additional £80 million will support Sovereign AI’s R&D Procurement Scheme to create more opportunities for innovative British AI companies to work directly on some of the government’s most significant challenges across the health and care system and in AI security, assurance and safe adoption, as well as delivering innovative approaches to warfighting.

Building on a £1 billion commitment earlier this year to procure large-scale quantum computers, the government will now go further with a quantum sensing and PNT Procurement Catalyst backed by £138 million from the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) and the Ministry of Defence (MoD). Starting with £30 million from Defence, this investment will create a route for successful capabilities to enter future Defence programmes. The Procurement Catalyst will also fund public service challenges, such as new methods for detecting defects in bridges to reduce delays in the transport system. The Department for Health and Social Care (DHSC) will explore opportunities to support the acceleration of scaling and adoption of quantum technologies to cut NHS waiting lists through more effective health diagnostics.

Promoting international investment and trade

The UK has a long history as an attractive destination for global investors – with the second largest inward stock of foreign direct investment (FDI) in the G7.[footnote 151] The next International Investment Summit will take place in spring 2027 in Newcastle.

The government is supporting businesses in all regions of the UK by striking trade deals across the globe.
