5.7 Building the UK’s AI future

AI is an age-defining general purpose technology, transforming the economy, society and national security. The OECD estimates that AI could add between 0.4 and 1.3 percentage points to annual UK productivity growth over the next decade.[footnote 154] If realised, these productivity gains could significantly raise living standards across the UK.

AI brings risks that must be addressed, including to online safety, cyber security and jobs. The UK must build on its strengths as Europe’s leading AI economy – raising capability and leverage in areas of strategic importance, whilst reducing dependence on other countries. The UK starts from a position of strength with some of the best technology and AI talent globally and a world-leading AI Security Institute (AISI). The government will build capabilities at home and work with international partners to manage the risks of AI.

At this Budget, the government has invested over £700 million to:

  • Strengthen security, resilience and sovereign capability to build public trust.
  • Accelerate productive adoption in businesses, public services and communities across the UK.
  • Launch a new Data Centre Covenant – setting tests for approving new strategic data centres and the contribution these projects must make to the UK, matched by a stronger offer of government support on energy connectivity for the projects that contribute the most to the UK’s objectives.
  • Build British capability in AI hardware, including advanced chip design.

Strengthening security, resilience and sovereign capability

AI offers profound opportunities, but these can only be realised if it is trusted and secure. The risks increase as AI becomes more capable and widely deployed. The government will therefore invest around £500 million to build the secure foundations for an AI-enabled economy.

To strengthen the UK’s AI security, the government will:

  • Strengthen AISI with an additional £120 million to ensure the UK remains at the forefront of understanding AI capabilities and advance the technical best practices for secure AI.
  • Strengthen AI security expertise outside London by establishing a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence in Manchester.

To deliver a step change in UK cyber defence, the government will:

  • Establish a new £70 million National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre at the National Cyber Security Centre to strengthen the UK’s ability to understand and reduce national cyber exposure.
  • Expand the public sector AI defence programme, investing an additional £24 million to systematically harden the public sector technology estate and ensure benefits are felt across local authorities, hospitals and schools.
  • Invest £60 million into the first phase of a national Cyber Shield to develop agentic cyber defence capabilities, in partnership with the UK cyber security industry. This will include a £25 million AI and Cyber Security Challenge Fund to support UK innovation, alongside scoping for a regulatory deployment sandbox to help organisations deploy new technologies.
  • Invest £40 million into a new National Agentic Security Unit to develop new capabilities to detect, investigate and respond to cases of rogue agentic systems. This will integrate monitoring and incident response functions with new operational capabilities.
  • Building on the Law Commission’s product liability consultation, the government will consult next year on how to tackle insecure technology at source and consider where liability for cyber breaches should sit.

The government is launching a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, building on the commitments made in the UK Biological Security Strategy, demonstrating continued UK leadership. This includes:

  • £100 million to establish the AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL), a new organisation to harness AI to protect against emerging biological threats, working with UK Health Security Agency, Animal and Plant Health Agency, and Defence Science and Technology Laboratory. AIBL will be supported by up to £200 million in AI model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic, and partnerships with Google DeepMind and London-based AI life sciences pioneer Basecamp Research.
  • £50.5 million towards cutting-edge bio-surveillance and a £14.5 million initial investment to support proof of concept development of novel medical countermeasures, working in partnership with the UK’s life sciences sector.

In order to strengthen national resilience and support the defence of the UK, MoD is assessing opportunities to increase the UK’s sovereign compute and data centre capacity through its secure estate, including the potential for a facility co-located with existing defence innovation, testing and technology infrastructure. In time, this could also provide scalable, secure access to compute for UK SMEs, supporting the growth of the UK’s Sovereign AI industrial base.

Unlocking the opportunities of AI

With these strong foundations in place, the UK can capture the benefits of AI for economic growth and improved public services.

The Budget therefore confirms:

  • £30 million to pilot local partnerships, starting with West Yorkshire Combined Authority, South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority, and York and North Yorkshire Combined Authority to develop locally led approaches to AI adoption. Building on the experience of Barnsley, the UK’s first Tech Town, these will work across local councils to help small businesses grow, equip people with the right skills, and transform local public services.
  • A £60 million AI Pathfinder Fund to support practical cross-government interventions to respond to emerging barriers and opportunities from the AI transition.
  • An additional £60 million for the Sovereign AI Fund from 2027‑28 to invest directly in promising UK AI companies to support them to scale, succeed and maintain a meaningful presence in the UK. This includes a new focus area: physical AI to build on the UK’s emerging strengths in areas such as robotics, autonomous systems and advanced manufacturing.
  • An additional £23 million for the AI Economics Institute (AIEI), the world’s first government-backed research institution dedicated to analysing the economic impacts of AI. This will examine how AI is affecting productivity, growth, jobs and living standards, including the regional, generational and socio-economic implications.

Delivering the infrastructure needed for AI

The government will ensure the UK has the data centres, energy connections, advanced chips and digital infrastructure needed to support national resilience, and the development and adoption of AI. Building the next generation of data centre capacity in the UK will reduce reliance on infrastructure overseas and ensure British businesses and public services can access the compute they need.

The government is announcing a new deal for the development of data centres, set out in a Data Centre Covenant published today. All data centres are encouraged to meet the tests set out in the Covenant, with data centres required to meet them where they are seeking enhanced government support:

  • Lower electricity bills: pay for their fair share of energy – covering any energy costs they create – so households, communities and other businesses do not pick up the bill. Their growth should help spread energy system costs across a larger base, reducing the share paid by households and businesses. They should also support grid resilience, flexibility and clean power.
  • Invest in improving local communities: communities that host nationally important infrastructure should share directly in the rewards. Strategic data centres should agree a Local Benefit Plan that commits to substantial investment, developed with the local community and linked to the development’s size. This can be spent on local priorities, like transport, parks and town centres.
  • Adhere to the highest environmental standards: protect nature, minimise water use and publish annual energy and water consumption reports. They should also capture the heat they produce for nearby homes, schools, hospitals or businesses wherever practical, rather than letting it go to waste.
  • Create jobs, apprenticeships and drive reindustrialisation: create jobs and invest in paid apprenticeships and training places, supporting young people into the AI, digital and infrastructure jobs of the future. They should also prioritise UK suppliers and technologies and make a meaningful contribution to the development and deployment of British AI hardware.
  • Strengthen Britain’s security: provide secure and reliable access to the compute the UK needs, including for the NHS and other public services. They should work with the relevant national technical authorities, including the National Cyber Security Centre, to enhance resilience against cyber and hybrid threats beyond baseline requirements.

In return, a new Ministerial Control Centre will accelerate time to power for strategic data centres. The government will:

  • Reserve and reallocate connections: using new Planning and Infrastructure Act powers to prioritise strategically important demand projects, including data centres, by reserving future capacity and reallocating capacity released when other projects leave the connections queue.
  • Identify additional capacity: working with NESO and network companies to identify locations where capacity may be available before 2030 and may use Planning and Infrastructure Act powers to access this capacity.
  • Accelerate connections before 2030: where there is a need to go further, using new Planning and Infrastructure Act powers to facilitate the transfer of pre-2030 data centre connections contracts.
  • Enable access to temporary power to bridge the gap to grid connections: by developing a tightly controlled framework to permit on-site generation until a grid connection can be secured. This will only be available for exceptionally strategic projects and only where the measures set out above cannot secure the required capacity in time, and subject to conditions such as ensuring energy security.

The government will set out further details in due course on the definition of strategic data centres and the additional criteria such projects will be expected to meet, including their contribution to local communities and impacts on the UK’s national and energy resilience.

In addition, the government is moving forward with wider reforms to support viable data centre projects to build faster and with more certainty while meeting expectations to support sustainable growth, protect communities, and conserve resources. This includes publishing a draft Data Centre National Policy Statement for consultation, which sets out the decision-making framework for data centre projects seeking development consent through the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project regime. Further detail is set out in the published Covenant.

The government is backing UK AI hardware through an advanced market commitment to bring British chips into public compute. A further £20 million will support reindustrialisation and jobs in AI hardware, including a UK advanced Chip Design Academy led by the University of Edinburgh, linking academic chip research to commercial silicon manufacturing.

The government will work with the Public Financial Institutions and Sovereign AI to provide a stronger and more coordinated financing and funding offer for strategically important UK AI hardware companies. This will give businesses a clearer route to accessing support, which could include a combination of public finance products, alongside bespoke financing solutions where needed. A referral approach will ensure businesses can navigate to the best solution, regardless of which institution they contact first.

6. Hope for the future

The government’s decisions at this Budget pave the way for the decade ahead. Fiscal responsibility underpins its promises and commitments; adhering to the fiscal rules enables the government to sustain the highest public investment in over four decades and target spending on priorities, while easing pressures on families and businesses. Strong public finances and stability create room to plan for a more hopeful decade. The government will outline its vision and next steps in its 10 Year Plan, ahead of the next spending review. The next spending review will take place in 2027.

The government is prioritising housing investment to support families to thrive with a secure place to live. It is sustaining public services and communities, with targeted investment at this Budget that gives support to individuals and families, creating opportunities and hope for the future. The government is committed to reforming the welfare system, prioritising the support people need to overcome barriers to work and participate in society, whilst putting the State Pension on a sustainable basis for decades to come. The government’s investment in defence and security protects the UK at home and abroad.

6.1 A secure place to live

Having a place to call home is foundational. It provides safety, stability and security. At this Budget, the government is prioritising housing investment, supporting families across the country to thrive.

The government is providing an additional £1.5 billion to deliver around 10,000 homes in England.[footnote 166] This funding will be prioritised for Social Rent, especially council homes. This takes total investment in the Social and Affordable Homes Programme to more than £40 billion over 10 years.[footnote 167] This funding will be allocated between 2027‑28 to 2030‑31 and will increase over the period to allow councils to build capacity. The government is also:

  • Supporting local authorities to build new council homes by providing a one‑year extension to the preferential rate from the Public Works Loan Board, keeping loans at 40 basis points below the normal rates.
  • Exploring options to establish a greater role for mayors in making decisions about how the public estate is used to unlock growth and deliver public services and housing in their areas. This will be supported by a revised approach to Strategic Asset Management Planning across government, as set out in Chapter 2.
  • Introducing a new VAT relief on land sold to registered social housing providers to expedite the construction of social housing.
  • Taken together, these measures represent progress towards the Prime Minister’s commitment to deliver the biggest boost to council house building since the post-war period, helping more people benefit from a safe and secure home and driving up private sector housebuilding. Next steps will be set out in the 10 Year Plan.

The government is also supporting people without access to the ‘bank of mum and dad’ to buy their own homes. The new £4.7 billion Your First Home scheme will help around 70,000 households in England to take their first step onto the housing ladder and support the delivery of an estimated 20,000 new homes. The scheme will provide 20% equity loans to first-time buyers who would not otherwise be in a position to purchase a residential property. Income caps will be set at £110,000 per household outside London and £140,000 inside London. Price caps will be set based on local authority median prices to ensure support is targeted at those who need it, with inner and outer London caps of £650,000 and £500,000 respectively. The deposit requirement will be set at 2.5%, with a maximum deposit of 15%. People will be able to access equity loans with a five-year interest free period, with a gradual increase after five years. That means those who use the scheme could save hundreds of pounds per month compared with a standard mortgage. Developers will be expected to make a contribution when signing up to the scheme to help cover costs, set on a sliding scale to protect smaller developments. Funding will be capped annually but government will work with developers and lenders to monitor demand.

The scheme will open for pre-registration by the end of December 2026 and full applications from February 2027 with the first loans issued from April 2027. In the near-term, the scheme will be delivered by Homes England drawing on the support, expertise and capitalisation of the National Housing Bank, which will take on responsibility for the scheme in the medium term, subject to the necessary legal and regulatory changes, with a review point next autumn to take stock on progress. To enable this, MHCLG will legislate as soon as Parliamentary time allows to provide an appropriate legislative and regulatory basis.

The £4.7 billion scheme has been funded through reprioritisation of departmental Financial Transactions. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero will reallocate Financial Transactions, including from the Warm Homes Fund, alongside exploring the use of guarantees rather than loans. The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs contribution reflects an updated delivery pathway for the Woodland Carbon Purchase Fund.

To support savers to save for a deposit for their first home, the government will introduce the new First Time Buyer ISA from April 2029. The product will retain the generosity of the Lifetime ISA, allowing contributions of up to £4,000 a year with a 25% government bonus. The bonus will be paid on the value of the account balance when funds are withdrawn for a qualifying first home purchase, up to the value of £450,000, so avoiding the need for any withdrawal charge. The new product will have no upper age restriction.

In recognition that some Lifetime ISA holders may wish to purchase a property above the £450,000 property price cap, the government will from 29 October 2026 allow Lifetime ISA funds to be withdrawn for such purchases which otherwise meet the qualifying rules, with a reduced withdrawal charge of 20%, ensuring the value of individual contributions is protected if the value of the property is above the price cap.

6.2 Public services

The government is committed to ending rough sleeping – there were 4,793 rough sleepers on a single night in autumn 2025.[footnote 168] Since July 2026, £442 million of additional funding has been provided to ensure a route off the street for rough sleepers, alongside targeted wraparound support and longer-term settled accommodation units to help rough sleepers and those with complex needs to stay off the streets long term. This includes funding to support people who are sleeping rough with a route off the streets in time for Christmas. The Budget goes further by announcing an additional £432 million across 2027‑28 and 2028‑29 to extend this off-the-streets offer, ensuring that people sleeping rough have a route off the streets, not just this year but every year.

Homelessness is not confined to rough sleeping, and the government also recognises the significant challenges associated with wider homelessness, including temporary accommodation. The government’s Value for Money Review into homelessness funding is ongoing and will conclude in 2027. Through the review, the government is considering the most effective ways to reduce homelessness, including by looking at temporary accommodation and supported housing delivery models.

The government is committed to halving violence against women and girls within a decade. To support this, the government is prioritising £55 million of funding over two years to accelerate delivery of the Violence Against Women and Girls strategy. This package includes £13 million in 2027‑28 which will strengthen law enforcement activity to improve protection for victims and to identify and disrupt harmful behaviours by perpetrators of abuse. The government is also providing £15 million to the Office for the Impact Economy to work with businesses, investors and philanthropists to mobilise additional funding to support women and girls and underpin the work of the National Taskforce for Tackling Misogyny, chaired by the Minister for Women and Equalities.

This government is supporting the NHS with record day-to-day spending and capital investment over the spending review period. The Budget provides a further £190 million in 2026‑27 for the NHS in England. This funding will support the NHS to manage the additional pressures it is facing over the winter and the rest of this year. This builds on the recent announcement of 25 new or expanded urgent care sites opening in time for winter, which are boosting NHS capacity and easing pressures on accident and emergency services.

The government will invest £100 million to accelerate the adoption of robotically assisted surgery across England. This investment will support an increase in robotic-assisted procedures from 70,000 a year today to 500,000 in 2035, enabling more patients to benefit from less invasive procedures and reducing geographical and gender inequalities. The programme will also improve NHS efficiency and productivity, supported by a world-leading national robotics registry that uses data and AI to improve outcomes and drive innovation in surgical care.

As well as supporting technological innovation, the government is supporting patient access to innovative treatments by removing VAT on medicines donated free of charge. This will help ensure early and expanded access programmes continue, supporting thousands of patients across the UK living with serious illness.[footnote 169]

6.3 Welfare reform

The government inherited a broken welfare system that has been letting too many people down and pushing costs up. The government is reforming it, prioritising the support people need to overcome barriers to work and participate in society, whilst putting the State Pension on a sustainable basis for decades to come. This is the best way to bring down the welfare bill in a sustainable and fair way.

The government has already acted:

  • Rebalancing Universal Credit to tackle the incentive for people to be labelled as too sick to work.
  • Increasing face-to-face assessments for health and disability benefits. The government has more than doubled face-to-face assessment rates since July 2024.[footnote 170]
  • Reforming Motability, with tax breaks restricted to save over £1 billion over the next five years, and Motability Operations removing luxury vehicles from the scheme.
  • Committed to stopping claims management companies from charging to help people to claim benefits, helping to reduce inaccurate claims and supporting vulnerable people.
  • Doubling down on tackling welfare fraud, with new measures expected to save an additional £1.4 billion over the forecast, bringing total savings from fraud and error to over £20 billion over the forecast.
  • Removing entitlement to Universal Credit, Pension Credit and Employment and Support Allowance from offenders detained in hospital that are convicted of the most serious violent and sexual offences.
  • Reducing the financial cliff edge for claimants in supported housing and temporary accommodation, to ensure that work pays.
  • The government is committed to further reforming the welfare system so that it proactively supports those in need, while supporting those who can work into work to bring down the welfare bill in a sustainable and fair way.
  • There are nearly one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (NEETs).[footnote 171] The current welfare system is failing too many, providing cash payments but not the support needed to help young people achieve their potential. Alan Milburn is right to say in his interim report into Young People and Work that “the welfare system should be more than a safety net. It should be a springboard.”[footnote 172] An entirely new approach is needed.
  • The government also takes seriously the conclusion of the interim report of the Timms Review, that Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is “no longer fit for purpose” and has failed to keep pace with how disability, health and work have changed.[footnote 173] This is not good enough when disability can affect anyone at any stage in their lives and almost one in four of the working-age population is classed as disabled.[footnote 174] Following the final report of the Timms Review, the government will bring forward changes to how it supports people with disabilities and health conditions.
  • The government looks forward to the final reports of the Milburn and Timms reviews, and this Budget confirms that the government will set out its response before the end of this year. A White Paper will follow early in 2027 ahead of legislation later that year.
  • This Budget confirms funding to provide new opportunities for young people, including through:
  • The Youth Employment and Skills Package, which in Spring 2026 announced: the £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant for businesses hiring eligible young unemployed people, an extension of the Jobs Guarantee to those aged 22 to 24, and a £2,000 apprenticeship hiring payment for new young apprentices taken on by non-levy paying employers (typically small and medium-sized enterprises) in England.
  • £100 million over two years to expand local apprenticeship services so that all current mayors are able to deliver tailored local support that helps young people access apprenticeships and supports employers to create apprenticeship opportunities.

Alongside reform of working-age welfare, the government has announced plans to put the State Pension on a sustainable footing for the decades ahead, giving people confidence that a rising State Pension will be there for them when they retire. In line with the government’s commitment to the Triple Lock throughout this Parliament, the State Pension will continue to rise by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth each year through to April 2029. This is set to see the annual rate of the full new State Pension increase by more than £2,000 over the course of the Parliament, taking the State Pension to a record high relative to earnings. The government is committed to delivering a sustainable State Pension system that people can trust will rise every year and be available for current and future pensioners. That is why the government is making those gains permanent by adjusting the Triple Lock from April 2030 so that the State Pension rises each year by the highest of 2.5%, inflation, or the amount required to maintain its value relative to earnings as reached in April 2029.

This adjustment will generate significant savings to help build up a high-quality, preventative National Care Service in England that will provide older people with personal care free at the point of use. To help prepare for these changes in the next Parliament, the Prime Minister has agreed with Baroness Casey that her Independent Commission on Adult Social Care will now report in 2027.

This is a new settlement for older generations. A sustainable footing for the State Pension will ensure it remains a cornerstone of retirement incomes for future generations. Alongside this, the Pensions Commission’s final report will be published in February next year and recommend steps to ensure the private pensions system delivers retirement outcomes that are adequate, fair and sustainable.

It removes the ‘ratchet’ effect, whereby the State Pension rises ever higher relative to earnings. Taken together, this is a comprehensive reform strategy for the UK’s social security system. It rewires the welfare state, prioritising not just cash payments but the support, care and opportunities that people need at all stages of their lives, whether struggling to get established in the world of work or living with dementia. It is through structural reforms to social security – rather than crude cuts – that the government will bring the welfare bill down.

6.4 National security

The first duty of government is to defend the nation and deter our adversaries. Russian aggression, conflict in the Middle East and rapidly changing technology demand even greater urgency in strengthening the UK’s armed forces, alliances, and defence industrial base. The government is prepared to take the strong decisions to make the UK more ready, secure and resilient.

The government has driven the highest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War and is fully funding the Defence Investment Plan at this Budget by reprioritising public spending. This will strengthen front-line military capability while creating skilled jobs, supporting British businesses and expanding growth and opportunity across the UK. Since the Defence Investment Plan was published, the Ministry of Defence has made significant new investments, signing around 370 new contracts worth over £2.7 billion. That includes:

  • Announcing £300 million of investment in the UK’s new Collaborative Combat Air programme, StormFighter, which will operate with crewed platforms like the Typhoon. This will coincide with broader investment of £5 billion on advanced uncrewed systems over the rest of this Parliament.
  • Launching the capital grant window for the Energetic Materials programme, to kickstart production at scale in UK for the first time in decades. This follows seed funding for 24 feasibility studies of new energetics factories, with initial construction nearing completion in the South West and spades in the ground in the Midlands.
  • Investing £400 million to equip the Army with the latest drone technology, bolstering Britain’s defence manufacturing base in South West England, and test, evaluation, and training activity in Wales.

At the spending review next year, the government will also set out the details of how it will meet its NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030. This is necessary for the security of the UK. It presents an opportunity to do things differently, working more closely with the private sector to build defence industry capacity alongside delivering new and innovative defence capability.

To support this, the government is launching a new Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce, charged with maximising the contribution of private and international finance to UK defence, and to further procurement reforms that support innovative financing. The Budget confirms immediate progress in these areas:

  • The government has been developing with partners in the Netherlands, Finland and Poland the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) to aggregate demand and enable joint procurement across partners. This will reduce costs, give industry greater certainty, deliver much better value for money and improve joint NATO capabilities. The government has announced today that the MDM partners will be commencing treaty negotiations, respecting individual members’ national processes, with the aim of having the MDM up and running in 2027.
  • A new commitment for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual use and other sectors that support UK national security, sovereign capability and resilience. This will support investment and lending across the defence supply chain to help strengthen the UK’s defence industrial base.
  • The government will expand the UK’s defence industrial base and develop a pipeline for private finance opportunities – including public private partnerships – where they are value for money, with more detail to be set out in the forthcoming Defence Financing and Investment Strategy.

The government also recognises the nature of threats facing the UK is rapidly changing. The government is investing nearly £500 million to build the security foundations for an AI-enabled economy. The government will continue to draw on all the levers of the state to boost the UK’s military capability, including the contribution of AI, technology and cyber security spending to the NATO mission.

Alongside increased investment, the government is maximising the value of every pound spent by accelerating defence reform, focusing resources on front-line capability rather than back office costs and cutting procurement costs. That includes:

  • Continuing to reform procurement under the new National Armaments Director. That means establishing defined capability portfolios, matching procurement routes to capability, and reducing the time to contract by two‑thirds for major platforms.
  • Accelerating the delivery of cutting-edge innovative technology. UK Defence Innovation – the Ministry of Defence’s innovation agency – was launched last year with a ringfenced budget of £400 million per year, and the government can now confirm Tony Reeves as the new permanent Director General Innovation.
  • Publishing a new Counter Fraud Strategy in November, with investment in fraud and error analytics and closer working with the Public Sector Fraud Authority set to deliver £250 million of benefits.
  • Investing in over £500 million of investments to improve productivity this year alone. That means protecting investment that will modernise the way the Ministry of Defence operates, with around £30 million on new digital tools – including “digital twin capabilities”– and around £29 million on automation and AI.

The government will also make better use of the defence asset base, unlocking Ministry of Defence land for housing and growth while ensuring the estate continues to meet Defence’s needs. The Defence Housing Strategy identified capacity for over 100,000 new homes on defence land. The government is accelerating delivery through:

  • Re-establishing the Defence Housing Tripartite Taskforce, with joint working between the Ministry of Defence, HM Treasury and MHCLG on housing and land release.
  • Setting up the Defence Housing Service to work more closely with local and Mayoral authorities on strategic sites, such as Feltham and Chetwynd Barracks, with military housing as an anchor for the wider development where possible.
  • Signing a new Strategic Partnership Agreement between the Ministry of Defence and Homes England, alongside working with the National Housing Bank to explore approaches to available funding programmes to unlock delivery.
  • Reforming the “Crichel Down” Rules, which slow down release of surplus defence and public sector land and which have not undergone significant change in 20 years with updated Rules to be brought in by spring 2027.

The government will build our defence industrial base, prioritising British firms and workers, as part of a new “Back British” approach for the defence sector. The government will give industry greater certainty to invest by setting out where it will build sovereign capability, partner with allies, buy competitively, and grow the skills, technologies, capacity and supply chains required. This will ensure Britain is the best place to start, grow and sustain a defence company. The Defence Investment Plan will create approximately 60,000 new jobs by 2029‑30 compared with 2023‑24.

6.5 Ukraine

The government is steadfast in supporting Ukraine to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion. This is in the UK’s national interest. A secure and stable Ukraine helps protect European and NATO security, deter future aggression and reduce the wider economic pressures that conflict creates for families and businesses in the United Kingdom.

Russia’s continued attacks are placing growing pressure on Ukraine’s economy, public services and security. Following President Zelensky’s visit and the Prime Minister’s commitment to step up UK government support, the Budget will make available over £10 billion of additional financial support to Ukraine, underlining the UK’s position as a leading partner amidst illegal Russian attacks. This is on top of the UK’s enduring commitment to £3 billion a year of military support for Ukraine until 2030‑31 or for as long as needed. The funding will include:

  • £7 billion of economic support over three years including up to £5.5 billion in loan guarantees through the World Bank. The government is also using the World Bank International Development Association’s crisis facility to mobilise £1.5 billion of development funding to support Ukraine’s recovery.
  • £500 million in additional military support to Ukraine’s air defences this winter. Together with £750 million already committed from the UK’s Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration loan to Ukraine, this takes UK military support provided this year to Ukraine to £4.3 billion.
  • A £3 billion increase in UK Export Finance (UKEF) credit capacity available to Ukraine prioritised for military support, bringing total UKEF cover to £6.5 billion.

The government has committed a further £3 million in 2027‑28 to support Ukrainian efforts to facilitate the tracing, return and reintegration of children forcibly deported by Russia, taking UK funding for this work to £7 million. The government has also confirmed a £17 million grant from Official Development Assistance to fund crucial repairs to the New Safe Confinement at the Chernobyl nuclear plant.

The government will work with international partners to consider all lawful routes to ensure Russia pays and Ukraine gets the financing it needs, building on the success of innovative initiatives like the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration loan which used profits from sanctioned Russian sovereign assets.
