7.3 The economy and the public finances

Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) remit 2026 – The Chancellor has reaffirmed the MPC’s primary objective of maintaining price stability, defined as a 2% CPI inflation target, and its secondary objective of supporting the economic policy of the government.

Financial Policy Committee remit 2026 – The Chancellor has made recommendations to the Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee (FPC) on responsibilities and priorities in relation to the Committee’s primary financial stability objective and secondary objective to support the government’s economic policy.

7.4 Public spending

Administration budgets – Government administration budgets will be reduced by 20% in real terms by 2029-30 compared to 2025-26 saving an additional £595 million in year 2029-30 compared to SR25 plans. £50 million of those savings will be reinvested in a new Civil Service AI transformation fund for AI deployment across the Civil Service to reduce unnecessary administrative burdens and improve outcomes.

Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) winter pressures – The Budget provides £190 million for the NHS in England. This funding will support the NHS to manage the additional pressures it is facing over the winter and the rest of this year.

Independent review of productivity and AI in the NHS – The Chancellor and Health and Social Care Secretary have asked Mark Bailie to lead an independent review on NHS productivity and AI, which will inform the next spending review. Reporting in early 2027, it will focus on the practical opportunities presented by AI and technology to transform services for patients and boost NHS productivity.

Specifying the savings to fund the 2026 police pay award – £150 million of savings from the Afghan Resettlement Programme is being repurposed to support the costs of the 2026 police pay award in England and Wales, as part of the rigorous reprioritisation announced by the Home Office in July.

Welfare: removal of benefit entitlements from serious offenders in hospital – From 6 April 2027, individuals convicted of a number of serious offences who are detained in hospital will no longer be entitled to benefit payments in Great Britain. Overall, this is expected to save around £5 million in 2031-32.

Universal Credit: surplus earnings threshold – The government will maintain the surplus earnings threshold at £2,500 for Universal Credit claimants in Great Britain for a further year until the end of March 2028.

Parental pay: establish a parental allowance for fathers, partners and adopters – The government is extending parental pay to eligible self-employed fathers, partners and adopters in Great Britain from April 2029. Those who are recently employed or unemployed, or with a broken or irregular pattern of employment, and therefore do not qualify for statutory paternity or adoption pay will also benefit providing that they have sufficient work and earnings history.

Carer’s Allowance: introduce a taper on excess earnings – The government is replacing the cliff edge withdrawal of Carer’s Allowance at the Weekly Earnings Limit with a 100% taper on earnings in excess of the limit. The taper is planned to be introduced in 2030-31 and apply in England and Wales.

Help to Save reform – The reformed Help to Save scheme will be introduced in Spring 2028. It will move to a multi-provider model, offering Help to Save accounts from a wider range of savings providers, including some with an established high-street presence.

A change to the tax treatment of the Immigration Skills Charge and Certificate of Sponsorship fees – The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 so that an employer’s payment of an Immigration Skills Charge or Certificate of Sponsorship fee is not treated as a taxable benefit in kind. The change will apply to payments made on or after 28 October 2026.

UK Asset Resolution (UKAR) pension schemes – Continuing progress towards winding down UKAR, the government expects to lay enabling secondary legislation in early 2027, with the transfer of the pension schemes for former Northern Rock and Bradford & Bingley employees to central government to occur by the end of 2027-28.

Ending surplus sharing in coal pension schemes – The government is changing the surplus sharing arrangements in the Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme and British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme, so the members receive 100% of the surpluses generated from the schemes’ performance. The government will work with the trustees toward full transfer of the remaining Guarantor’s Fund.

Asylum accommodation – The government is providing £150 million capital investment in 2027-28 to fund additional large sites to accommodate asylum seekers and facilitate the government’s commitment to end the use of asylum hotels.

DWP fraud and error: increase preventative checks in Pension Credit – The government will provide prompts to Pension Credit claimants to redeclare the correct amount of capital they hold.

DWP fraud and error: invest in 2,000 specialist fraud staff – The government will recruit over 2,000 specialist fraud staff in DWP to prevent fraud in new and existing Universal Credit claims.

DWP fraud and error: clamping down on welfare fraud for those living abroad – The government will strengthen DWP’s ability to identify cases where customers remain abroad longer than benefit rules allow.

DWP fraud and error: Universal Credit advances – The government will restrict access to a repeat New Claimants advance to claimants where previous New Claims Advance debt remains. Appropriate exemptions will be applied to protect those in exceptional circumstances.

Official Development Assistance (ODA) update – The government remains committed to restoring ODA spending to 0.7% of Gross National Income (GNI) as soon as the fiscal circumstances allow. The OBR’s latest forecast shows that the ODA fiscal tests are not due to be met within the Parliament. The government will continue to monitor future forecasts closely and, each year, will review and confirm, in accordance with the International Development (Official Development Assistance Target) Act 2015, whether a return to spending 0.7% of GNI on ODA is possible against the latest fiscal forecast.

7.5 Energy bills

Household Energy Payment: £100 council tax rebate for households in bands A to D – The government will provide a £100 Household Energy Payment for households in bands A to D in England, alongside £100 million of further funding for local authorities to provide targeted support to households acutely impacted by rising energy bills. This will be delivered by local authorities from January 2027.

Abolish gas standing charges – The government has asked Ofgem to abolish gas standing charges on domestic energy bills in Great Britain, aiming for delivery by the end of 2027 or as soon as possible after then. The government is also committing to reform electricity standing charges and will set out details next year.

Debt relief scheme – A strategy to tackle energy debt in Great Britain will be implemented starting this year, including reforms to prevent debt building up, improve repayment and strengthen household support, and a one-off targeted debt relief scheme for eligible households to launch next year.

Gas Shipper Obligation – A new levy on gas bills in Great Britain will no longer be implemented. Instead Hydrogen Allocation Round 1 funding will be met with a £27 million uplift to DESNZ RDEL in 2027-28 and the government will publicly fund any future hydrogen contracts – for example Hydrogen Production Plant 1 – if the government commits to them and subject to value for money.

Cost Control Framework – The government will introduce a new comprehensive Cost Control Framework at the spending review in 2027 that will set budgets for components of energy costs, including policy costs.

Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) Mandate – The government is announcing an intention to publish the UK and devolved governments’ response to the ZEV Mandate Review consultation by the end of 2026, with a view to any changes taking effect from 2027.

Cost of living tariff suspensions package – From 26 November 2026, the government is suspending tariffs on a selection of food products and kerosene heating oil until 31 December 2028, and fertiliser until 31 December 2027.

7.6 Targeted support for businesses and the self‑employed

British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme (BICS) funding – Applications are now open for the scheme, which from 1 April 2027 will exempt eligible businesses in Great Britain from the indirect costs of the Renewables Obligation, Feed in Tariffs and Capacity Market schemes. The government is also providing an additional payment to eligible businesses in 2027 to reflect the support they would have received had the scheme been in place sooner. The Northern Ireland Executive is being funded to deliver a comparable scheme.

Review of duty suspensions due to expire and opening of new window – The government is extending tariff suspensions across chemicals, plastics, hydrogen, automotive, and food and drinks industries that were due to expire in December 2026 and June 2027, until 31 December 2028 and 31 December 2027, respectively. The new window for applications for business suspensions will be open between 11 November and 3 February.

Outcome of 2025-26 business duty suspensions window – The government suspended tariffs on a range of products applied for in 2025-2026 by businesses and other interested parties across the chemicals, plastics, fibres, metals, automotive, and food and drinks industries, from 5 August 2026 until 31 December 2028.

India Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA): reduce tariffs on imports from India – The UK-India CETA entered into force on 15 July 2026. This measure costs the impact of preferential tariff rates on a range of goods including clothing, footwear and food now available to traders under this agreement for imports from India.

Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP): Canada and Mexico ratification of UK membership – Following ratification by Canada and Mexico, the UK’s accession to the CPTPP is now in force with all CPTPP Parties. This measure costs the impact of the preferential tariff rates now available to traders under the agreement for imports from Canada and Mexico.

Regulatory administrative savings – The government has published the detail of up to £640 million of new gross regulatory administrative savings, which contribute towards the government’s target to cut the administrative cost of regulation for businesses by 25%, or £5.6 billion, by the end of the Parliament.

Small Business Regulation Taskforce – The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) has published the government’s response to the Small Business Regulation Taskforce report, confirming the government will take forward the vast majority of its recommendations to reduce regulatory burdens on small businesses.

Regulatory innovation – The government has set out further detail on new cross-economy powers to ensure regulation keeps pace with innovation, including a pipeline of potential use cases the government is preparing to have ready to deploy once the new powers are in place.

Better Regulation Executive – The government is establishing a new Better Regulation Executive, which will set the direction and drive implementation of the government’s vision for a streamlined and proportionate regulatory system that better enables growth, investment and innovation, and frees up public sector workers to focus on the frontline.

7.7 Devolution and regional growth

Publishing the Fiscal Devolution Roadmap – The government is publishing the Fiscal Devolution Roadmap, which sets out its plans to reform the way that regional government is funded. This includes bringing Mayors into the Business Rates Retention system from 2027-28 and providing them with a share of income tax from 2028-29, as well as enabling strategic authorities to introduce visitor levies with local leaders able to set out plans for how revenues will be invested by March 2028.

Confirming progress towards new devolution agreements – The government confirms it is in the final stages of agreeing new devolution agreements with 10 areas. Final arrangements will be confirmed in due course, subject to agreement with local areas.

Increasing Business Rates Retention as part of fiscal devolution – From April 2027, mayors will receive a share of business rates income in exchange for Investment Funds, Mayoral Capacity Funding and Local Growth Funds, alongside a 20% share of growth in their areas on a permanent basis.

Business Rates Retention Zones programme for Mayoral Strategic Authorities – Subject to Full Business Case approval, the government is supporting nine Strategic Authorities by establishing new Business Rates Retention Zones. Within these zones, the relevant billing authorities can retain 100% of business rates growth above an agreed baseline for 25 years, allowing them to invest in local priorities.

Good Growth Funds – The government is supporting Mayors and local leaders in England to establish Good Growth Funds, giving local leaders greater flexibility to invest in local growth priorities with £285 million in transitional seed funding for one year in 2027-28, accompanied by a devolved borrowing facility for MSAs of £1.5 billion from April 2028 to catalyse investment into regional growth priorities. This facility will include a mechanism for subsidised lending.

City Investment Funds – The government announced funding as part of the 2026 Mais lecture, comprising grant, loan and patient capital funding for mayors in Greater London (Housing Accelerator Fund only), Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, the North East, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire and the West Midlands to deliver city densification at a local level.

Capacity and capability funding uplift for strategic authorities – The government is providing an uplift to Mayoral Capacity Funding of £150 million in 2027-28. Funding allocations across strategic authorities will be set out in due course. The government will undertake a fuller assessment of MSA capacity and capability, including accounting for any new responsibilities which are confirmed in the ‘Rewiring the State Delivery Paper’ and consider the results in setting MSA baselines at the spending review in 2027.

Strategic Authority rural proofing guidance– The government is developing, for the first time, new non-statutory guidance with strategic authorities and rural stakeholders to set out expectations for rural proofing at strategic authority level in England. The guidance will be published in early 2027 and help to ensure that devolution works effectively for rural places.

Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) lending limit extension – The government is raising the statutory limit on the total amount of loans that can be issued to local authorities from the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) from £135 billion to £155 billion, with the option to increase it to up to £175 billion in the future via statutory instrument.

Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) debt relief for councils in severe financial distress – The government is providing debt relief totalling £500 million for Woking Borough Council and £200 million for Thurrock Council for debt owed to the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB), to support the councils in their recovery from severe financial distress.

Reindustrialisation strengths – The No10 North Priority Projects Programme will support work to strengthen sectoral clusters across the UK by joining up agencies across government, business and academia and aligning plans with wider action on infrastructure, skills and investment.

Northern Growth Strategy package – The government is recommitting to boosting growth in the North through the Northern Growth Strategy with up to £7.8 million of funding to deliver on the commitment to develop the Northern 500 and backing the next stage of the North’s bid to host the Olympics and Paralympics.

Northern Olympics – The government is funding £7 million to conduct a feasibility study for a potential future bid to host the Olympics and Paralympics in the North of England during the 2040s.

Supporting regional growth priorities – Subject to business cases, the government is providing: i) £3 million for an inactivity pilot to support NEETs into Plymouth’s defence industry, ii) £11 million for the replacement of the Aberavon bridge in Port Talbot, iii) £3 million to provide match funding for specialist innovation space for early-stage companies in the Don Valley Corridor, iv) £10 million to unlock private investment in Bristol Temple Quarter, and v) £15 million to expand the Leeds College of Building campus.

Local Renewal Fund – The government will continue to support local projects across the UK through a new £80 million Local Renewal Fund to invest in local economic regeneration, support job creation, maintain heritage assets and back local initiatives that boost economic growth.

Growth Mission Fund: Stafford – £10 million from the Growth Mission Fund will support the refurbishment of Stafford Market Hall and an SME business incubation hub, subject to final business case.

Growth Mission Fund: Liverpool – £20 million from the Growth Mission Fund will support the restoration and redevelopment of the long-derelict Littlewoods site in Liverpool into a 260,000 square foot creative campus for film, TV, gaming, immersive technology and digital screen industries, subject to final business case.

Growth Mission Fund: Bury – £10 million from the Growth Mission Fund will support local regeneration in Bury focused on the restoration and reactivation of the indoor market building, subject to final business case.

Greater Cambridge Development Corporation government financing pilot – The government will provide repayable finance for infrastructure investments, with an ambition for long-term certainty and flexibility for access to government finance. The pilot could be extended to a development corporation in Oxford, subject to consultation.

Cardiff Parkway station – The government is bringing Cardiff Parkway into DfT’s Rail Enhancements Portfolio and providing £30 million to progress delivery with the Welsh Government and private sector.

Mass Transit Taskforce – The government supports the findings of the Taskforce due at the end of 2026. The government will explore ways to unlock mass transit schemes, including new powers to help mayors.

A66 project start of works – The government will deliver a continuous 50-mile dual carriageway between the M6 (Penrith) and A1(M) (Scotch Corner), starting works from November 2026 and with a revised nine-year delivery schedule.

TransPennine route upgrade – The government has awarded a £1.2 billion contract to Alstom’s Derby Litchurch Lane Works to build 29 new battery-powered trains.

Leeds Existing Station Programme – The government is confirming over £300 million for the Leeds Existing Station Programme (LSEP), set to be delivered by 2030.

London Deal – The government is confirming London transport measures including Greater London Authority’s (GLA) delivery of a Business Rates Retention Zone at Euston; exploratory work with the GLA to aim to enable international rail at Stratford International.

Collaboration for a Sustainable Future – UKRI has committed £19.75 million to support university partnerships that bring together complementary innovation strengths, building on the £4.8 million Cambridge-Manchester Innovation Partnership announced at Spending Review 2025.

Industry investment in life sciences – Convatec will invest over £500 million over the next decade, supported by government grant funding from the Life Sciences Transformational R&D Investment Fund, in a new global R&D hub in Manchester to accelerate evaluation of innovative products and its end-to-end research and manufacturing capability.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals investment – Vertex will invest over £300 million, supported by government grant funding from the Life Sciences Transformational R&D Investment Fund, in a new facility in Oxford to accelerate research into creating transformative medicines for people with serious diseases.

Kindeva investment – Kindeva will invest £200 million, supported by government grant funding from the Life Sciences Innovative Manufacturing Fund, in Loughborough to strengthen manufacturing of respiratory medicines.

Wales M-SParc expansion – The government will provide £2.5 million investment starting from 2026-27 to support expansion of the M-SParc science and innovation park in Anglesey, subject to business case. This will deliver more incubator space and support to SMEs and start-ups in North Wales.

Northern Ireland Investment Summit –The government will provide £1 million to deliver a Northern Ireland Investment Summit to promote investment, showcase opportunities in high-growth sectors, and highlight Northern Ireland’s unique dual market access.

Scotland SEC regeneration (Glasgow) – The government will provide £6 million investment from 2027-28 to fund the creation of a new outdoor events space at the SEC in Glasgow, subject to a business case.

Devolved government Financial Transactions (FT) offer and PuFIn designation – The devolved governments will access a share of the UK government’s FT expansion in AME where they have a public finance institution (PuFIn). The UK government will support the devolved governments in setting up their own PuFIns, should they choose to.

7.8 Public control and leadership

Rail infrastructure cost review – The government will launch a review chaired by Rachel Skinner CBE reporting in six months.

Procurement reform: innovation and procurement – The government intends to appoint an external chair to BIST’s Commercial Innovation Hub to accelerate efforts to drive innovation through public procurement.

Procurement reform– A new National Procurement Policy Statement will be laid in Parliament in March 2027, prioritising delivery of high-quality jobs, fair pay and skills opportunities. The government will publish a new definition for a “UK supplier” in public procurement by January 2027, to get a better understanding of UK suppliers and sub-contractors across public supply chains. The government has published new guidance on applying social value in central government procurement, and is using procurement to proactively shape strategic markets.

Green Book reform – The government is continuing to implement the actions in the Green Book Review 2025 by publishing new guidance on developing place-based business cases, new guidance on developing proportionate business cases, and the government’s response to the independent discount rate review.

Misogyny prevention funding – The government will provide £15 million to the Office for the Impact Economy to work with businesses, investors and philanthropists to mobilise additional funding to support women and girls, and underpin the work of the National Taskforce for Tackling Misogyny, chaired by the Minister for Women and Equalities.

Heathrow expansion – The government will provide an update as soon as possible on its position on a third runway at Heathrow.

Steel tariffs – On 1 July, the government introduced a steel trade measure, cutting the overall quota volume of steel that can enter the UK tariff free by 51% compared with the previous “steel safeguard” and increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate to 50%.

Co-operatives and mutuals – The government has appointed Andrew Pakes MP as Co-operatives and Mutuals Champion to act as a conduit for the co-operatives and mutuals sector within government and identify opportunities to support the sector’s growth.

Drone regulation unit– The government is launching a new Ministry of Defence-led drone regulation unit working across the government, which will take a targeted approach to cutting red tape and create clearer routes for testing uncrewed and autonomous systems.

7.9 Backing business and British Industry

British Business Bank recapitalisation – The British Business Bank’s total financial capacity will be increased by £5 billion, enabling increased commercial equity investment activity, a new venture debt product for innovative firms including defence and dual-use technology companies, and additional support for community lenders across the UK. It also delivers the Growth Guarantee expansion announced at Mansion House.

National Wealth Fund (NWF) recapitalisation – The government will provide the National Wealth Fund with an additional £15.4 billion of capital to continue investing in UK businesses and projects, which includes a £2 billion down payment for the Energy Wealth Fund.

UKRI big bets – UKRI will concentrate £1 billion of investment on “big bets,” channelling funding towards priority clusters across the country, in alignment with the Industrial Strategy sectors.

UK Export Finance ‘flexible finance’ guarantees – UK Export Finance will pilot a new guarantee product to improve the competitiveness of UK exports. Guarantees with more flexible terms will be offered to select overseas buyers who show significant potential to increase their procurement from the UK.

Rolls Royce next-generation gas-turbine technology cooperation agreement – The government is announcing a plan for a multi-decade cooperation agreement with Rolls-Royce starting with co-investment in a joint, 10-year, £2.5 billion programme for next-generation gas turbine technologies for civil and defence aerospace. The cooperation agreement provides the framework under which any future support will be provided. This has not been contracted and funding is subject to award, negotiations and relevant legal processes.

UK Advanced Chip Design – £18 million in funding will be invested to establish a UK Advanced Chip Design Academy led by the University of Edinburgh. This will support advanced semiconductor design capability and skills development in Edinburgh from October 2026 to March 2032.

Women in Tech standards – Two new voluntary industry standards developed by the Women in Tech Taskforce, ‘Tech Forward’ and ‘Inclusive Investment’, will drive more inclusive employment practices in tech and fairer access to investment for female entrepreneurs, supporting women to start and scale businesses and build careers in tech.

Widening SME access to export finance – Small and medium-sized businesses will have greater access to UK Export Finance working capital guarantees with expanded eligibility, faster approvals for larger facilities and a new SME export finance scheme launching in 2027 supporting smaller loans.

Robotic-assisted surgery – The government will invest £100 million of the £300 million NHS Transformation Fund to expand access to robotic-assisted surgery in the NHS across England.

Ceramics Industry Support Scheme – The government is introducing a £120 million Ceramics Industry Support Scheme to support energy efficiency and decarbonisation in the sector. The fund will be launched by the end of this year.

Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund – The government is confirming the £350 million Critical Chemicals Resilience Fund to support strategically important chemicals producers and sites, strengthen critical supply chains and help support thousands of skilled jobs. The fund will be launched by the end of this year.

Reform of non-compete clauses – The government will introduce legislation so that non-compete clauses in employment contracts do not prevent startups and scaling firms from hiring, or workers in the everyday economy from moving jobs. These reforms will apply across the whole economy. The government will consult shortly to understand the wider use of restrictive practices, to ensure that action it takes is proportionate, evidence-based and supportive of both dynamism and intellectual property. The government will set out a detailed position on all of these issues in early 2027, ahead of bringing legislation.

Implementing Migration Advisory Committee (MAC) recommendations on visa salary requirements – The government is implementing MAC recommendations on visa salary requirements from spring 2027. These comprise: reducing occupation-specific minimum salary thresholds from the median to the 25th percentile of wages; uprating the general threshold based on 2026 wage data; annually updating salary thresholds using the latest ONS wage inflation data (ASHE); levelling new entrant discounts into a single figure for those studying, recently graduated, or in professional training; removing the PhD discount.

Extending visa curtailment to six months – The government will allow the highest skilled workers to access a visa curtailment period of up to six months. This will give highly skilled workers longer to find a new job, with the duration varying depending on how long they have worked in their previous, highly-paid job, with implementation in 2027.

Expanding the High Potential Individual visa – The government is expanding the High Potential Individual visa route to the top 150 global institutions. There will be a proportional increase to the cap under this scheme.

Extending the graduate visa from 18 months to two years for eligible universities – The graduate visa duration will be set at two years for individuals who graduate from high-compliance universities where there are strong labour market outcomes.

Strategic Sites Accelerator – The government is announcing the formal launch of the Strategic Sites Accelerator (SSA). The SSA will mobilise around £700 million through the Office for Investment and National Wealth Fund to unlock the development of strategic commercial sites across the UK. The scheme is now open for applications from qualifying sites and is on track to invest in its first sites by the end of March 2027.

7.10 AI

Sovereign AI Fund – The £500 million Sovereign AI Fund (SovAI) will expand its direct investment activity by an additional £60 million between 2027-28 and 2029-30. This will include SovAI investing in a new focus area of Physical and Industrial AI.

AI Pathfinder fund – £60 million of funding will be provided between 2026-27 and 2029-30 on a needs-led basis to test solutions to cross-government barriers and opportunities arising from the AI transition.

Local AI partnerships – The government will provide £15 million funding for Local AI partnerships to pioneer place-based approaches to AI adoption from 2026-27 to 2029-30.

Chancellor’s AI Challenge Prize – A new Chancellor’s AI Challenge Prize will launch as an annual competition focused on a different public service priority each year with funding provided from 2026-27 to 2029-30. The first competition will focus on the NHS, with a top award of up to £2.5 million for the most promising solution to a priority healthcare challenge.

Strengthening the AI Security Institute – The AI Security Institute will receive an additional £120 million of funding over 2026-27 to 2029-30 to strengthen the UK’s frontier AI evaluation and testing capability.

Quantum Sensing procurement commitment – The government is making a new £138 million commitment from existing Budgets to catalyse quantum sensing procurement, led by BIST and including £30 million of co-investment from MoD for military-relevant innovation.

Expansion of Sovereign AI (SovAI) procurement scheme – The government is funding an additional £80 million to support SovAI’s challenge-led R&D procurement scheme. The scheme will back innovative AI companies to develop solutions to challenges including across the health and care system and in AI security, assurance and safe adoption, as well as delivering innovative approaches to warfighting, in addition to those already announced.

National Agentic Security Unit – A new £40 million National Agentic Security Unit will build world-first capabilities to detect and respond to misaligned agentic activity, increasing resilience to agentic incidents.

National Cyber Shield – A new £60 million National Cyber Shield will develop agentic capabilities to automate the UK’s cyber defences, including a £25 million AI and Cyber Security Challenge Fund to foster UK innovation.

National Biosecurity Initiative – The government is investing £100 million between 2027-28 and 2029-30 to establish a new AI Biosecurity Lab which will use advanced AI tools to understand and counter AI-enabled biosecurity threats, and a further £65 million to enhance metagenomic surveillance and partner with industry to develop medical countermeasures.

AI NERV centre – A new £70 million National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre will deploy AI tools to identify cyber vulnerabilities across our critical infrastructure and the wider economy.

Centre for Cyber and AI in Manchester – A new Centre for Cyber and AI Excellence in Manchester is being created to train the next generation of cyber and AI security expertise outside of London.

NI Cyber-AI Hub – The government will provide £7.5 million for Phase 2 of the Centre for Secure Information Technologies Cyber-AI Hub at Queen’s University Belfast, supporting collaboration between academia and cyber security firms to develop AI-enabled security technologies.

Progressing Data Centre Build – The government will launch a new data centre covenant for new strategic data centres and the contribution these projects must make to the UK, matched by a stronger offer of government support on energy connectivity for the projects that contribute the most to the UK’s objectives.

7.11 Housing

Your First Home Scheme – The government is introducing a new £4.7 billion equity loan scheme, supporting 70,000 first-time buyers with up to 20% government equity loans. Participants will benefit from a reduced deposit requirement and a five year interest free period, which will save the typical buyer hundreds of pounds a month.

Social and Affordable Homes Programme uplift – The government is providing further funding of £1.5 billion for the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, taking total capital investment in social and affordable housing to more than £40 billion over 10 years. This will complement the £9.6 billion allocated earlier this year and support delivery of around 10,000 additional homes.

Supported housing licensing scheme – The government is introducing a licensing regime in 2027-28 to enforce national standards for supported housing in England.

Extending council preferential access to the Public Works Loan Board for council housebuilding – The government will extend the preferential Public Works Loan Board rate for a further year, to 2027-28, at 40 basis points below the PWLB normal rate. The rate will continue to remain under review.

Supporting adoption of AI planning tools – To enable adoption of AI planning tools, the government will mandate Local Planning Authorities to digitise and publish key planning documents as open data by the end of 2027, and confirm its commitment to make MHCLG’s PlanAssist frontier AI tool available to all councils in England by the end of 2027, subject to further testing.

Housebuilding regulations – The government will not make major changes to building regulations for the remainder of this Parliament – except to continue improving building safety, including implementing the recommendations from the Grenfell Inquiry. In addition, the government will continue to consider how to amend regulations where doing so would support development, by being more proportionate.

Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) reforms – Residential brownfield developments on sites up to 1.5 hectares in England are being exempted from BNG requirements, reducing costs and ensuring the government’s ‘brownfield-first’ ambitions directly support the delivery of more homes. The full government response to the consultation and impact assessment will be published in due course. This will also set out the timeline for implementing the new exemption. In parallel, BNG will become mandatory for Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects from November 2026, ensuring the country’s largest developments make a strong contribution to nature recovery.

Rough sleeping – Over July and August, the Prime Minister announced £442m of funding to deliver a route off the street to rough sleepers in England before Christmas, alongside longer-term accommodation and intensive support. The government is now announcing additional funding to ensure that people sleeping rough in England have a route off the streets, not just this year, but every year, taking total additional rough sleeping funding to £874m from 2026-27 to 2028-29.

7.12 Public services

Accelerating implementation of the Violence Against Women and Girls Strategy – The government is providing a funding uplift for law enforcement activity and victim support services over the next two years in England and Wales.

Books for children – The government will provide £5 million a year for three years from 2027-28 to increase the provision of books for pre-school children, supporting organisations such as the Dolly Parton Imagination Library and BookTrust.

Higher education franchising reform – From academic year 2028/29, franchised higher education providers in England with 300 or more students will be required to register with the Office for Students for the courses they deliver to be designated for student finance.

School Physical Education (PE) & Sport funding – Funding to the Department for Education will increase by £60 million per year to contribute to the cost of new PE & Sport partnerships, due to be rolled out in England in 2027.

7.13 Young people and labour markets

Youth employment and skills: expanding local apprenticeship services to all current mayors – The government is providing £100 million of funding across 2027-28 and 2028-29 to expand Mayoral Apprenticeship Brokerage Pilots from 7 to 14 Mayoral Strategic Authorities across England. This will enable all current mayors to provide tailored support to young people and employers, particularly SMEs, to create more apprenticeship opportunities.

Young Entrepreneurs Allowance – The government will pilot a Young Entrepreneurs Allowance in England, providing successful applicants with support towards their living costs during the first year of their business.

Apprenticeships and skills: re-establish the Union Learning Fund – The government will re-establish the Union Learning Fund in England. The scheme will have a budget of £15 million per year from 2027-28 to allocate to projects put forward by unions to support learning and training among workers, supporting upskilling to the changing needs of the economy.

National Living Wage and National Minimum Wage – On 1 April 2027, the National Living Wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 per hour; the National Minimum Wage will increase by 3.9% to £11.27 per hour for 18 to 20-year-olds and by 3.9% to £8.31 per hour for 16 to 17-year-olds and eligible apprentices; and the accommodation offset will rise by 3.9% to £11.53 per day.

Requiring apprenticeships in large government construction and infrastructure projects – The government will require at least 3% of the workforces of all construction and infrastructure large government projects to be apprentices.

Support for women-led scale-ups – This new scale-up women’s programme will test how best to overcome barriers to fundraising and investment for women founders, which could include peer learning, investor networks and practical support on finance and governance.

Socio-economic and regional representation in financial services – HM Treasury will commission Progress Together to examine the drivers of workforce and skills attrition in financial services, focusing on how career progression, socio-economic background and regional factors affect retention, to report by the Chancellor’s Mansion House speech in 2027.

Global Talent Visa Expansion – To drive regional R&D-led growth, UKRI will work with organisations in regions across the UK to identify additional R&D-intensive businesses in Industrial Strategy sectors who could act as host organisations on the endorsed funder pathway of the Global Talent visa route by spring 2027.

Erasmus+ – The UK will participate in the Erasmus+ study scheme for 2027, from 1 January 2027. The government is accounting for the student loan impacts at this Budget, as well as providing for delivery costs.

7.14 Defence

NATO defence spending commitments – At the spending review next year, the government will set out the details of how we will meet our NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.

Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce – The government is launching a new taskforce, charged with maximising the contribution of private and international finance to UK defence, and to further procurement reforms that support innovative financing.

Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) – MDM partners, including the UK, will be commencing treaty negotiations, respecting individual members’ national processes, with the aim of having the MDM up and running in 2027.

NWF and BBB defence commitment – The National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion of investment and lending over the next 4 years into defence, dual use, and other sectors that support our national security, sovereign capability and resilience.

Defence private financing – The government will develop a pipeline for private finance opportunities, including public private partnerships, where they are value for money.

Expanded Public Sector Defence Programme – An additional £24 million will be invested between 2026-27 and 2029-30 in hardening our public sector AI defences and making AI-enabled cyber defence tools available across public services.

Emergency support for Ukraine’s air defences – The government is providing an additional £500 million of military support this winter to support Ukraine’s air defences.

Defence Investment Plan delivery – The government is putting the Defence Investment Plan into action through contracts with industry, supporting skilled jobs, strengthening UK supply chains and expanding the industrial capacity needed to deliver vital defence capabilities and drive economic growth.

Defence reform and efficiency – The government is maximising the value of every pound on defence to deliver stronger defence and better value for taxpayers. This includes reforming procurement under the National Armaments Director, publishing a new Counter Fraud Strategy and investing over £500 million in productivity improving investments this year.

Defence skills investment – The government is establishing new Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland and Wales, and working with the Northern Ireland Executive on a region-wide defence skills and apprenticeship programme.

Ukraine economic support – The government is making available a package of over £10 billion in future UK support for Ukraine from 2026-27 onwards, including up to £7 billion delivered through World Bank lending, £3 billion in increased capacity for UK Export Finance and £500 million of military support for this winter. The government will also provide £17 million for Chornobyl repairs and £3 million to support efforts to help return stolen children to Ukraine.

7.15 Measures to close the tax gap and modernise the tax system

E-invoicing – The government will require VAT invoices to be issued in a specified electronic format from 1 April 2029. The government has published an implementation roadmap, which sets out the key elements of the e-invoicing regime, and by April 2028 will provide full details on the policy and technical design of e-invoicing. The government has also published a consultation on potential future uses of structured invoice data generated through e-invoicing.

Reforming how taxpayers claim for employment expenses – The government will remove the £2,500 Income Tax Self-Assessment expenses threshold from 6 April 2028. This will allow more taxpayers to claim tax relief on non-reimbursed employment expenses through PAYE and ensure more claims are subject to evidence before relief is issued. The government will keep under review whether there is a case for mandating use of the PAYE route for taxpayers claiming solely employment expenses.

More timely payment for self-assessment –The government will require Income Tax Self-Assessment taxpayers who make payments on account to make more regular in-year payments towards their final tax bill from April 2029.

Requiring direct debit arrangements for VAT and PAYE return liabilities – The government will require taxpayers to set up a direct debit instruction for VAT and PAYE return liabilities from April 2029. Businesses will continue to be able to use other payment methods to pay their liability before a specified cut-off date. The direct debit instruction will be used to collect any unpaid balances.

Enhancing HMRC’s debt management capacity – The government will introduce a new power enabling HMRC to recover lower value tax debts through regular instalments directly from the bank accounts of individuals and companies who can afford to pay but repeatedly fail to do so from July 2029. The government will work with stakeholders to develop a Code of Practice setting out the safeguards and operational framework for the policy before being introduced to legislation in a future Finance Bill.

Investing in HMRC’s debt management capacity – The government will invest a further £70 million over the next five years in HMRC’s existing partnerships with private sector debt collection agencies to collect more tax debt.

Investing in additional HMRC compliance staff – The government will recruit an additional 670 HMRC compliance officers, building on previous commitments to recruit 5,500 additional compliance officers, by 2029-30.

Making Tax Digital (MTD) for income tax – Taxpayers joining MTD for income tax in April 2027 will not receive penalty points for late submission of their first four quarterly updates for the tax year 2027-28. The government is also deferring the roll-out of Making Tax Digital for Income Tax to several taxpayer groups until further notice.

Tax treatment of image rights payments – As announced at Budget 2025, the government will clarify that image rights payments related to an employment are taxable as employment income and taxed in the same way as wages. To provide affected sectors with additional time to adjust to this change, the measure will now take effect from 6 April 2028. This will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27.

VAT online marketplace liability (OMPL) – From October 2027, VAT OMPL rules will be extended to UK businesses. Online marketplaces will be responsible for collecting VAT on sales by UK VAT-registered businesses and any other UK business with a minimum annual sales threshold per platform of £90,000. The rules will not apply to non-business (i.e. personal) sales, second-hand goods, or business-to-business transactions.

Reforming civil tax information and inspection powers and modernising the definition of computer records – The government will modernise HMRC’s civil information and inspection powers by updating the rules for issuing information notices and revising the definition of computer records to reflect modern ways of storing and accessing information. This will ensure HMRC continues to have access to the information it needs to support its compliance work. The measure will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 and will take effect from Royal Assent.

Business systems integration –The government has published a Summary of Responses to the Business Systems Integration Call for Evidence. The government will work with industry to test practical ways to encourage greater integration between the systems that businesses use.

Making better use of third-party data – The government has published a consultation on modernising how property income data from third parties is collected and used by HMRC to help customers get their tax right first time.

Improving tax intermediary markets through an intermediation roadmap –The government will publish an intermediation roadmap in spring 2027, setting out HMRC’s long-term approach to working with tax advisers, software providers and others that support taxpayers to interact with the tax and customs system. The roadmap will include measures to help taxpayers choose advisers, support advisers to help their clients get expenses right, and strengthen standards for tax software providers. The roadmap will also help HMRC identify emerging risks and tackle harmful intermediary activity, including through a clear route for reporting harmful activity to HMRC, and set out an approach to tackling tax misinformation and incorrect tax advice online.

Modernising the correction of errors in tax returns –The government will introduce new requirements for taxpayers to correct tax returns and documents where inaccuracies are identified. These will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 and take effect from 1 April 2028.

HMRC’s approach to wealthy compliance – The government has published HMRC’s plan to modernise its approach to ensuring the wealthy meet their tax obligations, building on HMRC’s Transformation Roadmap.

Nicotine Approval Scheme consultation – The government has launched a 12-week consultation on the policy design of a Nicotine Approval Scheme (NAS). The NAS will introduce controls on the supply of high-strength nicotine in the UK to help tackle the illicit domestic manufacture of vaping liquid and subject to consultation will be implemented from 1 April 2028.

Excise wrongdoing penalties – The government will introduce a targeted civil penalty for deliberate conduct intended to evade UK excise duty before an excise duty point arises. The amendments will have effect from the date of Royal Assent to Finance Bill 2026-27.

Tackling the tax avoidance market –The government will shortly publish a consultation on a package of measures to tackle the promotion and use of tax avoidance.

Clamping down on till fraud – The government will introduce mandatory software standards for Electronic Point of Sale and Mobile Point of Sale systems to tackle electronic sales suppression. HMRC will engage with stakeholders and publish a technical consultation in summer 2027, setting out detailed implementation proposals.

Addressing persistent non-compliance by a small minority of larger businesses – The government will review its approach to persistent non-compliance and egregious behaviour by a small minority of larger businesses, including through the Special Measures regime. The government will engage stakeholders on any potential changes.

Reforming the publication of details of deliberate defaulters – The government will strengthen the framework for how HMRC publishes the details of deliberate tax cheats to bear down on those who default on their tax liabilities and will bring forward changes next year.

Policy maintenance package to tackle promoters of tax avoidance –The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 to amend the Promoters of Tax Avoidance Schemes legislation to ensure that the regime works more effectively and will make a typographical amendment to the legal professionals legislation in Finance Act 2026.

Offshore penalties reform consultation announcement – The government will publish a consultation later this year on reform to the offshore penalties framework.

Stamp Duty Land Tax group relief – The government will amend SDLT group relief rules to ensure that relief is withdrawn as intended when a purchaser leaves a corporate group, where the vendor company has been wound up. The changes will apply to transactions of property situated in England and Northern Ireland from 29 October 2026 and will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27.

Preventing protected cell company avoidance and clarifying the tax treatment of termination payments – The government is making minor technical changes to the rules that apply to gains made by non-resident close companies that are attributed to UK resident individuals, trusts and companies. The government is also clarifying the legislation around the tax treatment of termination payments. The changes will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 and take effect from 28 October 2026.

Close company reporting – Following consultation on company payments to participators, the government will not implement the proposed new reporting requirements at this time.

ISA manager compliance – The government will strengthen the compliance framework for Individual Savings Account (ISA) managers. From 6 April 2028 HMRC will be able to suspend non-compliant ISA managers and there will be new penalties for breaching ISA regulations, including points-based penalties for failures to submit required ISA reports and returns.

7.16 Tax administration, modernisation and simplification measures

Tax Update event – The government will announce further measures to simplify and modernise the tax and customs system at a Tax Update in 2027.

Corporate Tax simplification for business investment – The government is publishing a consultation exploring opportunities for targeted simplifications to the Corporate Tax system that could improve certainty and support investment, growth and competitiveness. The government will work with stakeholders over the next year to develop and prioritise reforms.

Modernising the administration of Corporation Tax – The government is publishing a Call for Evidence on the future administration of Corporation Tax, seeking views on how a modernised Corporation Tax administration system could better support companies to report and pay the right amount of tax first time.

Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) – The government is publishing a Summary of Responses to the Call for Evidence on the future of ACT and confirms it will repeal ACT legislation on 1 April 2031, which would extinguish existing surplus ACT balances, with legislation in a future Finance Bill.

Advance Tax Certainty Service – The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 to reduce the minimum expenditure threshold for HMRC’s Advance Tax Certainty Service from £1 billion to £300 million, expanding access to the service from 4 November 2026.

Summary of Responses to tax treatment of predevelopment costs consultation – The government is publishing a summary of responses to the call for evidence on predevelopment costs. Next steps set out include exploring potential changes to guidance to clarify the tax treatment of such costs; and considering wider challenges for some infrastructure investment under the capital allowances regime.

Stamp Duty taxes on shares – modernisation – Following consultations in 2023 and 2025, and the publication of draft legislation in July, the government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 to introduce the Securities Transfer Tax from late 2027. The Securities Transfer Tax will replace Stamp Duty and Stamp Duty Reserve Tax.

Review of Benchmark Scale Rates and Overseas Scale Rates – The government will reform and simplify the outdated rates used by employers to reimburse employees for domestic and overseas business travel and subsistence expenses without requiring receipts to be checked. From April 2028 Benchmark Scale Rates (BSR) will be modernised to better reflect current subsistence costs for domestic business travel. Overseas Scale Rates (OSR) will be simplified, replacing the current destination-specific framework with a tiered approach that reduces administrative burdens for employers.

Modernising the distributions framework – The government will reform the tax treatment of distributions and related rules to ensure they are consistent, regardless of legal form, company residence or transaction structure. The reforms are designed to protect capital treatment for genuine changes in ownership, including families passing down their business, and in some cases make the relief more generous for demergers. The government will continue engagement with stakeholders and will publish draft legislation for technical consultation in 2027, with the changes taking effect from April 2028.

Income Tax: Pension Tax Allowance – The government will introduce the Pension Tax Allowance (PTA), ensuring that pensioners whose total income is up to the value of the full new State Pension do not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax. The value of the PTA is calculated by applying the basic rate of income tax (20%) to the difference between the full new State Pension and the Personal Allowance. Individuals over State Pension age are eligible for the automatic tax deduction if their income, regardless of source, is below or at the value of the full new State Pension. For those with incomes just above the value of the full new State Pension, the allowance will be gradually withdrawn through a taper. The allowance will apply from 6 April 2027 until 5 April 2030 and will be uprated in line with the full new State Pension across this Parliament. It will be legislated for in Finance Bill 2026-27 and the government will consider arrangements beyond April 2030 in the usual way.

VAT treatment of cross-border services – From April 2027, the reverse charge on cross-border supplies of services will be restricted to VAT-registered businesses. Where overseas providers make supplies of services to non-VAT registered UK businesses, they will be required to account for VAT in the normal way. This will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27.

Offsetting Child Benefit overpayments – HMRC will automatically offset Child Benefit overpayments against the High Income Child Benefit Charge (HICBC), simplifying administration for affected customers by reducing unnecessary payment and repayment transactions. This will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 with retrospective effect from HICBC’s introduction in January 2013.

Temporary Staffing – The government will amend Group 7 of Schedule 9 to the VAT Act 1994 to restore the tax treatment of medical deputies to its previously intended position from 1 May 2027. This will be introduced through legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27.

Exploring the use of HMRC data in Open Finance – The government will explore the use of HMRC data in Open Finance, working with regulators and industry partners to test feasibility while safeguarding the integrity of the tax administration system.

VAT zero-rate for donated medicines – The government will introduce a new zero-rate of VAT for medicines donated in qualifying circumstances, including through early and expanded access schemes. The zero-rate applies to qualifying donations made on or after 23 June 2026.

Withholding tax exemption for Scottish Government bonds – The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 to provide an exemption from the duty to deduct sums representing income tax from interest paid on Scottish Government bonds, the issuance of which is subject to Treasury approval. The exemption will apply to any interest paid on or after 28 October 2026.

7.17 Business rates

Business rates: relief for pubs, social clubs and live music venues – The government is increasing the relief for pubs, social clubs and all but the very largest live music venues in England by 20ppt, from 15% to 35% from 1 April 2027. The very largest live music venues (with a rateable value of £1 million or above) will not receive this increased rate of relief, but will continue to benefit from the previously announced 15% relief in 2026-27 and real-term freeze in 2027-28 and 2028-29, as announced in January 2026. This will provide ongoing support to qualifying properties, with the level kept under review alongside the 2029 revaluation.

Business rates: Small Business Rates Relief thresholds for Retail, Hospitality and Leisure (RHL) – The government is increasing the SBRR eligibility thresholds for qualifying RHL properties in England from 1 April 2027. The threshold for 100% relief will increase to a rateable value of £18,000, and the threshold for tapered relief will increase to a rateable value of £21,000. These thresholds will provide ongoing support to qualifying properties, with their level kept under review alongside the 2029 revaluation.

Business rates: freeze bills in real terms for RHL properties for two years – The government will ensure that business rates bill increases for qualifying RHL properties in England are capped by CPI inflation in 2027-28 and 2028-29. This does not apply to increases in rateable values resulting from improvements, or losses in other reliefs such as improvement relief or hardship relief post 1 April 2026.

Business rates: Supporting Small Business (SSB) scheme – The government is extending the 2026 SSB scheme to those who were in receipt of 2023 SSB, for one year from 1 April 2027 in England.

Business rates: Transitional Relief Supplement (TRS) – The government is extending the 1p TRS for two years from 1 April 2027. This will be paid each year by those seeing bill increases otherwise below the Transitional Relief and SSB caps.

Business rates: Valuation Tribunal removal of appeal fees – The government will abolish the £150 and £300 fees charged by the Valuation Tribunal in England for non-domestic rating appeals. This will apply to the 2026 rating list and future lists and will enable fees already paid for appeals on the 2026 list to be refunded.

Business rates: removing reliefs for vape shops and Adult Gaming Centres – From April 2027, Adult Gaming Centres in England will no longer be eligible for the retail, hospitality, and leisure (RHL) multipliers, and vape shops in England will no longer be eligible for the RHL multipliers and the Small Business Rates Relief.

Business rates: General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR) – The government will introduce a GAAR for business rates in England as soon as possible, following a consultation on design and delivery.

Business rates: funding local authority costs for anti-avoidance litigation – From April 2027, the government will reimburse local authorities for external legal costs incurred in unsuccessful cases that challenge business rates avoidance and test a point of law.

Summary of Responses publication: business rates and investment –The government is publishing the findings from the Business Rates and Investment: Call for Evidence, summarising views on how business rates affect investment in England and setting out the government’s response.

Business Rates: GLA Business Rates Supplement – The government will legislate to enable the Mayor of London to establish a successor to the Elizabeth Line Business Rates Supplement with ballot arrangements no more restrictive than the general ballot provisions in the Business Rates Supplements Act 2009 as originally enacted.

7.18 Transport and environmental taxation

Vehicle excise duty (VED) support for heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) – Since July, a reduced annual VED rate of £1 has been available to the majority of HGVs. The reduced rate applies to VED licences or renewals taken out between 1 July 2026 and 30 June 2027. The government is introducing legislation to ensure that, from 28 October 2026, where this reduced rate is obtained for more than 12 months, any excess benefit may be recoverable from the vehicle keeper as a civil debt.

Vehicle excise duty (VED) upratings – The government will uprate VED rates for cars, vans and motorcycles in line with the Retail Prices Index (RPI) from 1 April 2027.

Vehicle Excise Duty (VED) exemption for search and rescue vehicles – At Budget 2025, the government announced that search and rescue charities will receive an exemption from VED for eligible vehicles. The government will introduce legislation for the exemption through the Finance Bill and it will come into effect from 1 April 2027.

Annual uprating of the Van Benefit Charge for 2027-2028 –The government will increase the Van Benefit Charge and the Car and Van Fuel Benefit Charges in line with CPI from 6 April 2027.

Cost of public electric vehicle (EV) charging – The government is publishing the response to the cost of public EV charging review, and announcing (i) the tariff porting taskforce and (ii) funding to reduce the cost of local, lower powered public chargers across Great Britain.

VAT on public electric vehicle charging – The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2026-27 to clarify that electricity supplied through publicly accessible, and workplace electric vehicle charging points is subject to 20% VAT and is not considered domestic use for the Climate Change Levy. The legislation will take effect from 1 November 2026.

Corporation Tax revenue recognition deferral for gas network operators – The government will introduce legislation in Finance Bill 2027–28 to introduce a Corporation Tax deferral for the one-off impact of changes to revenue recognition on qualifying gas distribution activities where this would otherwise be passed on to consumers.

Benefit in Kind Appropriate Percentage Rates for 2030-31 and potential for ULEV SalSac reforms – The government will set Company Car Tax Appropriate Percentage rates for 2030-31. Rates will be 1 percentage point above 2029-30 rates across all vehicle bands. Appropriate Percentages for zero-emission vehicles will increase from 9% to 10%, rates for cars emitting 1 to 50g CO2/km will increase from 19% to 20%, and all other rates will increase by 1 percentage point, subject to a maximum of 40%.

Carbon Price Support – The government will end Carbon Price Support rates in Great Britain from April 2028.

Climate Change Levy rates 2028-29 – The main rates of Climate Change Levy for electricity and liquified petroleum gas will be frozen from April 2028, at 2027-28 levels. The main rates for gas and solid fuels for 2028-29 will be uprated in line with RPI.

Temporary VAT zero-rate on electricity –The temporary 0% VAT rate for domestic electricity (six months from 1 October 2026) will be extended for a further three months, to 1 July 2027. This is expected to apply UK-wide from April 2027.

Fuel duty: 2027-28 main rates – The government will extend the temporary 5p-per-litre fuel duty cut for a further six months to 1 July 2027. The government is also deferring the planned RPI inflation increase to 1 July 2027.

Red diesel rate for fuel duty 2027-28 – The government will extend the temporary 3.7p-per-litre red diesel duty cut for a further six months, along with the proportional reduction in red diesel duty resulting from the 5p cut to the main fuel duty rate. Red diesel duty will then return to its pre-March 2022 rate and be uprated in line with RPI from 1 July 2027.

Mileage rates review – As announced on 27 October, the government is permanently increasing tax-free mileage rates for employees and self-employed people who use their own car or van for work. The tax-free, per mile rate will be 55p for the first 10,000 miles and 35p per mile for mileage above 10,000 miles.

Income Tax exemption: Department for Energy Security & Net Zero (DESNZ) Electricity Bill Discount Scheme –The government will exempt payments made under the DESNZ Electricity Bill Discount Scheme from income tax, with retrospective effect from 6 April 2026. This will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Revert to reduced rate on energy saving materials (ESMs) as planned and include heat batteries in scope – The government will add heat batteries to the list of materials that qualify for the reduced rate of VAT of 5% applying to energy saving materials from 1 April 2027, when installed in residential accommodation and charitable buildings. This will be legislated for via secondary legislation and take effect from 1 April 2027.

Electricity Generator Levy (EGL) – As previously announced, the government will extend the EGL past 2028. The EGL will remain for the lifetime of the longest Wholesale Contract for Difference (WCfD), on which DESNZ is launching a consultation. The exemptions for new investment and CfDs will remain, and CfDs will include WCfDs. A consultation on future EGL policy design will follow next year, and changes will be made in a future Finance Bill.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) country-specific default values (CSDVs) – The government will introduce CSDVs for the UK CBAM from 2029, replacing the initial global default values used in 2027 and 2028. CSDVs will more accurately reflect emissions associated with imports from different countries, strengthening the environmental integrity of the regime.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) sectoral scope expansion – The government intends to expand the scope of the CBAM to include refined products, subject to consultation on the feasibility and impacts of doing so.

Private hire vehicle operators – The government will deem the larger operators with annual fare turnover above a certain threshold liable for 20% VAT on the full value of their fares from 2 January 2028. The government will shortly publish a consultation to confirm the level of this threshold, with £50 million annual fare turnover as the lead option, and to support final policy design and implementation.

Plastic Packaging Tax (PPT): mechanically recycled plastic and certification consultation – Following consultation, from 1 April 2030 the government will introduce mandatory certification for mechanically recycled plastic used in plastic packaging for the purposes of PPT. The government has also published a summary of responses to the consultation.

Landfill Tax rates – The government will increase the standard rate of Landfill Tax by RPI and the lower rate by the cash amount of the increase in the standard rate in England and Northern Ireland, preventing the difference between the rates getting wider.

Landfill Communities Fund (LCF) value – The government will increase the cap of tax credit claimable by landfill operators in respect of contributions to the LCF from 5.3% to 8.3% of their Landfill Tax liability, to help sustain the LCF and support local communities.

Landfill Tax rebate for Defra-funded illegal waste sites – The government will provide funding for Defra to meet Landfill Tax liabilities arising from the planned clearance of six illegal waste sites between 2026–27 and 2028–29.

Landfill Tax rebate scheme for local authorities – The government will introduce a three-year pilot scheme, starting in 2027, to fund local authorities’ Landfill Tax liabilities arising from the clearance of illegal waste sites in their areas.

7.19 Duties and upratings

Machine Games Duty (MGD) – The Government will increase the rate of MGD from 20% to 25% for machine games with stakes over £1 or prizes over £100 from 1 April 2027. The consultation will close on 20 January 2027.

Alcohol duty – The government will increase alcohol duty rates in line with RPI to maintain its real terms value. The government will also increase the relative value of Small Producer Relief compared to the main rates, by moving to a more generous discount taper for products under 3.5% ABV and uprating the marginal discount for products between 3.5% and 8.4% ABV by RPI plus an additional 10%. Guest beer – The government intends to legislate to introduce a ‘Guest Beer’ provision to support brewers to continue to access pubs covered by the Pubs Code in England and Wales, building on existing voluntary action taken by Pub Companies in order to offer tied tenants greater flexibility on the range of beers they stock.

Gaming duty bands – The Gross Gaming Yield bandings for gaming duty will be frozen from 1 April 2027 until 31 March 2028.

Soft Drinks Industry Levy uprating – In line with the uprating strategy announced at Autumn Budget 2024, the SDIL will be uprated on 1 April 2027. The Levy will be increased in line with Consumer Price Index plus one fifth of the ‘catch-up’ increment to reflect the 27% CPI increase between 2018 and 2024.

Air Passenger Duty 2028-29 uprating – The government will increase all rates of Air Passenger Duty in line with RPI from 1 April 2028. These rates will be rounded to the nearest penny.

Married Couples Allowance (MCA) and Blind Persons Allowance (BPA) uprating – The government will uprate the Married Couple’s Allowance and the Blind Person’s Allowance by CPI. This will be legislated through a Treasury Order and take effect from 6 April 2027.

Qualifying Care Relief uprating – The government will uprate Qualifying Care Relief, the amount of income tax relief available to foster carers and shared lives carers, by CPI. This will be introduced through a Treasury Order and take effect from 6 April 2027.

7.20 Property taxation

High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS) – The government has published a Summary of Responses to consultation, confirming it will introduce a deferral scheme, a series of discounts and exemptions, and a 100% premium on properties left empty and unoccupied for 12 months or more. HVCTS applies to England only and this measure will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Annual Tax on Enveloped Dwellings (ATED) – The annual charges will increase by 3.5%, in line with September 2026 CPI, for the 2027–28 charging period. This uprating is provided for in existing legislation and will be confirmed in a Treasury Order.

Stamp Duty Land Tax Relief for the Local Government Pension Scheme – A relief will be introduced for the pooling of Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS) debt assets, situated in England and Northern Ireland, to support LGPS reforms, applying to transactions from 28 October 2026 and before 1 April 2032. This will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Removing Stamp Duty Land Tax on rent under assured tenancies – The government will remove Stamp Duty Land Tax on rent paid under assured tenancies in England, effective from 1 May 2026, following the introduction of the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. This will be introduced in Finance Bill 2026-27.

Zero-rate on land sold to social housing providers –The government will implement a zero-rate of VAT for land sold to registered providers of social housing (relevant Housing Associations). This will be introduced through secondary legislation in early 2027 and take effect from 1 April 2027.

First Time Buyer (FTB) ISA – The government will introduce a new FTB ISA from April 2029. The product will replace the Lifetime ISA (LISA) for new savers and provide a 25% government bonus, paid on withdrawal, towards the purchase of a first home worth up to £450,000. The maximum value of the bonus will be capped at £20,000. Existing LISA holders will be able to continue contributing to and using their accounts under the current rules. In addition, the government will reduce the withdrawal charge for existing LISA holders who use their savings to purchase a first home above the £450,000 property price cap.

Reduce Lifetime ISA (LISA) withdrawal charge for properties above the Property Price Cap – From midnight 29 October 2026 the withdrawal charge for purchases of properties above the LISA property price cap will be reduced to 20%. The charge for unauthorised withdrawals will remain at 25%.

7.21 Personal taxation

Guided Retirement and Retirement Collective Defined Contribution pension schemes – The government will make changes to enable the consolidation of Defined Contribution schemes and the introduction of the Guided Retirement framework and Retirement-only Collective Defined Contribution (RCDC) pension schemes. This will be introduced through Finance Bill 2027-28.

This will apply to any payments made on or after 28 October 2026 and will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Collecting tax due on excess lump sum death benefits – The government will make changes to the way tax is assessed and collected where a deceased member’s lump sum death benefit allowance has been exceeded to provide greater certainty to individual beneficiaries. This will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Inheritance Tax: preventing unintended deductions for liabilities in trust arrangements – The government will amend the inheritance tax rules to clarify when liabilities relating to trust property may reduce the value of assets for inheritance tax purposes, align the treatment of liabilities affecting trust property with personal liabilities, and strengthen anti-avoidance provisions. This will take effect for deaths and other chargeable events occurring on or after 28 October 2026. This will be introduced through Finance Bill 2026-27.

Changes to tax on property income – The government is increasing all the rates of income tax applied to property income by 2 percentage points. These rates will apply across England, Wales and Northern Ireland. This will be legislated for in Finance Bill 2026-27 and take effect from 6 April 2027.

Changes to tax on savings income – The government is increasing all the rates of income tax applied to savings income by 2 percentage points. The savings basic rate will be 24%, the savings higher rate will be 44%, and the savings additional rate will be 49%. These rates will apply across the UK. This will be legislated for in Finance Bill 2026-27 and take effect from 6 April 2027.

Maintaining the cash ISA limit at £20,000 – The government is retaining the annual cash Individual Savings Accounts (ISA) subscription limits at £20,000.

New ISA incentive – The government will work with industry to explore a new ISA incentive for people investing in a stocks and shares ISA for the first time. The detailed design will be developed with industry.
